===== Articles\Segment Math and Symmetry.docx =====
[normal] Segment Math and Symmetry
[normal] Symmetric tiling patterns are both deeply compelling, and mathematically unsatisfying. They have been used throughout the history of civilization, from the 12000 year old Göbekli Tepe onwards. These symmetry patterns hold deeper insights into how we calculate, how we think, and indeed how the world works.
[normal] Frieze patterns are a type of line group, with patterns that repeat only in one direction. These have been mathematically described with many rule sets and notations, and personally I’ve found them all a bit arbitrary. They all enumerate the patterns, but it feels more like classification than insight. Caveat, maybe I’m just too thick to appreciate it. And no doubt I’m adding one more rule set to the pile here. Apologies.
[normal] My take is these patterns are not base primitives to build on, but a visual embodiment of the rules needed to compare ordered things.
[normal] The segment number system I’ve been working on for the last five years (yikes!) make symmetry much more intuitive, as the four basic transformations (identity, negate value, negate number line, and negate both) are the same transformations used to construct segment numbers themselves.
[normal] TLDR, in the table below, each of the dots has an associated action that means the same as the encoding it represents. Notice how the seven dot patterns form 7 distinct shapes: nothing, point, horizontal, vertical, diagonal, corner, and everything. This is not a coincidence. With horizontal and vertical transforms, all 16 possible four bit bool patterns can be created. Finally, extending these binary actions to be ‘weighted’ creates various number systems – fundamentally a comparison using a basis and a value.
[normal] If you look very carefully at this diagram, you can probably skip the rest of this article.
[normal] Onward.
[Heading 1] The Four Units of a Measure
[normal] To start, let’s have a first-principles review of a line. A line can represent anything ordered. A line has two directions, and anything moving along it can move with or against those directions. For example, a line going up measures height, and a line going down measures depth. Positive numbers are either up or down, depending on the context (positive height is up, positive depth is down). Of course the same is true for horizontal lines, you can be travelling east, or travelling west. And you can be moving in those directions with the car in forward or reverse. Therefore, values on lines have four natural orientations.
[normal] We can’t just use arrows to indicate direction here, because travelling east → would be the same arrow as travelling west in reverse →.
[normal] Instead, imagine sitting on a cart with a swivel chair. You are facing the direction you want to go (east), and pointing in the direction of travel (east) with your left hand. So your arm is on the north side, pointing east (as in the top right image). There are four things that can happen here:
[normal] ⥬ Nothing happens at all, leaving your arm on the north side pointing east (identity, top right).
[normal] ⥪ The cart reverses, so your arm is still on the north side, but pointing west (negate progress, top left)
[normal] ⥭ You swivel around to face backwards, the cart keeps going. Now your arm is on the south side, still pointing east (negate goal, bottom right)
[normal] ⥫ You turn around and the cart reverses, putting your arm on the south side, pointing west (negate both, bottom left).
[normal] As you can see, there are four possible units here, combining forwards and backwards as well as east or west. The direction on the line, and the direction of the line.
[normal] And it isn’t just here, all measured values have these four perspectives, and not surprisingly, all symmetry is based on them as well. This is because lengths can only be measured relative to other lengths, and every length is created from two positions, totalling four measures. You can think of these as the four units used in every comparison, because, well, that’s what they are.
[Heading 1] The Meaning of Units
[normal] Now what do each of these mean? Our regular numbers only use the ‘east encoding’ (values increase to the right). This requires a value to measure, and a unit. For our numbers, the start point of both the value and unit is at zero, and the unit defines ‘1’ regardless of its length. 7 is 7 * 1 unit. This is how we can compress the four values into one.
[normal] It is easy to imagine an identical system that is ‘west encoded’. If you transform things horizontally and vertically, everything flips and now points west. This is similar to viewing it from the other side of the table, or rotating everything by 180 degrees.
[normal] It is important to understand that both of these perspectives are equal, nature doesn’t prefer right over left. Even though what is called the ‘negative unit’ here seems like it has a value of -1, it is a unit of value 1, just like all other units. A unit means ‘one of a certain thing’, like 1 inch, 1 degree, or 1 distance in the leftward direction. This is why we call them units — they don’t represent values, they represent context.
[normal] Notice also a positive unit can indicate a negative value, it just means the value grows in the opposite direction as the unit. -7 is 7 unit lengths in the opposite direction of the unit.
[normal] Back to the cart. Now we can ask, what would have to change to move the hand from pointing forwards to pointing backwards? This is ‘negating’ the gear you’re in, which negates the direction of progress. Changing from forward to reverse. And if already going in reverse, the same negating operation would change to forward. You are changing your direction on the line. This is multiplying by -1.
[normal] What would it take to get your arm to be on the south side of the car if it is currently on the north? In this case, the direction you are moving remains the same, but you negate the direction you are facing by swiveling your seat. If you were going forward facing east, you now have to face west. Forward was east, now forward is west. Even though you are moving in the same absolute direction (east), you have changed the direction of the line, as you are now going backwards. Numbers now get smaller going east. We don’t have a term for this, I’ll call it changing the polarity of the line. This is multiplying by -i.
[normal] So there are two operations here, negate your progress, and negate your goal. I promise this leads to symmetry! Negating progress is what happens when multiplying by -1, it negates a value. Negating the goal (toggling the polarity of the line) happens when multiplying by -i.
[normal] If we do both, we switch from moving east in forward to moving west in forward. We could call this -1*-i, but this double flipping causes the unit to be ‘upside up’ again, so it is no longer negative. This leaves 1i, or just i. It seems like a 180 degree rotation, but it is specifically a double flip, not a rotation.
[normal] So these are the base units for all measures, and all symmetry, 1,-1, -i and i. Both -1 and i will negate a value, and both -i and i will negate the polarity of the line. Note the choice of putting 1 in the top right corner is arbitrary. It is done here to map to our familiar numbers, with values increasing to the right. Any transformation of this cube is a valid orientation. Going west is just as valid as going east, positive up Y axis is just as valid and positive down. And, as much as it pains be to admit, driving on the left is just as valid as driving on the right. You can choose any orientation, as long as you’re consistent. I chose this one as it maps cleanly to our number system, and complex numbers.
[Heading 1] Encoding as Memory, Prediction and Action
[normal] Stepping back, notice how a number records a value. This value store can be used to recall or predict a value in a similar situation. If eggs are $5.00, then next time you see them you can predict they’ll be $5.00. Less obvious, but it does this by recording a ‘recipe’ that can be used to create that value from a unit. Numbers are actually very simple mini equations. For example the number 7 is the unit stretched away from zero, to end up 7 times the original unit length. In the same way, -7 is the unit stretched in the opposite direction, so it stretches to the left.
[normal] There is a subtle but important distinction when you multiply by a unit instead of a value. These will toggle the unit portion only. Multiplying by -i will flip the unit vertically (in reference to the diagram above), so a bottom unit will become a top one, and vice versa (-i→1 or i→-1). Multiplying by the unit -1 will flip the unit horizontally, where -1→1, or i→-1, and vice versa. And multiplying by i will flip things diagonally. Our math conflates units and values so this is confusing at first. Essentially we need four ‘yard’ units, one for each direction on a yardstick, and then the same thing for a yardstick where the values increase to the left. With this in mind, you should be able to convince yourself that transforms can change the units as easily as the values, and that they work as described above.
[normal] These transforms can of course be applied to things other than the unit. If you apply 7 to 3 instead of the unit 1, it stretches the length of 3 to 7 times its length (to 21) instead of stretching the unit. In the same way, if you multiply (2i+3) by (0i+7) you get (14i+21), just you are stretching two point segments instead of single numbers.
[normal] It doesn’t stop at numbers either. If you apply -1 to the letter ‘d’ you end up with the letter ‘b’, a flip across a zero point, just like negation of numbers. If you apply -i to ‘d’, you flip the polarity and end up with ‘q’. And multiplying ‘d’ by i, you get ‘p’, which looks like a rotated ‘d’. We can therefore create these four symmetries just using simple multiplication of units. This will make it much easier to tease apart and interpret the symmetries mathematically.
[Heading 1] Action
[normal] We’ll use a grid of four dots (bits) to represent the units of transform. Having them in a square rather than a single row allows them to visually line up with their actions (again, this is not a coincidence). The top row is bit 2 (negate value), bit 1 (identity), and the bottom row bit 4 (invert), bit 3 (negate line direction). The order is TR (1), TL (2), BR (4), BL(8).
[Heading 1] The Seven Symmetries
[Heading 2] No Transform
[normal] If we do nothing, whatever pattern we input will just repeat. A small point, but if a shape has a natural orientation like a heart ❤︎, the ‘do nothing’ action doesn’t correct a sideways heart ❥ to be normal. This literally means, ‘do nothing’.
[Heading 2] Point Transform
[normal] With a point, or single bit set, the input pattern will transform the same way every time. It is important to note here, that the input is always the output of the previous step. This is what causes the alternation. There are four of these patterns. The identity pattern doesn’t alternate, and initially seems similar to the first ‘do nothing’ pattern. Subtly though, it means ‘add the pattern untransformed’ rather than ‘add the pattern as is’. It is applying an action each time, just in these symmetries the input is always considered ‘true’, so it’s resetting things that don’t need to be reset.
[Heading 2] Horizontal and Vertical Transforms
[normal] Next is the horizontal and vertical lines. With two bits, they will always have two transforms. In the stripe patterns, we always have the identity copy, and then a horizontal or vertical flip, establishing the initial shape. This shape then gets re-input into the algorithm, causing this copy to get flipped in the same way, leaving the same shape. Flipping a ❤︎ left to right leaves a ❤︎. Flipping a ❥ up and down leaves a ❥.
[Heading 2] Diagonal Transform
[normal] The diagonal line is similar, other than the pattern mirrors. This is like creating an S, and then flipping it both horizontally and vertically and ending with S. Note this is not a rotation, it is a double inversion. It looks like a 180 degree rotation, but shapes can’t rotate in one dimension. Note to create a diagonal from top left to bottom right, you would just need to add whitespace to your initial pattern (by moving the vertical line that defines the ‘zero’ point of the left/right flip).
[Heading 2] Corner Transform
[normal] The corner pattern is the trickiest, as it creates a contradiction. It says, keep the initial shape and flip left/right, then also mirror that. This fills every quadrant, full symmetry. However, the missing dot in the bottom right says ‘there is no up and down symmetry’, which we’ve already created. This is an impossible request, at least within our constraints so far.
[normal] A missing dot is a ‘MUST NOT’ in logical terms, and is as much of a requirement as the ‘MUST’ actions. To satisfy the NOT condition, we must break the up/down symmetry. The ‘breaking’ can be done by shifting to the right (or left). Technically you could also rotate, shift upwards, or expand the bottom to break symmetry. However, these operations are not available using only units, in only one dimension.
[normal] The corner operation looks like two steps, however the symmetry breaking is just applying the NOT action in the same step. The key truth here is that any three dot pattern will create a contradiction, and only three dot patterns create a contradiction. It’s like someone asking you to put on both of your shoes, but make sure you aren’t wearing both shoes. Something has to give, and a ‘translation horizontally in time’ is ‘that something’ (put on your left shoe, take it off, put your right shoe, take it off, etc.). Notice how all the other dot patterns are linear in some way, while corners ‘break’ symmetry. Like in math, design and metaphor, corners are the entry point to new dimensions.
[Heading 2] Transform All
[normal] Last is the ALL pattern. This is self explanatory, however note you can imagine a lot of overlapping duplicates or repeated instructions present here. This is specifically ok, because there are no ‘MUST NOT’ instructions forbidding them. It is saying put on both shoes, also put on your left shoe, also put on your right shoe.
[normal] Here again are all the symmetries together.
[Heading 1] Why the Filter?
[normal] There are naturally 16 patterns with 4 bits, yet with Frieze symmetry there are only seven. On the surface, this filtering is caused by the repetition moving in a single direction, when there are in fact four cardinal directions encoded in the bits. You can see the filtered patterns map to the primitive patterns, albeit with some nudging and squinting. At a visual level, these are due to logical rules. Applying the same transform action twice will always lead back to the original state, making the result visually identical (if not the process). Add to that, a pattern tiling vertically may be similar to a different pattern tiling horizontally, and both are valid. But at its core, these symmetries arise from the same logical truths required to compare and create values. Symmetry presents the results of transforms, hiding the process, so it describes relations of the transforms, not the transforms themselves.
[Heading 1] The primitives of numeracy
[normal] Logic requires that any measurement is a comparison (there is no universal yardstick), and all numbers represent measurements of some form. Every comparison must use two ranges, one to calibrate (the basis) and the one to be compared (the value). This requires two ranges, denoted by four positions. Symmetry is a rule set that exposes these truths visually, with no assumptions about starting points or units. Symmetries aren’t core truths, they are a way of examining the relationships of core truths. Line symmetry has 7 primitive patterns and 16 total patterns It’s useful to examine what the filtered sets tell us, and why they naturally fall into existing groups.
[Heading 1] A Look at the Redundant Patterns
[Heading 2] Points
[normal] First we’ll look at the single points. Here is the bottom right (up/down flip), and you can see that with shifting it turns into the up/down symmetry pattern. This shifting is actually just shifting the pivot point (the zero point). This is always a choice, as there are no universal reference points to measure things from. You can see if tiling vertically you can come to a similar conclusion.
[normal] That said, all the four one-dot patterns represent repeatedly applying a single transform. The fact that they map to other patterns isn’t a coincidence, but this isn’t the core concept of a ‘point action’. The point action is about making a selection, choosing an orientation, or making a change. One. The repetition comes from the fact that we are tiling, not from the action the dot represents.
[Heading 2] Stripes and Diagonals
[normal] Two-dot patterns expose the behavior of symmetry pairs. There are six of these. The three that include identity: vertical, horizontal and diagonal. These three are primitive shapes in the seven listed above. The other diagonal (\) has no overlapping instructions, no identity, so it is the equivalent of a ‘both’ transform. The last two (left stripe, bottom stripe) alternate because they create ‘double instructions’ (flip and flip both), meaning the output will be a flipped version of the input.
[normal] Here is the alternation of the left stripe. This is a horizontal transform of the template, which is then inverted. This creates the \ diagonal, and when that output is reinput and transformed, it ends up the opposite / diagonal. While this looks similar to a contradiction (corner), it is actually alternating input – there is no forced break of symmetry.
[normal] Again, the idea that this is equivalent to a corner pattern is significant, but this isn’t the core symmetrical meaning. A useful analogy is to think of a toy car on a piece of track. It can go backwards or forwards in either direction, and when it gets to the end it can ‘bounce’ and drive back (alternate), or it can restart from the beginning (repeat). When the output is fed back into the transform pattern, either outcome is possible. Two-bit patterns are all about the symmetries of two combined transforms and the patterns they create, primitive or otherwise.
[Heading 2] Corners
[normal] Three-dot patterns are about contradictions. A corner that ‘bends’ on the bottom right (BR in the diagram) flips up/down instead of side to side. This is ‘glide reflection’ in other symmetry notation, and is considered the same pattern as the original TL corner. Glide reflection doesn’t discriminate between the type of reflection used, as these actions are already defined with two-dot symmetry. With three actions, the order of operations also changes the pattern. It may be easier to visualize the pattern similarities when tiled vertically, but ultimately the look of the pattern is just the hint.
[normal] The thing that defines corner symmetry is the contradiction of instructions, which forces the pattern to break into a new dimension.
[normal] Symmetry is focused on results, not process, so many of the results cancel each other. But that is not a dis! Prediction also focuses on results rather than the process, and with better-than-random prediction, you have the basis of intelligence. It is reasonable to think about these seven filtered patterns as building blocks of understanding.
[Heading 1] Symmetry as Action
[normal] This will be fleshed out in another post, but as you can see below, these symmetry primitives can also map to an instruction set for images and code. In the segment number system, the inverted line (positive left, bottom dots) represent the initial state, and the normal line (positive right, top dots) represents the goal state. This naturally leads to move-to, line-to, conditionals, branches, transforms, and transfer and return of control. Adding weights to these brings up a full system computation. Encoding in this system is not just interpretable, it’s executable.
[normal] Here are some simple Frieze patterns generated with three such numbers, each with slight tweaks to the encodings. You can see these are from a very similar base — with minor changes to the run order and symmetries you can generate near endless variety.

===== Articles\Sequential Math, Parallel Math.docx =====
[normal] Order of operations is a first class primitive in math that defines the sequence of operations, but parallel operations are mostly not specifiable. This is because we fixate on results rather than processes for equations. And it's one of the reasons calculus can seem so confusing.
[normal] This is easiest to see in 2D (parallel vs sequential matters). The operations down 1 and across 1 give an 'L' when done sequentially, and a '\' when done in parallel. Translating this to 1D (1+1) we can get two segments joined (sequential) or a single segment of length 2 (parallel) where every bit of each segment is piecemeal merged into a new one.
[normal] A better mental model of this is adding four rows of numbers together using column arithmetic (parallel), or adding up receipts on a calculator one after another (sequential).
[normal] The same is true for multiplication. 3x3x3 stretches a value to 3, stops, stretches that to 9, stops, and then stretches that to 27. If you imagine each of these steps taking the same amount of time, there are three distinct speeds. This is sequential.
[normal] An example of the parallel version of multiplication is powers. 3^3 starts with three values stacked in a column. As the first stretches to 3, the second tracks it to remain three times longer, and the third tracks the second, remaining 3x longer than it. There are also three speeds here, but they all happen at the same time on different values. We 'care' about the last value, which is a segment of 27 that was formed at a constant speed.
[normal] If you animate these, you'll find a lot of ambiguity, and a lot of things missing. Right off the bat, we distinguish between parallel/sequential versions of addition. We do with multiplication, but only with the same number (there is a parallel 3x3x3, but not for 3x4x7). Polynomials seem to be a parallel/sequential combination, where we sequentially step between each in increase in power. Even with 2D, where it is absolutely required, there is nothing in math that distinguishes an 'L' from a '\', that is just in the code or metadata somewhere.
[normal] This matters a lot when trying to encode motions. And encoding motions matters a lot when trying to encode concepts because so many thoughts we have are metaphorical 'change motions'. You can just make decisions and write code, but these are fundamental facts about combining values at the  level of other operations on numbers. Rules here can't be arbitrary or inconsistent, they need to be at the system level.
[normal] Thank you for coming to my talk.

===== Articles\The Mathematical Interpretation of Symmetric Numbers.docx =====
[Heading 1] The Mathematical Interpretation
[normal] As explored in the last article, “Boolean Arithmetic with Segments”, boolean values can be considered weighted values that have some true/false threshold. So when we see the four boolean units here, identity, negative-progress, negative-goal, and inversion, we should consider what the weighted version of these mean. They are at the heart of mathematical transformations, and core to defining numbers themselves.
[normal] Our numbers are defined by the unit segment that defines 0 to 1, and a second segment that starts at 0 and extends to some non fixed length. The number is computed by comparing the unit length to the segment in question.
[normal] For a ‘positive to the right’ numbering system like ours, the unit needs to start at zero, and move to the right. From the zero perspective, the goal position is one unit away. From the goal position, the start is -1 away. This suggests that the unit value is on the line with the opposite polarity. From our normal perspective it is position 1, and indeed from its own perspective it is also 1. All unit values are 1, it’s just the units themselves come in four flavors. The red unit’s location is ‘the negative side of the line that is positive-left’, so the unit is -i. This is confusing because of overloading the - operator here, imagine we have units of miles, and other units of ‘negative miles’. Really it is more like “1 negative inverted unit”, or <insert better name here>. It is the going-backwards-while-facing-left unit :).
[normal] When used to measure the green line, it can be converted by position into the green unit, and its position is 1.
[normal] There are reasons to prefer using -i as the unit of our normal numbers, rather than 1. It takes two segments to measure something, a unit and a length to measure. If they both use the same unit and are the same length, they are mathematically identical objects. Which is dividing by which in that case?
[normal] The only way to differentiate the two is to have them on different line polarities. It makes sense that a positive value moves towards the unit, and the unit is the landmark that positive things move towards. These are opposite perspectives, the unit starts at position 1 and goes to 0, the value starts at 0 and goes in whatever direction it encodes.
[normal] This final value is the only one that is variable (the 0, 0, and 1 are constants), so we can encode a number with one value. That value is the ‘goal’ or the ‘end point’.
[Heading 1] Segment Numbers
[normal] What about the numbers in the opposite polarity? This is the same system with everything negated. These will have their unit on the left side, from the -1 position, to zero. Of course this can be treated exactly as our own numbers, just flipped horizontally and vertically (akin to moving to the other side of the table). When combined together though, the inverted version will indicate the opposite values of the normal one. The meaning will be the opposite as well, measuring the distance from the start, rather than the goal. The progress so far rather than the final value. The starting position rather than the end.
[normal] So for segments not anchored to zero, the start position moves in the opposite direction as the end position. This makes sense, because a segment from 3 to 5 has a length of 2, not 8 (-3+5=2 vs 3+5=8). That implies the start point has had a head start, a distance that is skipped or subtracted. Putting the start point in the opposite perspective of the end point allows this. For example, below is a segment that starts at 2i in the inverted perspective, and ends at 4 in the normal perspective. Notice how these units map to the four symmetric transformations.
[normal] This segment number system actually only relaxes one extra constraint compared to normal numbers. The two units are a fixed value of 1, and are both the same length. The start point and the end point are variable. This is why it only takes two values to express a segment (aka a complex number) – the two unit values are a constant value of 1, and always the same length.
[Heading 1] Beyond Segments
[normal] What about relaxing a third constraint? At first this seems like it would be chaos, as the two units would not need to be identical. That points to where it would be useful though, environments without units.
[normal] Imagine a primitive life form has two light sensor eyes, one on each side. There is no universal lumens reference in this world, and each eye is imperfect. The darkest and lightest points of each aren’t always going to be the same, damaged or otherwise, so there isn’t even a common minimum or maximum for each eye. Perhaps even the resolution isn’t constant, one could see in ten steps of brightness, the other twenty. The constant here is they both belong to the same organism, so they will experience the same stimulus, unless there are local reasons for a difference. The organism needs to utilize this messy low resolution information to help maintain its balance of energy and internal conditions.
[normal] The first requirement is to have some reference point. Day and night are very different, so there isn’t an external constant. By keeping an average as it moves and spins around, it could get an average input over a certain period of time and use that as a ‘zero’ reference. Then each eye would move above or below that zero point as it swims through its environment. It needs to dynamically calibrate its sensors, meaning the reference point and the unit size both need to be flexible.
[normal] This creates a positive or negative segment value in each eye. Both segments are zero referenced, so there is no unit. The only option is to set one as the unit and compare it to the other. This allows calculating which is greater, as well as knowing if the total light is increasing or decreasing. The averaged zero point also gives an indication of how much ambient light is present. This system is something like our numbers, with the main difference being that both the zero and one positions of the unit are ‘floating’ over time, and the choice of which value should be used as the unit is arbitrary.
[normal] We get a truly floating system with a second sampling. Now there are two directed segments with a slowly floating zero point. All four positions of the two segments are floating, so while any area can be used as a unit, there can’t be a constant unit. There is a surprising amount of useful math that can be done with these floating quadrants!
[normal] We’ll go over this math in the next article, but suffice to say there is a lot of utility that emerges from the selections, comparisons and transformations of these areas. With the addition of resolution and the above symmetry actions, a basic pseudo organism becomes viable. With a minimal node count, a trainable prediction engine can steer through its environment and sustain itself.

===== Articles\Thinking in Directed Segments.docx =====
[normal] Thinking in Directed Segments
[normal] Directed segments work very well for encoding concepts. They are very simple, a start point and an end point, which gives you a range with a direction. And they have a surprisingly intuitive mapping to the type of complex structures you find in grammar. I've talked about this a lot, but now that I’m getting further into it, I have, perhaps, some better examples.
[normal] In all languages, tenses can reference future, current or past events, and they can do this from the perspective of the future, current or past. They can use the event‘s point of view or the speakers. And they can focus on different aspects of the event; before, beginning, during, completion, or after — or contiguous combinations of those. Imagine eating a meal (I ate, I’m eating, I’m going to eat). The segment describes the duration of eating, and the calibration (where the basis 0->1 is placed) describes the temporal position of the event. This is [time : time], but you could imagine [distance : distance] ("there’s a very long bridge in 5 miles"), or any combination ("a 10 minute delay in 10 miles", "the stock went down last week" etc). Here are some common English tenses, would you map them in a similar way?
[normal] There are many tenses available in English, but like all languages, there are many expressible tenses we don't have structures for. For these we just use extra words to describe the situation, but mathematically less common doesn't have to mean a more complex encoding.
[normal] The segment itself can be interpreted in different ways, due to the fact that it's made up of two zero anchored segments (zero to a start point, and zero to an end point). For example, the segment could be the event, it could be a description of a partially completed event, or it could two contiguous events. These interpretations determine the ways you can meaningfully combine segments, so it is important to codify this intent. Units as mathematical objects can help clarify this, as I talked about elsewhere.
[normal] Note that the direction of the arrow is also relevant. This polarity is lost in regular numbers (other than positive and negative), but it is common in both the real world and the math we use to describe it.  In fact the core of measurement, the basis itself, is a directed segment from 0->1. Here you can see directional encodings for gaining versus losing, a lot versus a little, as well as before versus after.
[normal] The basis unit has positive and negative aspects (and mirrored, but we'll save that for later). "The number goes up", means one thing for wealth, but another for debt. Most measure words in a language have this duality; either as a separate word (height/depth, strong/weak, calm/agitated), or with the prefix 'un' (happy/unhappy, fair/unfair). And as discussed in other posts, the start point of a segment is actually an inverted unit located at (-1->0), or (1->0). This gives us the 'i' in complex numbers.
[normal] This isn’t just a way to solve temporal encodings in language. Segments simplify encoding transforms from an initial state to a goal state (a ‘verb’), allow qualifying and comparing things (adjectives/adverbs), as well as categorizing objects (nouns). Even minor things like prepositions fit intuitively into segments. A segment has up to 7 distinct areas of interest. The focus can cover multiple contiguous positions, inclusive or exclusively, and involve multiple segments. This allows for a lot of combinations, and the human mind has evolved to make any such setups intuitive. Here are some examples of changing the focus to derive prepositions. This focus itself can of course be defined with a segment. And importantly, all these segments and focal areas can be trained for AI with things like attention mechanisms.
[normal] As you can see, there are may ways to interpret a segment. There also many ways to combine segments, whether through addition, multiplication, repetition, merges, and other operations. Yes — many ways to add, many ways to multiply. This may sound absurd, but that is actually pretty normal in math. Look at all the Boolean operations, there are 16 of them. Even in our regular number system there are different meanings for multiply. And in fact there are other 'intuitive' ways of multiplying that are considered wrong. For example, here’s a few interpretations of multiplying 2 with 3:
[normal] Imagine expressing all of these ideas with just our regular points-on-a-line numbers. Of course it can be done, but you’d have one system and I’d have another. The intuition would be lost in our personal encoding choices. Segments, however, bring a numeric intuition that maps to the way we think.
[normal] I'm convinced that segment math will start us down the path to interpretable AI. Working hard on it, hope you can give it consideration as well!
[normal] Follow along if you are interested, more to come -- up next, multiplication and boolean operations. These operations are extremely powerful and meaningful with directed segments. 🚀

[normal] Is Math Universal?
[normal] It is often claimed that math is a ‘universal language’ — that it was discovered rather than invented. Given our limited interactions with alien species, that is a difficult claim to test, but it certainly feels like at least parts of it would be similar in any form of intelligence. Being able to categorize things requires grouping, grouping leads directly to counting and measuring, which leads to adding and multiplying — and then all mathematics tumbles out. Or is this summary already so rife with human bias that it wouldn’t even be describable to another intelligence?
[normal] The best we can probably do is to imagine communicating it to another very very different life form. Maybe a smart octopus, a blank computer AI, or a giant smarty pants gas cloud that had no concept of time, space or pants. In this context base ten numbers and even Cartesian coordinates don’t seem so fundamental, but what about counting, adding, comparing and multiplying?
[normal] Ok, let’s imagine then that there’s an alien AI supercomputer gas cloud floating somewhere in deep space, and by some distant friend of a friend we can communicate with it. You say, “Hi, I’m a human and I come in peace”. And it says, “What’s a human, and what’s an I, and what’s a peace?”.  A few exchanges like this get nowhere, and then you remember the universal language that is mathematics. The impulse is to start with geometry, because other than having ‘geo’ in the name, it seems pretty universal (which has ‘universe’ in the name). But before triangles and all that you’ll need to explain positions, which implies relationships between things, which implies things. So we are going to need a thing.
[normal] Act 1
[normal] What is the simplest thing? Not an apple or anything like that - you don’t want to have to describe an apple. And rule of thumb, you should avoid talking about edible life forms to aliens. The ‘thing’ should be as unspecific as possible, as we have zero context of their existence. Lastly, out of an abundance of caution, we should make sure we’re starting with nothing else before we talk about this thing. This alien may live in a busy world where the quiet of nothing is a novel concept.
[normal] First message: “Start with nothing.”
[normal] “Ok, empty”, comes the reply. Wow, hello alien friend. Oh and a note from our intermediary, “The word ‘empty’ is a very crude translation, but close as will make sense at all to you. Expect more of this.”
[normal] This is good, if they’ve erased the board so to speak, we can start to build.
[normal] Second message: “Let there be something.” A little dramatic, but how else to put it? Maybe ‘Imagine something’, but what if they don’t have an imagination? ‘Produce something’, would work, but begs the question ‘from what?’ which is more information than something this general allows for.
[normal] The alien responds, “Ok, what next?”. Victory! You have just communicated at least one bit of information -- two bits if you count the nothing part. In a way you’ve still said nothing, for all you know it could be imagining a banana in nine dimensions, a large slice of time, or an undetectable fart smell. But you both have a thing that exists, at least in your minds, and that is a giant step. You have a noun (the thing), the verb ‘is’ (it exists), and ‘let’ means you share a way of bringing things into a context of some sort. These map nicely to an operation on an entity that produces a result (let x => x is).
[normal] Now, what next indeed? We could focus on the thing itself, trying to quantify it by measuring properties, but to measure anything you need a reference, and we only have the thing itself. The other option is to go for a second thing, and build up the ideas by organizing those things, and maybe even get to paths between things when they are organized in certain ways. Seeing as measuring requires a second thing anyway, a ‘second thing’ seems like the way to go.
[normal] “Let there be another thing.” Hopefully our friend of a friend can translate ‘another’, as this is addition, and addition is the basis for half of mathematics. The response presently comes.
[normal] “Wow. Two things. Impressive.”
[normal] Ok, that’s good. Hard to tell if that is sarcasm or not, if not it’s tempting to just say ‘that’s it!’ and wait a few millennia. Either way, we now have plural, and the ability to separate things from each other somehow. We might have repetition (apple plus apple), though can’t be sure it doesn’t have two very different things (apple plus orange). But we know it isn’t everything before the thing and the thing (no apple, apple) because we started with nothing (whew). Let’s go for a third thing, this should be obvious to it.
[normal] “Let there be a third thing.” We ask our friend to translate ‘third’, or just say ‘yet another thing’ if that’s impossible.
[normal] “I am very confused. These things have become hard to absorb.”
[normal] Hmmmm. Well this is perplexing, but perhaps it explains why the alien was so impressed with two things. Our friend assures us again that this is a very intelligent mind that is easily capable of learning math, so something is on us here. What three things would be hard to keep track of for us? Three blinking fireflies in the night, three spokes on a spinning wheel, three overlapping tree crowns, three zebras in front of one another, three fart smells in a large room… ok, not hard to get confused after all. It seems our alien friend needs to establish a way of separating things from each other.
[normal] “Can you make each thing small, still and unchanging? We will need many more things.”
[normal] “No I can’t. Can I use different things instead?”, the alien asks.
[normal] “Yes, it is not important what these things are, it is just important that you find them easy to acquire, easy to tell apart, and easy manipulate.”
[normal] “Ok. I have three things. This is easy again.”
[normal] This seems like progress - if the basis of math isn’t boringly obvious, the rest is impossible. Although, one has to wonder if we might have just ploughed over an entire undiscovered branch of math based on whatever it had before. Firefly math?
[normal] “Of these three things, what is the most similar thing about them and what is the most different?”
[normal] The alien responded quickly this time, “They are the same kind of thing, but each one is different”.
[normal] This is good. ’Kind’ means categories, which suggests multiple nouns, and yet each element is somewhat unique. It means we can eventually count different things, compare counts, talk of groups and sets, which leads to patterns, statistics, probability, and all of math, or at least all math involving whole numbers. Assuming these are ‘countable nouns’ that is (things like apples, cars or people), we should verify that.
[normal] If they are not countable nouns (things like water, traffic or courage), they are a single thing with continuous properties, which allows these properties to be combined, adjusted, stretched and measured, at least mentally. This leads to multiplication, geometry, algebra, calculus and all of math - at least all math without exact values.
[normal] “Take one of these things and partition it. Do you now have two things, or two parts of one thing?”. Hopefully this will make sense, and hopefully nothing ends up bleeding.
[normal] “There are now two parts of one thing.” Ok, perfect, count nouns. And because they all share a category, we can assume they are all count noun things - let’s imagine they’re apples even though they aren’t apples. That would now be two whole apples, and a third apple cut in two.
[normal] An interesting paradox with counting and measuring is that continuous things can not be partitioned, but can be adjusted to a specific magnitude, while discrete things can be partitioned, but are not bound to specific magnitudes. As an example, you can not draw half a line, but you can adjust a line to be as close to three inches long as your precision allows. On the flip side, you can have 68.2% of an apple, but apples can not be defined by a specific weight, diameter or color. The implication of this is the only way we can get an exact number (say exactly three) is with discrete things, but with these we lose the ability to have properties with consistent values. We can still use a single discrete thing as an exact unit of measure and get a continuous value, but then all comparisons to the unit will be measured, and limited by our precision (this apple is 1.153 times heavier than our unit apple, to three decimal places, not four). The only numbers that can be ‘infinitely’ precise are the ones that can contain no information about the values of their attributes. The declared membership in a category (including the unit category)  is the ‘true’ axiom, and is the only value with no error in its magnitude.
[normal] This means only discrete things can be added to get counting (because one line plus one line is still one line, albeit with a new length), and only continuous things can be multiplied (you can stretch or scale a continuous thing and get a new measure, but you can’t partition or append to a discrete thing without getting fragments or additional things).
[normal] An adding number line starts at zero, and pulls in one direction or the other. It doesn’t stretch anything, but everything it passes gets removed from existing field and added to the one being created. Eg white paper is removed and a black line is added. This is similar to the reciprocal in multiplication where you connect each end of the lines to each other, but in this case you start at zero, one side is positive value, the other negative. When adding to an existing line you can start at zero and ‘push’ to the positive, moving everything along (or start at max, and push to negative first). Now if that line is circular like in mod arithmetic for example, that becomes a rotation. If it isn’t circular, it is still sort of a rotation, just it doesn’t run out of ‘chairs’ so never circles back to the start. Contrast that with the stretching in multiplication, first one way then the other - if you would do that to a line it would fold up to a single point, and then unfold in reverse order. That is flipping. So multiplication is like flipping,and adding is like rotation. We can rotate by 90 degrees with multiplication using two perpendicular lines, but that is a flip that unwraps in the same direction (which is why it only works for the angles of the two lines, and you need cos/sin to actually rotate).
[normal] While adding in a mod system is like rotating (pushing the numbers around a clock a bit each time you add one), multiplying is going to potentially create gaps and overlaps (imagine all the numbers on the clock scale by 4, one becomes 4, 2 becomes 8, 3 becomes 12, 4 becomes 16=>4, 5 becomes 20=>8 etc). Some numbers will perfectly fill (1 always does because there is no change), and some will land all digits on the same number (*size always will). This should show certain patterns with primes, factors, symmetries and groups, and maybe even information, probability etc. Also if you keep track of the number of times something goes around as a place value system, you may get place value, exponents, multiple dimensions etc.
[normal] You use addition to create lengths (carve something out, negative, and push it out, positive), and then multiply using two of those objects, one as unit. With a single object, you can multiply (stretch), but it will be a flip end to end. You need to start at an end for the stretch because there is no unit (or the object is the unit if you prefer), and the end is zero rather than one. When stretching a single unit, the only landmark is the other point, so the points can either exchange (flip) or revert to how they were (identity).
[normal] Using category whole numbers, accuracy is as detailed as you want because fractions are valid. So PI is whatever large number over whatever other large number to get you 3.14159865… as precise as you want — but limited by how large your max number is. In this sense whole numbers are the ‘reciprocal’ of measured fractions, as they are also limited in precision based on how good your resolution (measurement) is. One is more samples, the other is a better ruler, but it comes to the same. Neither are groups unless you account for these limitations in closure (technically the answer is always in the group, just the correctness is limited, maybe similar to ‘mod’ in that sense).
[normal] Anything plural is continuous, anything singular is discrete? Combining continuous things is a ‘x combined into (by) y’ relation (in^2, mph, ‘watery milk’), where discrete is an ‘x to y’ ratio (4 apples to 5 oranges). The singular thing in a plural is always the unit category, and can be used in a ‘by’ relation (7.4 inches uses an inch as the unit). Some continuous things have no unit (water, air, dancing, courage), probably because it is too small, including time steps being too small. At a certain scale, all things break down and become other things (water>hydrogen, dancing to motionless, courage to inaction, gas to stars). Some have fairly meaningless units because they are so generally defined (clouds).
[normal] We use precision and estimation in language in a similar way. The unit is always present, if assumed (a really big dog, a tiny elephant - category size is assumed and used as unit). Our ability to differentiate things is probably somewhere around 7-20, after that we need new units or place value positions. We use our bodies and world as units (touch, manipulate, pinch, grab, hug, tackle, walk, run, journey…. thou, mm, inch, foot, meter, mile… ms, second, minute, hour, day, month, year)
[normal] We should establish how different these things are, because counting is a sequence, which requires an order, which requires you can tell one thing from another.
[normal] When dealing with discrete things, the two organization systems are cyclical (mod arithmetic, shapes), and estimation beyond precision (rounding, statistics, probability, and just greater/less than).
[normal] Creating something from nothing requires the removing of ‘the nothing’ (you can imagine one apple, but you can’t imagine an apple and keep the space an apple takes empty). So these things are always paired, and every operation in math is paired in a similar way. This is why equations are balanced etc.
[normal] As numbers/permutations grow, this is similar to going beyond the resolution of measurement. So a game like tic tac toe is in the resolution of a computer, and chess/go isn’t. This makes something totally ‘determinable’ more of a probability problem. At a certain scale things change state - this can be inherent in the object, or based on your ability to measure calculate it. Perhaps state changes in nature (water to hydrogen as it divides, matter to stars) can be framed as an object moving beyond the resolution of its state.
[normal] Some discrete things still can not be portioned, because their category is a continuous object. Cut one discrete ice cube, and you get two discrete ice cubes, even though an ice cube is discrete. It is discrete, with no information that distinguishes its parts.
[normal] List each decision point and possible optional decisions (start with one thing, move to two vs make a ray vs delete it vs move it etc)
[normal] When scaling there are no whole numbers due to precision, where in discrete objects (counting, adding) there are. This is because scaling down does not allow you to destroy information, where removing (subtracting) does.
[normal] Discrete values are nouns, attributes are adjectives (measured against a ‘unit’ of attribute), scaling is verbs, ratios are adverbs, formulas are statements(?), missing values or past precision are questions.
[normal] Multiplying is really just a form of zooming in and out, looking for more or less detail. Precision could be increased if the thing is measured then shrank, or scaled up then measured, depending on how the unit is treated. Being able to measure with higher precision is a form of zooming in, and being able to count higher is a form of gaining precision by using more bits. You only gain information if the scale is natural and not based on your numbers alone. If you have 100 things of weights exact beyond your measurement, weighing them all and averaging gives you more precision because the scaling is natural. Same with looking closer or increasing temperature/volume/distance or even stretching a rubber band - increasing a natural attribute of a thing gives you more precision. But, just multiplying your low resolution measurement does not - you will be out by the same ratio (same entropy overall), but will be worse off in absolute terms.
[normal] A question is, can you get more exact measurements with the whole number part, and scale to measure the fraction, or is the precision of your unit the limiting factor? This would depend on the case, but might be possible to clarify better.
[normal] The values past precision are the true values, and the difference is noise (in an information theory sense). So measurement = value + noise. The noise is valid information, and seems to line up with entropy type math in general. (The average uncertainty of the actual value after it is measured, X = Y + n).
[normal] When multiplying, the two types of units can always give an answer, but sometimes 0,1 or both are continuous/discrete. Eg. time X time can have one continuous and one discrete (open 9-5, seven days a week), both discrete (bus leaves at 1:00, 2:00, or 3:00, for the next three days) — but not both discrete because time is one dimensional. 2D space can be all - a grid of dots, a column of lines, or an area.
[normal] If something is discrete, it just means its resolution is lower than something continuous. So the 3rd and 10th of every month can be queried with the 7.86th of month two — month two is fine, and 7.86th is based on probability resolution (e.g. probably the 10th, but may be otherwise depending on resolution mechanism).
[normal] An area is created if both multiplied values are continuous. It is only a true area if both units are combined into a new unit though. 3” x 2” is 6” squared, because all parts of the area are part of the solution and the units are combined into a new inches squared. If you get $20/hour, it is a rate line to $60 for three hours work (or 3 hours for $60)— even though both are potentially continuous values. Rates like mpg, mph, horsepower, man hours etc have one continuous value and one fixed unit. The units combine, but one is normalized so it is a bit more like a rate than an area (though an area also throws away the actual dimensions, hmm). A grid style chart is more like an area (flight grid with cost and day, pressure), and three sliders akin to a volume (RGB sliders, yaw/pitch/roll). Consider a three way trade off, like ‘better faster cheaper, pick two’ (but on sliders) - this is a shaped volume with curves. Ultimately area needs to be filled, making things that don’t naturally combine not really work the same (dollars squared, time squared etc aren’t natural things). Does anything other than space combine like this? Maybe curves, acceleration etc?
[normal] The angle between two joined axis is ‘how connected’ they are. Perpendicular is fully connected, which means each is doing maximum work, which means they are fully independent of each other for information (like two dice, the outcome of each is independent). In matrix notation, it is possible to show these relations with more than two axis, though you could represent the same amount of information graphically, eg 3D, use color, quality of line, curves, concepts, shapes etc. In fact, in a very distant way, this is what we do with line drawing.
[normal] A curve is a line moving up and forward, with one moving at a different rate. If that is viewed on a grid you get a parabola, but if viewed from the perspective of the moving point you get a spiral. A circle is then moving forward and ‘to my left’ (or right) at a constant rate. The area triangles are also from their own perspective moving ‘to the line on my right’.
[normal] If two lines have no attach points they are unrelated and can only be compared. With one attach point, when one is extended to the other it stretches without affecting the other, so the unit doesn’t change. This is addition. With two attach points, any stretching of one will stretch the other, and relative to the original units this is multiplication. With three attach points, stretching from both ends makes the center attach point the origin with the positive and negative units potentially different sizes. With three lines connected, A->B and B-C this becomes a power of two scaling, which is also a curve when viewed with two axes. With two separated parallel lines attached with different unit sizes (a vertical connection and a second angled connection) this also will be a scaled power of two connections, but will result in a curve (one side longer but connect points and distance the same will pull one or both into a curve).
[normal] ** Stretching the unit causes all things measured by the unit to have more or less units per former unit, meaning multiply or divide. If the other elements move proportionally, a larger unit is ‘multiply’, and a smaller unit is ‘divide’. If the non unit elements don’t change size, then it becomes the opposite (reciprocal), where a smaller unit means a larger number of units fit in other elements (multiply), and a larger unit is ‘divide’. If non unit elements are scaled, they won’t affect the unit at all, so they just have room for more or less units depending on growth direction. This is just addition or subtraction.
[normal] Two options in a unit relation are 1) measuring from ‘unit’ or 2) sizing from ‘unit’. This leads to either addition or multiplication as the unit changes size. This can work the other way too if the connection is two way -- where ‘unit’ can be resized or not as other elements change magnitude. It feels more natural to have ‘unit’ be independent, but there are many examples where that doesn’t hold of course. For example levers and gears are two way, but also the reciprocal of every unit relation, where the non unit becomes unit, can be viewed this way. We know you can’t adjust your shadow size directly, but the relation to the object size or light distance holds from all points of view (just some are non causal).
[normal] When things stretch to zero (multiply by zero) they are NOT removed from existence, in fact stretching can’t create or destroy information. They are just perfectly correlated with your measuring system, so you can no longer measuring them that way. This could be the geometry lines up with your line of sight, or your red glasses can no longer see something exactly that red. Only addition creates something from nothing (and creates nothing from something in subtraction), and the amount of something + nothing is constant.
[normal] This is akin to rolling dice and using the bottom + top values (always seven) result in no information per roll, because the result values are perfectly correlated. The information available depends on what you are measuring - eg what happens to probability if you add all the visible sides from a set angle? If we reported both the top and north side value we’d get approximate rotation, and if the two north values were interpolated we may be able to get orientation. As it is we throw away the zero information results, as well as the higher information results that we don’t care about (rotation, dice color, dice size, temperature, bet value etc), and assume things like fairness, counting, flatness of table... So the ‘unit’ here is still a single dot on the dice, but the organization of them is very specific, and the measurement rules determine the possible results.
[normal] As happy as the moment is, there is a temptation to just send a third, “That’s it!” message and let it figure the rest out by itself over a few millennia. But weirdly it doesn’t seem to have clued into three et al, and it doesn’t seem to know you can connect the points with a line. We have a minimum for plural, and at least one repetition. We probably have the idea of proximity, either near or far by their discretion. And among other things, we’ve confirmed by the law of reciprocals how little we know about the physics of gas nebulae. But the next step. Should it be counting or lines?
[normal] You phone a friend, but they just wonder with a little too much concern whether this is the same aliens that built the pyramids. Never mind. It seems we could build up from either counting or geometry, but all those ‘points’ we are going to need for counting aren’t going to be lined up, or even necessarily the same size (small, but not equal). Probably better not to get a ‘number line’ scattered all over and then try to reign it in - let’s go with a line first. Or I guess a segment to start with, and we’ll ease into lines.
