===== Math 5.docx =====
[Heading 1] Universal Math from First Principles
[normal] <Code that explores this system available here.>
[Heading 2] Universals
[normal] Physics is the study of energy, mathematics is the study of magnitudes. Both have parallels to the study of information. Physics has discovered a small number of universal ‘first principles’ in the laws of thermodynamics. These laws can be interpreted for mathematics as well, giving many new insights.
[Heading 3] The Laws of Thermodynamics
[normal] Law 0: If two systems are both in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
[normal] Law 1: Energy can not be created or destroyed, but it can be changed from one form to another.
[normal] Law 2: All closed systems, including the universe, spontaneously tend toward an equilibrium state in which entropy is at a maximum.
[normal] Law 3: The entropy of a system approaches a constant value as the temperature approaches absolute zero. *Note the word ‘approaches’, Absolute zero (zero motion) can not be achieved as energy can not be destroyed (law 1). Energy can only be mixed and dispersed.
[Heading 3] The Laws of Thermodynamics Applied to Information
[normal] Law 0: If two magnitudes are both equivalent to a third magnitude, they are also equivalent to each other.
[normal] Law 1: Selected magnitudes can not be transformed to have more or less potential information, but they can be transformed in any other way that does not violate these laws.
[normal] Law 2: All measurements must be derived from a directed gradient, where the fluctuations while measuring are not greater than the stated precision.
[normal] Law 3: Change tends to obscure past states, and reveal patterns that may predict future states. As change approaches true randomness, information approaches zero in both directions.
[Heading 3] Implications of The Laws of Information
[normal] Definition: Potential information is anything measurable. Information comes from measurements that reduce uncertainty, so it is always relative to the existing knowledge of the measurer.
[normal] Definition: ‘Equivalent’ means compared measurements are indistinguishable at the resolution measured.
[normal] Law 0:
[normal] Measurements can and must be compared with each other to gain information. There is no universal yardstick
[normal] Law 1:
[normal] All parts of an equation must balance.
[normal] All values must be fully specified (infinite size or precision is created information)
[normal] Limits on precision require all values to be soft-bounded ranges of some form.
[normal] Law 2:
[normal] Static (non-fluctuating) values are a useful subset of mathematics, not the foundation.
[normal] Measurements lie on a directed gradient, therefore are made relative to a landmark direction.
[normal] We must be explicit about our frame of reference on a gradient when discussing measurements.
[normal] Law 3:
[normal] Measurements can come from any gradient, but information can only come from comparisons that reduce uncertainty.
[normal] Perfect randomness (zero information) can only be approached, not achieved.
[normal] It is possible to derive information (predictions with accuracy better than chance) from tendencies and structure (trends and patterns).
[Heading 2] Deriving Universal Math
[Heading 3] 1.0 Measurement
[normal] There are many paths to deriving universal math from first principles. Traditionally we start with something like an infinitely small point in space, an empty set, a basic symmetry, or even an apple. As simple as these seem, they are all complex concepts filled with prerequisite information.
[normal] This approach will use a simple sensor as a model. We don’t know where it is, we don’t know how it is calibrated, and we don’t even know what it is sensing. It could be biological or electronic. Finally, the output of this sensor is non numeric, it’s just a quantity that can be sensed (with a meter or a brain, it doesn’t matter). A signal along a gradient is the natural starting point for the study of math. This is a simple concept that we can eventually scale up into geometries, sets, symmetries, and even apple-detectors.
[normal] We take a measurement.
[normal] With a single measurement, we have no information because we have nothing to compare it to. We can’t say if it is high or low, because we know nothing about the precision and range of the signal, nor our ability to measure it. In much the same way, we can’t say if our universe is large or small compared to typical universes, as we only have one data point.
[Heading 3] 1.1 Precision
[normal] All things that can be measured, or even imagined, are not perfectly stable. They may be fluctuating rapidly like sound or light, or slowly changing like the cooling of the earth’s core. All measurements are samples over some duration, as nothing can be instantaneous. Measuring temperature is measuring the kinetic energy of atoms or molecules, and to measure this motion requires time. Other samples are over a much longer period, like the decay of carbon-14. Lastly, the measure needs to quantify this sample accurately, not just the ‘center’ of it, but the bounds as well. We usually do this with precision. The precision we use for a measurement can be limited by the traits we measure, by our instruments, or most commonly by our limited need for precision. The only hard limit is that precision must be finite.
[normal] Todo: point segment image
[normal] Knowing that all measures are some bounds of values that change over time makes it clear that measurements are ranges. A measurement doesn’t represent an infinitely precise value, because that would require inventing precision. Given that all values have limits to their precision, at a certain resolution they become segments or probability ranges. If we can’t tell two measures apart (or don’t care about the difference) they must use the same measurement. If we later find a way to tell them apart (or start caring about the differences), we can separate them and add precision to the system. A value isn’t an exact number, nor a segment with two endpoints – it is all potential measurements that are considered the same at the level of precision used.
[Heading 3] 1.2 Extents
[normal] Measurements aren’t just confined to a level of precision, they are also bound by their maximum potential extents in each direction. This can be a limit of the domain itself, of the instrument, or by the limits of our concern. Any measures two large to be distinguished (in the positive or negative direction) must also be considered the same. We are free to improve our instruments, take more samples, or even imagine greater extents. But this expanded domain will still be bounded, and subsequent transformations will still be limited by these new bounds. This is true even in domains where we can not articulate a bounds, such as with numbers. Numbers do not have a hard limit, but we know they eventually grow large enough that they invalidate any definition that can describe what they are. Mathematics that obeys the conservation law must work with a finite amount of total information, and that total will not change under transformation.
[normal] A bounded value, or a range between two measured values.
[Heading 3] 1.3 Units, Unots and Basis
[normal] All gradient measurements have a precision and maximum range, but we can’t quantify these with a single measurement from an uncalibrated instrument. The first step would be to acquire a second value, and the only requirement here is that we can tell it apart from the first one. This second value tells us the precision and limits are at least this range. We can also compare the two and call one signal ‘greater’ than the other. Everything measurable comes from some form of ordered gradient, otherwise we couldn’t measure it. Imagining we are measuring a voltage, greater voltage may mean extra electrons or fewer electrons. This directional choice is arbitrary but necessary. For any comparison we need to label one direction greater and one lesser, in order to specify what we mean when values increase and decrease.
[normal] Imagine our voltage meter has an indicator that swings from blue to red. Let’s say the first point measured was more red, the second more blue. We’ll arbitrarily label red to blue as the positive direction. A numeric segment can be created by calling the  first position ‘zero’ and the second position ‘one’. This segment forms a unit, where the positive direction is always towards blue.
[normal] If we would flip this numbering, moving towards red would be considered positive. This ‘negative unit’ segment will be called a unot in order to distinguish it from a unit. This is a new word, but more importantly, *this is an extremely important concept*. Note that this isn’t a negative number - that is a number with a positive unit that moves leftward. This is a number whose unit is negative. What does a negative unit imply? What would adding or multiplying a number with a negative unit do? This is worth pausing to think about. More on this later.
[normal] The term ‘basis’ represents either the unit or unot of a measure, whichever one it is using. The absolute direction chosen for a unit is arbitrary, but the unot will always be opposite. We normally only work in units, and they normally increase to the right. This would make unots point to the left. Keep in mind this is just a visualization. Measurements such as wealth vs debt, tallness vs shortness, heating vs cooling, or happiness vs sadness have no preferred basis, no preferred direction, and are not even naturally horizontal.
[Heading 3] 1.4 Comparisons
[normal] With three values, we can form two segments and compare them. There are actually three possible segments here, and they are all useful to consider.
[normal] Let’s call the latest value ‘x’. If the first two values (0->1) form a unit, then a second segment (0->x) can be created to compare to the first one. Depending where the x value is, the segment formed could be 2 times as long as the unit, 3 times as long, 0.25 times as long, or even -4 times as long. From the unot perspective these values would simply be inverted, but this will be covered in more detail later.
[normal] It is instructive to test what happens to the ratio of the x segment to the unit segment as you slide the x value along the scale. As x moves to the right the ratio becomes larger and larger until it hits the limit of its range. As it moves left it gets smaller, as it passes 1 you get fractions, and as it moves past 0 you get larger and larger negative numbers. These values are linear with motion - the numbers increase or decrease in direct proportion to the amount you move the x position. The motion of x gives us the familiar rational numbers - a fraction with the x segment on top and the unit segment on the bottom.
[normal] What about if you move the unit’s ‘1’ position? Here the unit is changing size, so as it moves left closer to zero the ratio of the x segment grows larger, and as it moves right, past the x position that ratio grows smaller. If the point moves to the left of zero, we get a negative unit. This means our perspective has flipped – where greater used to mean bluer, they now mean redder. The position just to the left of zero gives us a very small ‘unot’, meaning a large negative number in the unot perspective. As the point continues left the large ratio comes down until it is as small as we have resolution for.
[Heading 3] 1.5 Reciprocals
[normal] Graphing these sliding comparisons gives the reciprocal function (y=1/x). Whatever value you get by taking the first segment as the basis, you will get the reciprocal when using the other segment as the basis. They are fractions of each other, 1/3 becomes 3/1.  Any number multiplied by its reciprocal equals its basis.
[normal] It is useful to think of these segments as having a start point and end point rather than left and right. A basis segment is a unit if its endpoint is on the right side, and it is a unot if its endpoint is on the left. If it is a point rather than a segment, you can’t tell whether the start point is on the left or right. Remember a point isn’t zero length. It’s just that we can't tell apart the values it may contain, therefore we also can’t tell left from right. Another way of thinking about this is, a segment is positive if it points in the same direction as its basis, and negative if it points in the opposite direction.
[Heading 3] 1.6 Exploring Unot
[normal] A literal way to understand unot is to think of the dual interpretations we use for measure in everyday language. A normal day can be hot or cold, and everything in between. If warmer is the unit direction, then cooler is unot direction, and vice versa. Talking about temperature is usually done with a warm reference in summer (How hot is it? Very hot.) and a cool reference in winter (how cold is it? Very cold).
[normal] If a day goes from 10 degrees to 20 degrees, we can say the temperature was never more than 20 units, and never less than 10 units. But this doesn’t give us a direction. If we instead describe it in unot/unit terms, we can impose an order (unot->unit). That would be, from -10 unots to 20 units. If the start point is a unot, addition and also becomes straight forward, as we just add each element. Multiplication of two (non zero anchored) segments also becomes sensible, if not intuitive.
[normal] At a higher level of abstraction, you can think of the unot as the dual of the unit. If you select 3 out of 10 elements, the ‘unot’ is the 7 elements you didn’t select. If you multiply by a unot, it flips the meaning for forwards and backward as well as scaling. Mathematics contains duals throughout, due to the conservation not allowing the total information to change under transformation. The unot is a manifestation of that at the basis level.
[Heading 3] 1.7 Addition and Subtraction
[normal] Addition and subtraction are about total length. They require appending two lengths to form a new length. For addition of segments (in the unit perspective), the second segment is appended to the first segment’s endpoint. Subtraction is the same, only the segment being subtracted is flipped around its start point.
[normal] Note that the order here is the second element appends to the end. It could also be viewed as the second element emerging from the zero point (this might make more sense with segments that aren’t zero aligned). Addition mostly cares about total lengths, so it usually doesn’t matter. In more advanced situations, like when inspecting symmetry, it would be important to at least keep the rule consistent.
[normal] Addition and subtraction of unot segments works exactly the same, but the geometry will be reversed because the unot is pointing in the opposite direction. Again, we have to specify somehow this is all in the unot perspective.
[normal] Addition of mixed unit and unot segments reveals a bit more about the meaning of these segments. It is tempting to think of a positive unot value like a negative unit value, but they are different. They are often convertible to each other, but at minimum this requires a transform.
[normal] An example might help. If I have $5.00 (+5 wealth) and lose $3.00 (-3 wealth) I have $2.00 left. If I have $5.00 and you lend me $3.00 (+3 debt) I have $8.00. Even when I pay back the $3.00, I’ll still have $5.00. Wealth and debt are related but different. A negative is an opposite value, where a unot is an opposite perspective. Earning money and spending money are both dealing with the same perspective of the ledger (wealth). So are borrowing and paying back (debt). Combining both of them requires tracking both of them. This is true for all unit and unot measures. A very happy/sad moment feels quite different than an apathetic moment.
[normal] Adding mixed units (units and unots) requires us to conserve and track both values. We do this by joining the unot values to unot values, and joining unit values to unit values. Notice how the result will still have a unit and a unot value (with a shared zero point). In fact, we can describe all segments this way. In our normal numbering system we always assume a zero unot value, which creates a segment starting at zero. But these ‘full numbers’ (aka complex numbers) always fully describe the segment, even if both parts are non zero.
[Heading 3] 1.8 Complex Numbers are Segments
[normal] Complex numbers are directed segments. Normally complex numbers are transcribed with the unot side after the unit side, like 3+2i. Reversing that makes the segment read better, start point to end point, 2i+3. It also maps well to our existing numbers, which are all zero anchored, where”n” is actually “0i+n”. The numbers we are familiar with are the end point of a zero anchored segment.
[normal] Also notice these segments no longer need to be in the unit or unot perspective — the start point is measured by a unot, and the end point by a unit. The unit perspective is always the one we are viewing from, and unot is the one that ‘flips’ the perspective. This is why multiplying by unot (i) will flip the perspective and multiplying by unit will leave things as they are.
[normal] Complex numbers are normally visualized as transformed 2D objects with a rotation and magnitude. It can be useful to transform numbers like this, but untransformed complex numbers allow many visualizations that are not traditionally possible. At their simplest, they are just one dimensional segments along a gradient.
[Heading 3] 1.8 Multiplication
[normal] Addition and subtraction transform values through concatenation, while multiplication and division transform by scaling. You can think of it as stretching, as scaling up and down, or even zooming in and out. The important point is that all selected values scale linearly based on how far from the origin they are. Here is a simple number line, scaling up. It is much like stretching a rubber band with ticks on it, with zero at the center.
[normal] Notice how the 2i and 4 scale proportionally from zero as the number line stretches. If the original ‘1’ position became four times larger (by dragging it to the original 4), then all values selected would also become four times larger. If the ‘1’ was dragged to the left (became smaller), then all values would shrink. Lastly if the ‘1’ was dragged across the zero line to the -1 position, then all values would be negated.
[normal] We can measure this change if we hold the original basis units constant. In this case we are dragging values, not units. We always drag from the end of the basis (unit or unot) in multiplication, because the basis defines the scale of the number line.
[normal] With addition we concatenate from the zero point because we are appending, and therefore need to start at zero to include all the information in each unit direction. With multiplication we are scaling from the unit size to something larger or smaller, so we start at the one position to utilize the full measure of the unit. This explains why zero is the additive identity (adding zero doesn’t change the length) and one is the multiplicative identity (multiplying by one doesn’t change the length). Also it shows how zero can represent the absence of value in addition, but not in multiplication - something multiplied by zero is still there, it just at a scale that is less than we can measure.
[normal] Multiplication can only change the scale of an object, where addition can add or remove content to the element in focus. Addition results in multiple objects merged into one, so the end result has many similarities with scaling.
[normal] For scaling by a set amount, you stretch by that amount. All numbers are records of values, recipes to create these values, and for transformations by these values. In this case the *5 is the transformation that 5 causes.
[normal] To multiply 3 by 2 (3*2), you would drag the basis point to 2, and then remeasure the location of new ‘three’ point with the original unit.
[normal] What is happening in a multiplication is every section of the multiplicand is being stretched by every section of the multiplier. When one end of that segment is zero like in this case, the zero has no ‘pull’ on the result. This is a special case. Two segments are always multiplied by accounting for the four endpoints, just they do not affect the result when they are anchored on zero.
[Heading 3] 1.9 Multiplying by i
[normal] Anything multiplied by unit (1) doesn’t change. Anything multiplied by unot (a negative unit, or ‘i’), keeps the same value, but flips the perspective. So 5 becomes 5i, and 6i becomes 6. Note that 5i lies on the opposite side of the number line to 5 (flipped around zero), even though it has the same scalar. This is because ‘unot’ points in the opposite direction of ‘unit’, so its positive values grow in the opposite direction. To fully understand why this happens, we need to recap what a full number represents.
[normal] First, a full number represents a value as a directed segment, both the unit and unot amounts. Second, it is a recipe to create that segment. For example, ‘unit*10-4’ is a recipe to create ‘6’ from a unit by stretching and appending. Third, a full number represents the transformation itself. This transformation can be applied to any other full number or equation, and it will transform it in the same way. The part that is “*10-4” is a transformation applied to a unit that creates the segment 0i->6, but when applied to 2 (2 units*10-4) you get 0i->16. The transformation requires substitution to be applied elsewhere: n*10-4, 1*n-4 or 1*10-n. For this reason it is good to think of the transformation as including the operator, like +n, *n, -n³, or /ni.
[normal] Note: Negation is a mess, we use the same symbol to express negative numbers as we do to remove from a selection. It might be better to only have addition and multiplication. Then ‘-’ would only expresses negative numbers, and ‘/’ means “scaled by the reciprocal of", written as ‘*1/n’. Or at least to think about it this way.
[normal] For transformations, ‘+’ means append, ‘*’ means scale, ‘³’ (power) means repetition, ‘-’ means flip around zero, and ‘i’ (unot) means change the perspective. Note that our notation is always from the unit perspective, so multiplying by ‘i’ means “flip to the other perspective”, not change to the ‘i’ perspective. It will flip unit to unot, and unot to unit.
[normal] As an example, we can multiply 2i*3i. The value 2i represents a recorded value, and 3i represents how we want to transform it. These are both in the unot perspective, so their basis unit is -1. The transform is multiplication by 3i, so it will flip the perspective, and then scale by what remains. The 2i becomes 2 when it flips. This leaves the 3, but its position is now in the unit perspective, which makes it -3. Notice, nothing flipped the 3i, it just used up its ‘i’. This leaves us with (2*-3) in unit perspective, which is -6.
[normal] Multiplying by a negative unit flips the perspective of the multiplicand. As a bonus, we can now calculate that i*i=-1, rather than accepting this result as the definition of i.
[Heading 3] 1.10 Repeated Multiplies
[normal] Repetition is another fundamental operation in mathematics. We’ll cover it more later, but to really see how full numbers are equivalent to complex numbers, let’s look at what happens when repeatedly multiplying by i.
[normal] A segment can cycle through the positive and negative values of both the unit and unot directions by repeating a single transform: *i. This is the familiar cycling sequence 1, i, -1, -i, 1, i, -1, i… normally viewed as a rotation on a grid. It is easier to see how this works when multiplying by 2i as each operation’s output will be at a new scale. It may look complicated, but it is all just a consequence of the fact that multiplying by ‘i’ flips the perspective. Remember, multiplying by a negative flips the values around zero, and multiplying by ‘i’ flips the value’s directional orientation on the number line itself.
[Heading 3] 1.11 Resolution, Range, and Focus
[normal] Significant figures are of great importance in science and engineering, yet we have no way of encoding them in our mathematical notation. Even our base 10 numbering system is inappropriate for recording what is ultimately a binary phenomena. Fully defined basis segments specify both unit length and segment resolution, enabling computation to automatically track significant figures as it moves through transformations. Units (and unots) are created out of ‘ticks’ which are the smallest measure we are capable of – or more often just the smallest measure we care about for the given context.
[normal] Unit size is an arbitrary choice, but one with consequences. In pure math, where all values are imagined and therefore ‘perfectly measurable’, the unit resolution is mostly a matter of convenience. We choose units such as inches or light years because those are close to the values we expect to be working with. This avoids very large or small numbers that are not only awkward to work with, but convey a false sense of precision — especially important when our notation only ‘senses’ precision. Note that this is in no way claiming that avoiding a false sense of precision is a good way of measuring precision.
[normal] In applied math, where actual measurements have limits on accuracy and scale, choosing a unit in the appropriate range becomes more important. It also entails a lot of bookkeeping to ensure we don’t stray from that measured accuracy.
[normal] Intuitively, it seems the smallest element we can measure should always be the unit. This would be the distance between the smallest changes we can detect. The problem that arises is that the smallest measure is the least accurate signal we have, by definition. It is hard to get a precise value, and we have no way of making it more accurate. This inaccuracy will compound. If we estimate a micrometer, putting a million of them side by side is unlikely to be exactly a meter.
[normal] Making a unit the largest number that can be measured or imagined is problematic for the same reason. We think the universe is something like 13 billion light years across, but this is at the edge of what we’re able to measure, so it is very approximate and subject to change.
[normal] Much better would be to use a large number of those differences and divide them. Even if this measure isn’t perfect, the error is divided rather than compounded. A bonus is the unit’s magnitude can be made at whatever scale is appropriate, whether nanometers or miles. Note that these scales can be very very large and small. A computer can easily handle trillions and trillions of ticks in any configuration. The only requirement is that both the resolution and range be defined, and that both be finite.
[normal] Another important requirement of a unit basis is that it be simple to recalibrate. Not just to accommodate greater accuracies as we acquire them, but because the problems we work on have greatly varying resolutions. Having plenty of extra resolution for units to grow and shrink facilitates these conversions. We are used to having standard units we can measure with such as the meter. These units are calibrated very precisely, and they get more precise over time. However in actual usage the resolution must be allowed to vary widely. A tape measure does not give us the 0.1nm precision available from the meter definition, and the meter definition does not give us the numeric precision routinely used in computers.
[Heading 3] 1.12 Adding Two Segments
[normal] So far most of our segments have been anchored at zero. This creates very useful math – it is simple, and we can map it (with workarounds) to many of the magnitudes we deal with in everyday life. But it is not the full description of numbers, and it often breaks down without us even noticing.
[normal] Imagine a segment going from 0i->3, aka the number 3. What do we mean when we add ‘2’ to this? As we covered in the last section, this means appending the unit portion of ‘2 segment’ to the unit point (end point) of the original segment, and adding the unot portion of the ‘2 segment’ (zero in this case) to the unot point (start point) of the original segment. This results in a segment of length 5 (0i+5).
[normal] Now we can add segments that aren’t anchored at zero. The formula is the same (add the unit to unit, add the unot to unot), but you can see the second value is ‘split’. When segments don’t straddle the zero line, the formula is still the same, just both the start points and the end points are involved.
[normal] Here is an example of adding a segment where the endpoint is to the left of a start point. You can see why these complex-number segments are directed – the complex value represents the startpoint, not the leftmost point. A negative value shift the endpoint in the opposite direction. Ultimately the formula is simple, add the start points to get the resulting start point, and then add the end points to get the resulting endpoint.
[normal] What if we meant to shift the segment by 2 instead of add 2? In this case we want both the startpoint and the endpoint to move to the right by 2. This requires a segment with an end value of 2 (which moves the unit position to the right by 2), and a start value of -2i (which moves the unot position to the right by 2). Remember a unot value increases as it moves left, so -2 will move it to the right. This is normally what we consider a point rather than a segment.
[normal] So adding the segment 2 (0i->2) appends to the length of a segment, but adding the point 2 (-2i->2) shifts the segment. In normal math we consider these both to be ‘+2’ and differentiate based on context, but as you can see they are usefully different.
[Heading 3] 1.13 Multiplying Two Segments
[normal] Multiplying two segments that are offset from zero requires that every portion of the multiplier exerts a force on every portion of the multiplicand. This is simplified somewhat by the fact that the segments are linear. This allows us to interpolate these forces by just using the four endpoints. Multiply all the combinations together, and add the results up.
[normal] (ai+b)*(ci+d)= ai*ci + ai*d + b*ci + b*d
[normal] SegA*SegB    = endpt+startpt+startpt+endpt
[normal] = startpt+endpt
[normal] = Segment
[normal] It is still worth developing an intuition for this, and get a sense for the forces one segment exerts on the other. Try to see the tips of one segment acting on the tips of the other. It takes a while to feel intuitive because of the perspective flipping that the i multiplication does, but once dragging things around in an interactive program you do get the sense of it. Notice how you end up with two start points (unots), and two end points (units) that can be added together. Remember i*i results in the unit perspective, so the ai*ci results in a unit perspective endpoint.
[Heading 3] 1.14 Repetition
[normal] The last fundamental part of a full number is repetition. We normally assign repetition to multiplication, using powers. The value n^2 or n^3 means scale n by itself 2 or 3 times. This scaling can also be repeated 2½ times, -⅓ times, or even 2i+4 times. Naturally these repetitions can be represented as segments
[normal] Scaling up, these repetitions can be applied to repetitions, in multiple layers, which can be scaled up with repetitions, etc.
[normal] Scaling down, we get the repetition of addition. Counting from 1 to 7 could be written as an additive exponent (1)+7, where addition is repeated 7 times. We usually confuse this with single step multiplication (1*7), but the difference is apparent when looking at full number segments.
[normal] In order, there is repetion by addition, which is related to multiplication. Next repetition of multiplication that is expressed as powers. From there, repetion of powers, and powers of powers. Segments tend to lose meaning for us as levels of repetition grows, either exceeding the domain range, falling below the tick resolution, or just turning into seeming randomness.
[normal] There is also repetition with variation. We’ll cover that later as it is works in the context of equations.
[Heading 3] 1.15 Complete description of a value
[normal] Characterizing a trait we measure is as important as the measurements. The following is an example of characterizing an unknown source, where we have a dial to generate input and a meter to read output. This source will be linear, where the output value changes proportionally to the input. Of course not all traits will have linear values, and characterizing this is one of the main tasks of equations. This will also describe the limits of what is measurable of this source - it is much more common to only use the resolutions and ranges we care about.
[normal] A full description of a domain requires a minimum resolution (tick size), a maximum positive and negative range, a zero point, and a unit size. All of these can be described with directed segments (complex numbers). A domain also needs to belong to a trait, for example Celsius (a domain) belongs to the temperature trait. Any fully described value must belong to a fully described domain.
[normal] First we’ll consider the maximum range segment. Turning the dial all the way to the left, and then all the way to the right, will give us min/max readings. The meter might stop before the end, or it might reach the end before the dial is fully turned. It is always the meter that determines the domain (the output values), not of the capabilities of the measuring instrument. The limits of ranges do not have to be stated, just the ranges you care about. 32 bit integers go from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, and we can work with these even though we know there are numbers beyond this range.
[normal] Next we need a segment to measure the minimum distance that can be differentiated. We’ll call this a tick. Signals may well be coming in at a finer resolution, but because we can’t differentiate them this tick can not be subdivided. A tick is a segment, but it is a special case as it is the level where discrete changes are indistinguishable from continuous ones. Again, we usually limit this to a size we care about in a given context. Asking someone’s age has a tick size of years, not nanoseconds.
[normal] Lastly we need to choose a unit. This is somewhat arbitrary, but ideally it is somewhere where the resolution is informative, and the range is meaningful. If common values tend to cluster in an area it might be useful to locate zero there (like Celcius), other signals may make more sense to have zero at a natural start point (like Kelvin). An imperial tape measure has a unit of one inch, a tick size of 1/8th of an inch, and a range of 0-192 inches (16 feet, with feet and yards being optional units).
[normal] These three segments (tick, range, and unit) define the domain of a measurement. Now all values in this domain are meaningful. If later a tick is able to be more accurately measured, the same unit can just be split into more ticks. The existing values will not need to change, they just will be lower precision than newer values. The system can be similarly extended if values are eventually measured outside the existing range. Inversely, we can reduce precision in the same way. A tick can even be larger than a unit, such as when we use rounding. We say the population of a city is 750,000 (a tick of 50,000 and a unit of 1) to express approximation.
[normal] It may seem strange to couple all this domain information to a number, but domains are just like numbers – a context agnostic system to record information about magnitudes. Specifying ranges and units does not limit this domain system to specific categories, any more than counting seven apples ties our numbering system to fruit. Domains are just a more complete way of describing and relating values, with precision, ranges, and calibration.
[Heading 3] 1.16 Some Advantages
[normal] Before going deeper into equations, multiple dimensions, and concept encoding, it is worth looking at some of the practical advantages of using this number system rather than real numbers. Full disclosure, I’ve only used this system (while programming) for months, not years, so these thoughts are preliminary.
[normal] The main benefit to treating numbers as directed segments is the change in mindset it brings. With infinitely precise numbers we look for single correct answers, with flexible segments we try to narrow down possible truths. This is maps closely to how we learn and discover. These segments do not have to represent hard values at their endpoints either — they could just as easily represent a standard deviation. This mindset forces us to quantify our certainty, and avoid the hubris of a perfect true or false.
[normal] The fact that everything in this system can be expressed on a gradient makes iterating towards a result straight forward. This includes the traits themselves, the resolution, the maximum ranges and the value ranges. It also makes conversion of domains within a trait simple and accurate. There is also a clear path to combining simple traits into new traits, in non linear ways. E.g. the size and color traits of a context can be mathematically joined to express “apples can be red or green, and green apples tend to be larger”.
[normal] As a programmer, this system can be thought of as ‘typed numbers’ (something I’ve always wanted). A value range  belongs to a domain, which belongs to a trait (a range, in Celsius, measuring temperature). It becomes impossible to accidentally add a temperture to a counter, and temperture values can have custom methods that only relate to temperature. That said, it is still simple to convert across domains (C->F) with adapters, and across traits, by using the evaluated complex number. At the trait level, things can still be converted and compared with other traits. This allows metamorphical reuse of transformations, something fundamental to both math and language.
[normal] This system goes further with programming. Many common errors simply go away. Divide by zero is no longer an error, 4/0 just becomes a segment greater than the number of ticks in 4. If the domain has 10 ticks per unit, 4/0 is a segment from 40 1/10 to max. Null errors in math go away because ‘true zero’ (nothing selected) only exists in addition. For multiplication or repetition, we are using a selection, and these are methods on selections. If there is no selection there is no method available. Precision and auto conversion is simple for simple cases, and can be automatically learned from more complex data. Definitions of equality can be fully articulated, accuarte and bounded by defined precisions. All numbers and domains become fully differentiable. Continuous (floats) and discrete (ints) are combined into one system where ticks are continuous, and units are discrete. The list goes on.
[normal] In math, considering complex number to be one dimensional directed segments will at least make some visualizations possible that are currently limited (three complex numbers can be visualized in 3D space, where currently 2 complex numbers require four dimensions). Adding precision and type to numbers saves storing those things in the metadata of symbol chooses and footnotes. The advanced areas of many math domains end up with a version of complex numbers involved. Viewing existing domains of math with directed range rather than exact values could make many difficult concepts simpler to reason about.
[normal] While I know very little of physics, so much of it seems to use complex numbers as the primitive value. Oscillations, harmonics and rotations are the natural language of these directed segments over time. It seems like a better fit from a distance at least.
[normal] Lastly, and maybe most importantly, I feel this system adapts well to the much more abstract calculations of language and thought. It is very comfortable with the low precision of terms like warm and cool. The context of the statement is also quantifiable and diffable, so saying warm in an Arizona summer or Manitoba winter expects different ranges. Surprise can be a simple diff of what is expected in context. And key, concepts can be defined with ranges on a large number of traits, and context can be applied by filtering these expectations. This could lead to an encoding of concepts that is independent of language.
[normal] Lots of work to be done.
[Heading 3] <in progress>
[Heading 3] Equations
[Heading 3] 2.1 Repetition with Variation
[normal] All prediction is grounded in repetition. Some repetition is direct, such as the repeating +1 in 12345, or the repeating *2 in 25. Symmetry is repetition with reflections and translations. Patterns are repetition with variation. Repetition can be nested, self reflecting and recursive. Even unchanging measures can be described as repeated +0s or *1s. Because repetition is at the heart of all prediction, all ‘questions’ in mathematics are at some level trying to discover repetition.
[normal] Within a domain, there are some natural repetitions. A unit additively repeated the maximum range number of times gives counting up, and results in the maximum value of the domain. Additively repeating ticks by the number of ticks per unit gives us the unit. These are obvious, but repeated multiplication is more interesting. Taking the unit (the multiplicative identity) plus a tick and repeatedly multiplying that ticks-per-unit times gives us something like 2.71828, which is Euler’s number. This value comes up whenever you look at continuous compounding change – repetition that takes into account previous results. The same operation with a unit minus a tick gives us the reciprocal of e, 1/e. These operations are not infinitely repeating, they repeat to the limit of the resolution chosen.
[normal] Incidentally, repeated multiplication now allows us to have non-linear motion, where values changes are linked to the number line at rates other than zero (addition) or one (multiplication).
[normal] Combining additive and multiplicative repetition gives patterns like 1*2*3*4*5, known as five factorial (plus 1 times total, five times), written as 5!. This is a key series in statistics and information theory, as it represents all possible variations of a set of elements. For example, there are 120 ways (5! ways) to combine 5 different letters. Notice how this series reference the iteration index of the repetition, where notation could be something like (index)*5.
[normal] A power series also references the iteration index, for example ex is (xindex/index!)+number of iterations. Fibonacci is a sequence that references previous results, something like (two results ago+last result)+number of iterations. Repetition may require some aspects to be constant and others to be variable with a pattern – a pattern that also involves repetition.
[normal] Patterns that repeat can also be described with reflections or cycles. When we think of a bead on a wire, there are two possible repeating motions - it could move back and forth, or the wire could loop allowing it to cycle. One dimensional paths are typically defined as lines, but a path can be curved, it just can’t have forks. The loop path simply joins its tip to its tail, making cycles easier to visualize. It does not follow that these cycles need to be circular, and even if presented as circular it is still one dimensional. This also makes clear that even though we commonly view repetition as multiples of whole numbers, you can have partial repetition. You can easily go part way through a cycle if it has the resolution.
[normal] While beads on wires are intuitive, we know from our close study of segments as complex numbers above that there are actually four directions in one dimension. In bead terms, this would be like having a bead with a red and blue side, and being able to flip the bead - Imagine being able to remove the bead, a flattened loop, or a mobius double circle wire. In wealth/debt terms there is increasing wealth, increasing debt, decreasing wealth and decreasing debt. Segments will naturally cycle through these directions (1,i,-1,-i…) when repeatedly multiplied by a segment with a non-zero start point. It is very informative to look at cyclic systems in math and science as segments bouncing and cycling around paths. Things like the Fourier transforms, electromagnetic waves, or even tessellating patterns of wallpaper can all be described as cycling and reflecting segments. This is not the place to explore various branches of math in terms of segments, but it is a very useful exercise.
[normal] The last category of repetitions we’ll discuss here are symmetries. Creating symmetries is easy, simply repeat a series of operations with or without variation. Symmetry in one dimension can repeat, invert, reflect, or reflect invert, Like pbqd (again, 1, i, -1, -i). Finding the series of nested operations and repetition that can turn p into qqdbpp reveals much about the abstract structures of transformations. These symmetries turn up over and over in mathematics (Galois theory, group theory, topology), and indeed the real world.
[normal] Any mathematical operation or combinations of operations can be repeated. This includes selection, addition, scaling, evaluation, and repetition itself. This repetition can have variation, and these variations also have patterns formed by repetition. We have many ways to signify repetition, using exponents, Σ, ∏, or even just repeating notation, however it is more useful to consider all of these simply repetition of operations. Ultimately we can encode the number of repeats in the same way we record ranges, units and values - with segments.
[Heading 3] Selection and Evaluation
[normal] Addition, multiplication and repetition form the core of equations, but it is helpful to also have selection and evaluation as specific steps. These last steps on the face are things that only life can do, but they should be taken as more general concepts. If we calculate a trajectory for a rock falling off a cliff, the rock is ‘selected’ in the sense that the equation is focused on it. The rock will still fall without the focus, and the trajectory would be the same. Likewise if it strikes another rock on the way down, it can be thought of as evaluating some intersecting path, and ‘selecting’ the second rock. Selection in the broad sense isn’t possible without evaluation, and evaluation isn’t possible without selection, so these are intertwined concepts.
[normal] Even when doing something as trivial as adding apples to a bag, the apples must be selected before being added. A selection operation also has a reciprocal, which is everything not selected. The only true zero in mathematics is to select nothing, and its reciprocal is the closest we have to infinity  – to not select everything. Selection as a step is important because we need to specifically reselect elements in any repeat operation. It is obvious in the fibonacci sequence that we are reselecting previous results, but even in simple counting we are selecting the previous total before adding one. This does mean equations need access to the result stack, the iteration index, the original equation and any partial or nested results. Because all of these have linear order, they can be expressed along a gradient, and therefore can be selected with a segment. The selection segment can be part of the equations or even derived from a result. Lastly an equation can terminate on a condition or when it runs out of material to select.
[normal] Evaluation in this context means comparing segments. This can be boolean operations over ranges, perhaps testing if two segments overlap anywhere, everywhere, or nowhere. There are prepositional tests, for in front, behind, between, near. There is comparing lengths, offsets, scales, growth rates, or patterns of any sort. When looking at all the styles of comparison, you can see that they are similar to equations themselves. Asking if one segment is longer than another is akin to asking if a positive scaling could make it the same length (without needing to know exactly what scale would be needed). Because of this evaluation can also be expressed as expressions, which can be expressed as segments.
[Heading 3] Equations
[normal] Full equations consist of selection, transformation (appending or stretching), repetition, and evaluation. All of these steps can be expressed as segments on a gradient (a fully defined domain). In a sense an equation is a fully defined number. It represents a value, a transformation, and recipe that can be applied to other values.
[normal] There is an advantage to having all values and operations of an equation expressible as segments. A common format allows incremental changing, testing and improvement across all parts of an equation when searching for solutions. It also allows different aspects of an equation to influence the result, like when the iteration index creates future selections from the result stack. Techniques used in machine learning, from gradient descent to attention networks are very well suited to manipulating. While these will eventually allow us to quantify and even predict the behavior of a single sensor (one dimension), understanding the world requires us to do the same with many such sensors, all combining and interacting in semi-predictable ways.
[Heading 3] Multiple Domains
[normal] At this point, we receive another sensor. Again we don’t know what it represents, we may have heat and pressure, length and width, or second pixel for a microorganism. We can now explore how two separate domains can interact.
[normal] Our math so far was one dimensional, segments interacting in a single domain. Most situations involve more than one type of information. This second signal can be redundant, related, or independent. Redundant means one signal can fully predict the other, such as one reading in Celcius and the other in Fahrenheit, so no new information. This would be characterized by two parallel domains, perhaps with different units. Related signals would be where one partially defines the other, perhaps only for some ranges, or in conjunction with additional domains. Youth and beauty for example. Lastly the signals may be completely orthogonal, changes in one are fully independent of changes in the other. Length and width are examples of this, at least in the abstract. Redundant signals can be converted with the math in the last section, and related signals will be explored when we have more than two signals. This leaves independent signals.
[normal] Apart from being able to compare values on different domains, domains can be combined into ‘2D’ domains. It is useful to think of 2D as ‘2 domains’ rather than 2 dimensions. This wording makes ‘99D’ objects feel very natural. The difference between 2 domains and a 2D domain is that 2D domains are combined to give an area. A foot measures a distance, a pound measures weight, but foot pounds measure work (just as newtons and meters measure joules). Length and width measure perpendicular distances, and area measures their combination.
[normal] Like with segment values where the unot value is set to zero, it is common to normalize these domain combinations by setting one domain to be the unit. This can be seen with meters per second, or miles per gallon. Zero based segments and a unit domain allow these combinations to be expressed as a single value, but this is not the full picture. 1D values (segments) have a unot start value and a unit end value which are also segments. 2D values (areas) have a unot start values and unit end areas, which are also areas. This is best understood geometrically.
[normal] Two independent signals can be represented by making the two domains perpendicular, similar to the familiar x/y axes. Moving a value up and down the vertical domain does not move its position along the horizontal, and vice versa. Each of these domains still support all existing segment operations independently, just that there is now a new 2D connected ‘area domain’. Traditionally we create an area by making a segment starting from zero on each axis, and joining them into a rectangle. We consider each width and height segment to have zero area, and the rectangle to have width*height area. There is a lot wrong with this, in spite of getting the correct area answer. Looking at the mechanics in terms of domains and segments helps us see the motivations and shortcomings.
[normal] To join these, we traditionally make a rectangle with the coordinates and count up the area. In domain terms, each domain is duplicated (or ghosted?) and moved to align with a point on the opposite domain. The domains are then connected to each other. If we take the vertical axis to represent 6 miles (a line from 0 to 6), and the horizontal to be 3 hours (a line from zero to 3), the rate is determined by a diagonal arrow from zero to the top right corner. It has a a slope of 6/3, or 2 miles per hour. It isn’t clear what the filled in area represents. If 2 mph is the maximum speed, 6 miles in 1 hour is not achievable, even though it is part of the shaded rectangle. It may represent the maximum time and distance independently, but there would be no extra value presenting these as an area. Things went from 0 area to 18 area, from 2 domains to 4 domains, and a number of new joining rules were created. Something was created from nothing, more than once even.
[normal] Joining the same 6 miles and 3 hours using domains and segments clarify not only the geometry, but the meaning of this area. First, a segment viewed in 2D does not have zero area. There are no infinitely small lines, so a line viewed in 2D must have at least tick height. If we assume 10 ticks per unit, multiplying (0i+6)*(0i+3) = (0i+18), or a line one tick tall and 180 ticks wide (180 square ticks). We expect multiplying 3*6 in joined domains to also create an area of 180 ticks (18 square units), and indeed it does. Next we know from segment math that multiplying one segment by another requires combining the two start points, the two end points, and the two sets of start/end points. In the case of 3*6, there are only end points that are non zero, so we can combine them directly. The area isn’t created linearly like with 1D multiplication, so the scaling ‘pressure’ doesn’t scale the values, it just fills the area between them. This creates a triangle, that is half the solution. As with segment multiplication, we need to create both unit and unot endpoints. To get a unit area, we convert all the values to units, and for a unot area we convert all the values to unots. In this case, 3 and 6 are both already end points (units), and the unot points are both zero unots which is equivalent to zero units. Thus the initial triangle is in units. To get the unot triangle, we must first convert all points to unots. The zeros are already unots, and the unit values 3 and 6 become -3i and -6i. This triangle forms the unot area, and together they are the solution. You can think of these as a start area and end area, or a clockwise area and counterclockwise one.
[normal] Implied in this simple multiplication of 2D domains (simple because both segments were zero based) is we can also multiply point segments, segments pointing towards zero like (-6i+0), and non zero segments like (3i+4). It isn’t clear how you would declare this intent in regular area calculations, nor what those calculations would look like. Moving from 1D to 2D is a very crucial step, so we’ll go over a few examples with interpretations.
[normal] Imagine an electric car and its charge status. The car can go in forward or reverse (+ or -), and it can drive towards work or towards home (unit or unot). Home to work is a path, not a line, but as we only care about the distance it can be characterized as a line. Home will be left in this example, and work on the right. A segment describing a morning commute will start at zero (no miles driven towards home) and end at 10 (work is 10 miles away). If you get half way and realize you forgot your keys, you turn around (towards home) drive 5 miles, then turn back to work and drive 10. This creates a segment that starts at 5i and goes to 15. If for some reason you returned home driving backwards instead of turning around, it would be a segment from 0i to 10 again. The segment length measures the net distance driven forward regardless of direction, so turning around is net 20 miles. Each point of the segment measures the net position driven in each direction (towards work and towards home). Finally, if you drove all the way to work in reverse, you would have a segment that went from 10 to zero, or -10i+0. This means you faced the home direction (unot) and drove backwards 10 miles. A segment from 4 to 10 (-4i+10) could be interpreted as you started 14 miles from work, drove 4 miles in reverse to your home, then turned around and drove the normal 10 miles to work.
[normal] Lastly, notice how driving 4 miles in the unot direction is similar to driving backwards for 4 miles (-4 miles) in the unit direction. To convert a normal line (unot to unit, 4i+10) into a segment of only units, you need a segment with a net 6 miles of change that still ends up ten miles forward. This can be expressed as a segment from -4 to +10, where the positive and negative values aren’t evaluated (4 miles driven, or from 4 to 10, where the negative value has been removed.
[normal] Likewise, the same segment expressed as a fully unot segment would be 10i to 0i to 4i, reduced to an undirected unot segment between 10i and 4i. In this way the segment 4i+10 can be decomposed into a 10i,4i segment and a 4,10 segment.
[normal] The clearer the meaning of these segments are, the easier their area will be to interpret. If it is still confusing, imagine different scenarios, with subway trains between stations, with heaters and AC, with wealth and debt, hungry and full, or any others you can think of. Not all values have natural negatives or inversions so it is perfectly fine to use zero based segments. But remember, you can place the unit anywhere (like Celsius vs Kelvin), so any measure can turn into segments with two directions.
[normal] Our first segment is distance, and the second is charge. Charging your car by plugging it in adds potential (more charging increases charge), whereas using it is the inverse (more usage decreases potential). We’ll arbitrarily label ‘charging’ the unit and ‘usage’ the unot. The negative of a plugged in car would be the car helping to power the house, and the negative of using charge while driving the car would be regenerative braking or going downhill. Adding 100 kilowatt hours (kWh) of charge from the wall would be a segment going from 0 to 100. Later driving off 50kWh would now be a segment from -50 to 100 (50i+100). A case where you power your house with 20kWh, and then drive downhill to generate 30kWh (maybe you live on a mountain) creates a segment pointing left, from 30 to -20 (-30i-20). Lastly, as always, it is possible to convert units to unots if needed, 20kWh of charging is equivalent to -20kWh of usage - plugging in is akin to driving downhill. The segment remains in the same position, it is just interpreted from the opposite direction. We will need to do this with area calculations, so it is worth being comfortable with the idea.
[normal] Now to areas. This operation may seem counterintuitive at first, but it is just connecting all points as units to create a unit area, then connecting all points as unots to create a unot area.

===== Math backup.docx =====
[normal] Everything that can be done with a segment on a line
[normal] A line is like a path that can extend in each direction. A line has a width, but we are only considering the 1D aspect of it, so any width, height, or other surroundings are ignored. Lines have two directions, and we can choose one to be forward and the other backwards.
[normal] A trait can always be represented by a line. Traits are properties that have magnitudes ordered from lowest to highest in a linear progression. Once calibrated, the line represents the lowest and highest known values for the trait. If values are discovered beyond the limits of the line, it can be extended or made more precise.
[normal] This line does not have to be straight. We are only considering one dimension, but it could be a curvy line, the edges of a polygon, a satellite's orbit, or a path through the woods. The shape of this line is significant when it represents repetition or symmetries.
[normal] A focal segment is a segment of any achievable length on this line. The segment has a start point, and end point, so it can point forward or backwards. Note that points are also  segments, just they are the width of the smallest possible resolution.
[normal] A line with segments on it represents everything that can happen in one dimension. Because this is such a fundamental object, we will try to exhaustively enumerate all the unique operations that can be done with it.
[normal] Select
[normal] This can be done choosing an existing segment, or creating a new one. Creating a new segment can be done manually or algorithmically. The segment represents what has been selected.
[normal] Direction
[normal] Every trait has a linear progression of magnitudes, and every segment has a start point and end point. This means the segments have information about which direction they are pointing - low to high, high to low, or can’t tell (a point). Note this has nothing to do with how the trait line is drawn - the line could be vertical or circular. It is better to imagine the line going from red to blue, with the segment’s end point either redder or bluer than the start point. Neither red nor blue represent forward - that is defined elsewhere.
[normal] Repeat
[normal] Whatever we do, we can do again. If we select something, we can select a second thing. And a third. The same goes for any actions we do. Geometrically, repetition can be represented by multiple segments on a line, a line that joins onto itself (like a polygon or circle), or going back and forth along segments. Repetition is the second fundamental action in math, after selection. All patterns, and therefore all predictions are based on forms of repetition. In normal math, repetition is (in a very limited way) expressed using exponents.
[normal] Repetition implies steps done in order. This brings in the new dimension of time. Everything in the universe is in constant motion, so all things naturally exist in the time dimension.
[normal] Count
[normal] Being able to create more than one segment (using repetition) results in being able to count. Segments do not have to be the same length to count them - each segment acts as its own unit. We count segments without regard to length (half a segment is still a segment). This means we can only count whole numbers at this point.
[normal] The only 'natural' counting order is when the number of elements change over time. This is because time has a single fixed direction causing events in sequence. If we see a number of elements all at once, we must impose a counting system on them. Without a system, we can't keep track of what is already counted and what isn't.
[normal] With the tools so far, counting has to be addition by one (1+1+1+1=4). The ability to separate elements into groups while counting is important though. It bootstraps the idea of merging more than one element at a time into a total, also known as addition.
[normal] Addition
[normal] Addition of segments is the joining of two groups that have already been counted. In normal math, we think of whole number addition as the algorithm we preform in order to not have to recount everything. These are great skills to know, and probably among the most important inventions we’ve ever made. But it is important to remember that addition is really the joining of two groups of elements that we are able to count. There are a lot more decisions involved in joining two groups than adding two numbers, and they are all important at different times.
[normal] Sometimes when we add to an ordered set, we care more about the resulting set than the total. For example adding C,E to A,B,D we might expect A,B,C,D,E rather than ((C,E),(A,B,D)). Or we might want to copy the second set into the first, keeping the original. We might have counted each set differently, so need to clarify how the result should be ordered. We may want to ignore duplicates. All of this falls under addition.
[normal] When combining two groups into one, we gain clarification by filtering information that isn’t relevant to our task. This is a choice, and what is useful is context sensitive. As always, there are insights to be had whenever we notice we are making a choice, so it is important to keep a broad view of what something as fundamental as addition actually represents.
[normal] Note that with all this information so far, we still can’t count backwards or subtract.
[normal] Subtraction
[normal] At its most basic, subtraction is removing from a selection. If it is an ordered selection we are removing from, we traditionally remove from the ‘end’, or remove randomly and reinterpret the results. If we add 4 oranges to a bag (1,2,3,4), and then remove one, the remaining oranges could be (1,3,4). We usually consider oranges in a bag to be unordered, so we would either reinterpret the removed orange to be the fourth one resulting in (1,2,3), or reinterpret the oranges (1,3,4) to be (1,2,3). We would call this a bag of three oranges when focused on the unordered total, but if asked to count them we would have no trouble pointing to a first, second and third, in some order.
[normal] This may seem like hair splitting, but there are certainly cases where sets of things are ordered, and we want to delete a certain member. In these situations (1,3,4) is not the same as (1,2,3). It is important to keep a broad view of what subtraction actually is, or it will be hard to understand it in less intuitive situations. Subtraction is the removal of specified elements from a group. How elements are specified can be as important as how many are specified.
[normal] With ordered counts (like discrete numbers), it is tempting to define subtraction as just counting backwards, but that wouldn’t cover cases where you subtract one group’s count from another’s. Counting backwards with a one to one correspondence is closer, but we still need to define what ‘backwards’ means here. If we used a heuristic for ordered counting (like say smallest to largest) then we can reverse it (largest to smallest). One can imagine ways of subtracting by counting backwards with this set, but there are many other ways to get a one to one correspondence with set elements.
[normal] Corresponding elements can always have multiple interpretations here as there are multiple ways of defining how things should correspond. Traditionally this is just one to one for each element in its given order. But as with addition, there are many branches of mathematics where the identity of each element in a calculation matters more than its result. We also can run into a problem this correspondence method - we sometimes want to subtract more elements than exist in the target set.
[normal] Negatives
[normal] We can now add and subtract groups of segments using correspondence, however there is an unresolved problem when we try to subtract more elements than exist in the original set. There are two ways to think about these negative numbers. The first is they are selections that have been made, but not yet fulfilled. The second is they are positive selections, but of an opposite thing. For example a person could have ‘negative ten dollars’ or have ‘positive ten dollars of debt’. These are not two ways of saying the same thing.
[normal] The ‘negative operation’ mirrors a value at zero, so 5 dollars becomes -5 dollars. Adding 1 dollar here will still make you richer. This is what negative means.
[normal] The ‘debt operation’ mirrors the whole perspective of that +1 means without changing any values. The value is still 5, but it is of debt instead of credit. Adding 1 dollar (of debt) makes you poorer.
[normal] Negation is the operation that mirrors values. A negative number is mirrored around zero, and subtraction is addition of such a negative number. For example 5-3 is 5 plus three mirrored around zero (-3). Negation is not the second option, the one that mirrors the number line itself. More on this crucial point later.
[normal] Unit
[normal] Once a segment is selected, it can be used as a unit. So far have been using every segment as its own unit, which is how we can count them. As noted, these units do not have to be the same length. These types of units are very common, we do not expect three dogs to have the same weight, and we know three months does not mean each contains the same amount of days. This makes precise comparisons impossible - we have no way of dividing units, and we can’t say a single unit 1/3 is the length of three other units with any confidence.
[normal] What we are sure of is each unit (segment) has a start point and an end point. Traversing these, there is no unit at the start, and there is one unit by the end. Numerically this means the start point is zero, and the end point is one. The other number we can imagine here is -1. Negative one uses the same unit, but with the end point (1) mirrored around the start point (0). Again we don’t know anything about the true length of this negative segment (it could be millimeters or it could be miles), just it is the same length as the original segment. For both +1 and -1 the unit is pointing in the same positive direction. Think about what it would mean to have a negative unit.
[normal] Compare
[normal] Every segment is its own unit, but to compare things we need a calibration unit. There is no ‘correct’ calibration unit - comparisons are always relative, and any segment can be compared with any other. With addition and and a calibration unit we can now produce fractions. For example we could add the calibration unit to itself 5 times to form segment A, and then make segment B by adding the calibration unit to itself 60 times. We can now compare A to B because they use the same units, The first segments is 5:60 the length of the second, or 1/12th.
[normal] If we are given a segment of arbitrary length, we can find its ratio to the calibration segment using similar strategies. For example we could add copies of the shorter of the two until is it longer segment, then add copies the other segment until it is the longer one. Eventually the two segments will be the same length, to whatever level of precision measured. The ratio will be the number of calibration units to the number or arbitrary segment units.
[normal] Note that if we change the calibration unit to be the second segment, the only thing that changes is the order of the ration. So 5:60 (1/12th) would become 60:5 (12). This is the reciprocal, which is the neutralizing operation for a comparison. Anytime something is 12 time larger, something else is 12 time smaller. Like select and unselect, add and subtract, or negative and positive, comparisons have an ‘anti-comparison’. Every operation has a neutralizing operation, because energy is always conserved.
[normal] Jump and Slide
[normal] A point on a line can only be selected, unselected, or moved. Selecting multiple times is duplicating or counting up, while deselecting multiple times is deleting or counting down. Addition and subtraction encode selecting and deselecting. Moving a selection is a continuous operation, the equivalent of sliding. We can move the whole segment along the line, or just move the start or end point. Any motion will change the position of a segment, and changing an end point will also change the length. All motion is encoded with multiplication (including it’s reciprocal, division). Multiple moves are encoded with powers, which we will address later.
[normal] We can imagine a move to be a jump or a slide, which represent discrete or continuous motion. When looking closer though, a ‘jump’ move tends to be a continuous one that we ignore the middle part, or a new selection. It is useful to remember that at the limit of our resolution, continuous motion appears as a series of discrete steps. Conversely, every discrete distance can be traversed with a continuous motion. We can only be certain an operation is discrete if there is a known location between the start and end of a move, and the motion does not pass through it. We know 5 exists between 3 and 8, so if we move from 3 to 8 and don’t pass through 5, we know at least some part of the move was a discrete jump. This type of jump can only happen with selection, which means it can only happen with addition. For a real world example of such a jump, imagine selecting a six pack of juice boxes, then changing your mind and selecting a 24 pack. At no point were there 7 or 8 juice boxes selected, so this would be a jump, and therefore addition. We subtracted 6 and added 24. We did not multiply 6 by 4 because the transition wasn’t continuous.
[normal] When sliding segments or points we move through all the positions between the start and end positions. Imagine a segment from 0 to 2, and we slide it’s endpoint to 4. It is now twice as long, so we have multiplied (scaled) it by two. Note that we still have one segment, and it is still the same segment. In addition we start with the same segment of length 2, but then add a second segment of length 2. We can select both as a new single selection (we are assuming we place them tip to tail here), and have a segment of length 4. This is a new selection that was created from two selections. This is very different than stretching a segment, and the difference is crucial.
[normal] When selecting, we can select nothing, so zero is a valid value. When stretching, we need to stretch a selection, so the operation does nothing if nothing is selected. Conversely if a segment is selected and we stretch it to ‘zero’, it is still a segment. We can no longer say how long it is (it is by definition beyond our ability to measure), but we know it is there, and we know it has a start and end point. We also know if we stretch it larger it will eventually come back. If it was a series of segments that formed dashes, they will come back as the same dashes. Sliding elements never destroys them, which is why we can move and endpoint from +5 to -5 (through zero) and not have our segment disappear forever.
[normal] The other difference with selection and motion (addition and multiplication) is a selection does not need to be of the same elements. We started by selecting segments of different lengths, but we could even select segments of different lines (remember, lines are traits), or segments on completely different objects. It feels natural to select (add) 4 apples and 3 oranges, but it is less obvious how we would multiply 4 apples by 3 oranges. More on this later.
[normal] Geometric Interpretation
[normal] In the real world the segments we measure (property ranges) on paths (traits) aren’t usually lined up neat and straight. In spite of that, it’s still useful to have a clear and simple geometric interpretation. For the next few sections we’ll build this interpretation, but remember this is a useful abstraction, not a necessity nor a reflection of reality. When comparing two people’s hair length, we do not have to remove all their hair and line each strand up straight, tip to tail.
[normal] Measurement and Snap
[normal] As points on a segment slide along a trait, they can snap to other existing points. Like always, this isn’t an infinitely perfect overlap, just an overlap so close we can’t tell which point would be to the left and which to the right. With this we can line up multiple segments to easily measure the full length. It is also easier to imagine merging multiple segments into a single one, as we have been implying with addition. Lastly when stretching elements, it is easy to imagine moving a units endpoint to snap to the endpoint of a second element. All of these operations could be done with measuring, but it is more obvious what is happening with these mental models. This makes further abstraction possible, which leads to further understanding.
[normal] Add and Subtract Lengths
[normal] One can imagine snapping the start and end points to other segment points as you select or slide them. With snapping, a unit selected multiple times (multiple copies) allows adding and subtracting by length rather than just counting. Just take all the units, place them tip to tail, and measure. With the ability to compare units, we can also add segments of different lengths - put them all tip to tail, and measure how many times the unit fits into the total length.
[normal] This tip to tail sorting also deletes any whitespace and overlap information between the segment’s original positions. This is a simplification that we normally do in math, but eventually we will need to understand how to work with these gaps as well.
[normal] Repeated Add and Subtract
[normal] We can repeat selections which allows counting, and we can group selections. This means we can also repeatedly select a group. So 3+3+3+3=12. This is considered multiplication in normal math, but this is NOT multiplication because it is made of multiple selections rather than stretching a single segment. The final number is the same, but this is jumping from value to value rather than moving through all possible intermediate values. In 1D this could be a series of points rather than a line, and in 2D it could be a grid of points rather than an area. We usually write this as 3*4=12, but that confuses it with stretching. In fact it is addition repeated, so in exponent form it is  (+3)⁴, where stretching is (*3)⁴.
[normal] Stretch Segments
[normal] Segments can be stretched by moving their endpoints. This allows resizing a segment without needing a new selection. Segments can be resized into precise ratios of a unit. For example, take two unit sized segments, arrange them tip to tail, and then stretch them down to a total length of one unit. Each segment will now be half a unit. They stretched from one unit to half a unit. Also notice the unit itself is now be twice their length. It didn’t stretch at all, but it’s being compared to segments that did. We could have also stretched the unit up to be the size of the two segments. This is a different operation, but our final ratios would not change because all comparisons are relative. All rational numbers (fractions) can be created this way.
[normal] Our normal multiplication is always about stretching, but stretching is not limited to multiplication. It does not even need to involve comparisons or ratios. Imagine a segment that we only know the end point. If we move that end point (and thus stretch the segment) farther along the line, say by three units, it will change size. We still do not know the total length, we just know it is 3 units longer than it was. Of course the ratio of the full segment to the unit has changed, but we aren’t focused on that. This type of move is the same as adding to the end, except for the key fact that is this is a ‘continuous add’. There was motion here, it wasn’t a discrete jump like when you add a segment of three units. A stretch always passes through intermediate points on the way to its destination. Most importantly a stretch always adds or subtracts, continuously, from the total length of a segment.
