[normal] Comparing separate things is the heart of math. Every object is defined as a collection of traits with their probable ranges and relations. The only things that can be measured are these traits, and these measurements are used to separate things into categories we care about. In order to have two things to measure, the two things must have some trait that is separable. It may be at a different location, or measured at a different time, but at least one trait being separable is the first requirement for making a comparison. If there isn’t this, then there is only one discernable object.
[normal] Once we have two separate measures, they may be too close to know which is greater, or they may just be within some tolerance. When we can’t tell the difference, or don’t care about the difference, then we have equality. This doesn’t mean they are the same, just that we consider them equal in measure. We might have two eggs, one slightly larger, but we don’t consider this to be 0.9 or 1.1 eggs because our defined valid egg sizes are a range. Someone can make 100 dots on a paper, but we can only count them correctly if they are all in different locations. If there are 100 dots one on top of the other and we need to count them correctly, we devise testable ways of doing this, and from then on we have a new ability to see past our previous resolution. Much of science is looking for ways to improve our resolution - to move past an ‘equality’ that we feel is separable.
[Heading 3] Things diffuse from high concentrations to low
[normal] This is the second law of thermodynamics, total entropy can never decrease. Significantly, there is such a thing as high and low, greater and less, before and after – and there is a natural direction for these. A lot of what we care about, in fact life itself, is organizing against local entropy, so our natural ‘positive’ directions tend to be against entropy (build vs destroy, assemble vs disperse, grow vs wilt). Time itself has this direction, as well as cause and effect, which is important for continuous systems.
[normal] In one dimension, when something diffuses from a point it creates a line moving in both directions. In two dimensions it creates a circle, and in three dimensions a sphere. This is easy to visualize when imagining a hot spot dissipating from the center of a rod, a sheet of metal, or a large space. This makes a two direction line, a circle and a sphere the unrestricted default shapes for these dimensions. It is helpful to characterize all measurements of traits with these kinds of observations. For example time is one dimensional and only diffuses forward, so its default is a one directional line. Color can be thought of as three dimensional (RGB), and one can model its natural directions and diffusions in various helpful ways.
[normal] Discrete things are a collection of continuous ranges, one or more. Continuous things are discrete things that can be stretched.
[Heading 3] Everything is relative
[normal] There is no way to measure something without comparing it to something else. Imagine you exist alone floating in dark space. Would you have any idea how big you are? You would know your leg is larger than your arm, and your teeth are harder than your tongue, but you would have no idea how large you are overall.
[normal] There are no standard correct units of measure, so what we choose as a unit is a matter of convenience, and we can change that at will. Saying your arm is 3 times longer than your hand can just as correctly be stated as your hand is ⅓ as long as your arm. In fact it asserts it. Units are the primitive components of measure, and there is much to learn from exploring them exhaustively.
[Heading 3] Nothing is infinite
[normal] There is not one thing in the universe that we know to be infinitely small, infinitely large, or infinitely anything. There never has been an infinite number or infinite decimal places used in a calculation, by person or machine. You can not imagine infinity, but you can imagine you can imagine infinity. This makes it a concept, and you can do math on concepts. But you can’t do math with infinity.
[normal] Using infinity as a primitive feature of math was a mistake. It isn’t just because the primitives we use for proving the ‘truth’ of math contain a lie (an infinitely small point on an infinitely long line, or the infinite precision of real numbers). It is because it has led us to incorrect expectations, and obscured useful truths.
[normal] If we accept the reality that everything we can measure in the universe is bounded on the high and low sides, our math becomes about segments, confidences and probabilities. We look at what happens at the ends - do things just end, do they transform, do they fade or lose meaning, do they move beyond our ability to measure them? Much of the work of math, engineering and science is to explore these ends, quantify them, and discover ways of moving past them. There is much to be learned by acknowledging the world is finite, and calibrating our tools accordingly.
[normal] If there is infinite precision, we seek absolute truths. When this proves impossible we imagine the world a construct of our imaginations, the laziest thought a person can have. In reality, we are always trying to bound the truth, and narrow that bounds through effort, perseverance, imaginative and critical thinking.
[normal] Math that is not centered on infinity is larger, richer, correct, and wide open for discovery and innovation.
[Heading 3] Everything is changing, always
[normal] We can imagine something at absolute zero, where things become perfectly still, but in fact physics tells us that absolute zero is unattainable. Even at the ‘heat death of the universe’ things will not be still, its just energy would be so dispersed that it can’t do useful work. Remember energy can not be created or destroyed, and energy is always in motion at some level, it’s just that as it spreads out evenly there would no longer be gradients needed to do work.
[normal] This implies that math is always a dynamic system, even if we can snapshot things to get useful results. We may not care about the dynamic part, but we should be aware that a momentary equation is not the whole truth. Continuous systems with feedback are more complex, but are also more natural, much like a movie is more complex and more natural that a photo. We will learn more about the world with continuous feedback systems — our math should be built to naturally accommodate them.
[Heading 3] Traits are the primitives, not objects
[normal] Discrete things are made up of definitions. A definition is a probable range of a continuous thing. You can have a fraction of a discrete thing (half an apple), and you can count discrete things. The uncertainty with discrete objects is that the definitions are probable and dynamic, and therefore have ‘gray areas’. A small crab apple is probably an apple, but an apple bud is not. Any line that delineates an apple bud from an apple is an agreement on a definition. The same goes for apples themselves, and in fact any other object that exists.
[normal] Continuous things can not be divided into fractions - you can not have ‘half a length’ (a partial length is still a length) and it doesn’t make sense to ask ‘how many lengths are in a room’ without defining further what you mean by a length. Ultimately our ability to measure breaks down, or continuous things can end up discrete like grains of sand, so continuous does not mean infinite precision, it means continuous values at a certain level of precision.
[normal] Discrete things are defined collections of (continuous) trait ranges, one or more. Continuous things are traits of discrete things that can be stretched.
[normal] Therefore objects are made up of the probabilities of their traits. Some traits are more foundational than others, some have more variation than others, and which ones we focus on is also a matter of context. But certainly traits of objects are the primitives, and objects themselves the useful bundling of them.
[normal] Our math should reflect this. Counting is not the primitive operation, comparing magnitudes is. We can compare magnitudes without numbers — in fact the results of these comparisons is where numbers come from.
[Heading 3] Logic is universal
[normal] While logic can be derived from true or false (and thus bits), true or false themselves are results of comparisons. Comparisons of magnitudes are the primitive operations of this mathematical system, so logic flows directly from these. If a second magnitude is greater than a first one (measured true), and a third magnitude is greater than the second (measured true), then the third is also greater than the first (logically true).
[normal] There are certainly many ways of doing logic, and our rule set is certainly not the final word on it. But it is self consistent, and does seem to stand up to many inherent truths we observe. So it is, to the best of our understanding, universal. With the understanding that there is always room for improvement.
[Heading 3] Probability is universal
[normal] Probability is prediction of an unknown. When magnitudes move beyond our ability to measure them we can only characterize the possible results and their likelihoods, and then design new ways to test these expectations. Much of science is trying to discover things beyond our resolution. If math doesn’t contain infinitely large values, or infinitely precise measures, probability becomes an essential tool at the edges. It is important to characterize the ends of a measured segment - sometimes it is a simple termination, sometimes a transformation, sometimes a gradual change based on a definition. And very often it is something that passes our ability to measure, and we are unable to sense a pattern. At this point we must use probability to estimate what may lie beyond – a surprisingly powerful tool in this context.
[Heading 3] Symmetry is universal
[normal] Symmetry often implies bilateral symmetry, where one side mirrors the other. It isn’t just in life forms, but in any mirroring operation (negation), so it is a very fundamental operation in math as well. There is also ‘duality’ that seems to appear everywhere in math, with every operation having some sort of reciprocal or paired operation. Selecting something also ‘doesn’t select’ everything else. If a magnitude is 3 times larger than a unit, the ratio is ⅓ when making the larger object the unit. These ideas are found everywhere in higher geometry, logic and algebra, and may be as universal as ‘every action has an equal and opposite reaction’.
[normal] Symmetry is more general than reflection though. In 2D geometry there is also translation (non flipped motion) and rotation, as well as new symmetries built from combinations of these. These are most easily seen in ornamentation patterns used across all cultures since ancient times. They also play a large role in Group Theory. When there is a pattern, it implies there is some type of symmetry. Symmetry then becomes something held invariant while an operation repeats. Using these resulting objects in further patterns allows not only the generating of any pattern, but also a way of encoding predictions of patterns.
[normal] This broader idea of symmetry is the foundational element of operations, transformation, and indeed all predictable change.
[Heading 3] Binary is universal
[normal] The most basic operation when comparing things is to be able to tell one from the other. When measuring something, the measurement system breaks down when we can no longer separate readings. If there are a hundred dots on a piece of paper they can be counted, but if they are all made in the same spot counting becomes potentially impossible.
[normal] Every time we can separate one piece of information into two we double the information in that piece. Therefore the smallest piece of information in a system can be represented by a bit. Information theory shows us that things like compression, transmission, and existing information are also very important, but information is most naturally represented in bits.
[normal] This does not mean that decimal doesn’t work, or we can’t roll up bits into hexadecimal, just that the most natural system for measuring the world is binary. Other systems can work, but they are more likely to obfuscate truths, and make natural things seem unnatural.
[Heading 3] Complexity is inherent in simple things
[normal] Simple and straightforward rules can quickly turn into patterns, complexity, and even randomness when iterated. Emergent behavior can be completely uniform or impossible to predict. This implies the future doesn’t have to be knowable, calculations aren’t always calculable, and simple systems can break down at scale.
[normal] Take numbers, that can always add one to get the next one. It seems obviously infinite. But if you take a million to the power of a million a million times, you end up with a number so big that you can’t generate the next one. You can’t add numbers of that size, or take a random number between two of them. It would be hard to define anything about a number that still can be shown to hold at that scale, because it is so many times larger than all the plank lengths in the visible universe.
[normal] So while we can make rules and usefully use these to make predictions, we need to remember that these systems can also go their own way to defy perfect understanding. The world can be neat and orderly, and also chaotic and messy. That is why it is so interesting.
[Heading 3] Dimensions are traits
[normal] Dimensions are most easily imagined as spatial, 1D, 2D or 3D. However, anything measurable is a dimension, and every dimension is a unique and measurable trait. A ten dimensional object isn’t some impossible to imagine geometric abstraction, it’s simply an object where ten traits have been considered.
[normal] It is possible to define any object or concept using a collection of valid ranges of traits, and information on how those ranges relate to each other. There are obviously a lot of traits to choose from in the world, but we only care about a much smaller subset of them, and even then we only consider a few at a time depending on context and metaphor. In fact, context could be defined as the traits we are currently focusing on, and metaphor defined as transferring traits from one object to another.
[normal] Traits are always continuous at their discernible resolution, definitions are based on probability ranges of traits, and instances are based on the measured value of traits. It is possible to sample the traits of a limited number of instances to estimate the ranges and relations of traits for a category. More samples will refine the understanding of the category, but with this type of encoding good results can come from many fewer samples than traditional machine learning. Additionally, existing machine learning networks can be leveraged to measure and weight traits based on their utility to people. There is no need to hand craft these networks, but because they are interpable, they are able to be debugged and ‘taught’ without large scale retraining with new data.
[Title] What is the Human Part?
[normal] Some things are, to the best of our knowledge, universal - but that isn’t the whole story. We exist in a very local environment in this universe, and our intelligence is well adapted to it. Specifically we have gravity, ten fingers, a body that runs on food and desire, and a very strong social dynamic. The thing that really sets us apart from the impartial universe of atoms and galaxies is we are surrounded by life. Life is anti-entropy, an inverting of the natural order of energy itself. It requires a new layer over the pure math of physics, that has its own local rules. In our case, this math is the human layer.
[normal] Having our human perspective reflected in our math is not a mistake. It’s a continuously evolving way of adapting to the world and times we live in. The reason to separate it out from universal math is not to remove it. Rather it’s to better understand parts of the world that are, and are not, subject to the forces of our everyday experience.
[Heading 3] Base ten
[normal] We have ten fingers, so we mostly use base ten numbers. Babylonian calculation was based on tables of ratios, so they used a very divisible base 60 (sexagesimal). Mayans used base 20. But by and large we seem to prefer base 10 for everyday use, and certainly it is the dominant base in use today. Computers however use base two (binary), so it could be argued that we use binary for calculating, and translate to decimal for display. The Romans used the abacus for calculating, and translated to Roman numerals for display.
[Heading 3] Squares, angles and gravity
[normal] We consider squares and rectangles very core geometric shapes, more so than triangles or circles. This is because we live in a gravity field on a planet large enough that it seems flat. Anything that needs to stand up needs to be perpendicular to the surface, the rectangle is a very natural shape. 90 degree angles are certainly very important - the most a pair of lines can diverge from each other’s direction is 90 degrees. But four-sided figures require a lot of rules to define, and a lot of rules to specify how they change as lengths and positions change. Compare this with changing a circle’s radius, or the length of a triangle’s side. Ancient geometry is filled with triangles and circles, as they worked from minimum axioms, but it is good to keep in mind our bias to squares. For example, a length and a width naturally forms a triangle, not a rectangle.
[normal] Because of gravity we are also very aware of angles. This fits quite well with our perceptions, and we have extensive branches of mathematics presented in terms of angles. Angles ultimately represent ratios of traits, height to width in geometry, but any two traits can be compared and related in the same way. The phase angle of electricity uses trigonometry adapted from geometry when it is really just describing relations. The electricity won’t ‘fall down’ like a leaning building would, but our math evolved in gravity, and we use the tools we have.
[Heading 3] Poor non-linear intuition
[normal] Most aspects of our lives take place in a fairly linear way. Time ticks on, the world seems flat, dropped things don’t reach crazy speeds. This is sensible. If something grows or shrinks exponentially for too long it would replace everything else or disappear completely. Given that we exist, normal things aren’t going to have long term exponential growth. The result of living in this environment is that our intuition for exponential things is pretty weak. Perhaps our emotions are exponential, things like panic, rage and love. Maybe it’s how we deal with those rare instances of compounding stakes, not overreaction as much as exponential reaction.
[normal] There are many other areas of math that our intuition can easily mislead us. Things like probability, very small or large scales, emergent behavior, or even paradoxes and optical illusions, are all based on tricking our intuitions. And there are many more things that seem intuitive now but were anything but at the time of discovery. And many more we’ve gone back and forth on. Intuition is certainly baked into our minds, but it is also possible for us to adapt to new ideas so completely that they become intuitive for us. Here is a very human pattern - imagine an idea that seems counter intuitive, adapt it, and then remake the world to fit the idea. Sounds crazy, but what are currencies, national borders, video games or sports teams? They are ideas that have been made into real things with real consequences. We do the same in math, where some things are real and some are constructs, and we can’t tell which is which.
[normal] It is important that we use our intuition as it usually serves us well, but we shouldn’t encode it in the low levels of our tools. And we should get used to right answers derived from first principles not always ‘feeling right’. At least not at first.
[Heading 3] A sense of the divine
[normal] We can sense divinity, the all seeing, the all knowing, and it shapes how we see the world. This is one of our superpowers in fact - imagination, creativity and perseverance are directly linked to this faith in the unknown. It obviously helps us in many ways, but it does leave us with the impression that there are perfect answers to every question if we look hard enough. Our math, with its ‘infinite’ precision, and infinite expanses reinforces this.
[normal] In reality we are only ever narrowing the bounds of truth, not finding perfect answers. Recognizing this makes the world much more understandable, and our goals much more tractable. There are things we can confidently say are true because they are well within the bounds of what we know to be true. Other things are gray areas, and others are confidently false. That reality is neither perfection or ‘a pure construct of the mind’ feels right when paired with our experiences, but it also feels that things beyond our understanding should have clear and exact answers. But we know that even in our current math that already isn’t true, and our math only covers a tiny amount of our reality. A math focused on bounding and quantifying truths would feel less precise, but it would be able to usefully inspect and qualify many aspects of reality that are currently too ‘squishy’ for algorithms.
[normal] What is amazing is how much we have been able to narrow down aspects of the world that are far beyond our normal resolution. The sense of limitlessness, along with honest methodology and correct calculation, is a very powerful combination.
[Heading 3] We have history, so does our math
[normal] Math was created by the first city states, or perhaps it caused them. It was used
[normal] to manage these states, tracking land, trade, taxation and astronomy. Some of this was just recording information and simple arithmetic, but surveying and calendars required deeper understanding of the relations between measurements. This led to the need for ‘recipes’ transformations and their calculations.
[normal] The discoveries in math were first and foremost about ways to make difficult calculations tractable. What started as a tally system became a number system, what started as counting ticks became addition and then multiplication. Every time we figured out a better way to calculate (tables to abacus to slide rule to computer) it profoundly affected our number system and algorithms.
[normal] The Babylonians used ratios tables to calculate, and their number system was based on the very divisible 60. Later the Greeks and Chinese used multiplication tables, and moved to base 10. The Romans extensively used the abacus, and their numbering system reflects how the results are encoded – 8 is 2 less than 10, 12 is two more than 10, etc. Just like an abacus. Note that all of these systems used zeros in calculations (an abacus has the concept of zero), they just didn’t record the results with a positional zero.
[normal] Hindu/Arabic numbers were base 10 positional systems, which is where the current decimal system comes from. They also used the abacus, but their math was getting very symbolic by this time (~900AD) which required the more algorithmic decimal number system. By the 1600’s logarithmic tables and soon after the slide rule were invented, making multiplication almost as easy as addition. This allowed (or was caused by) great advances in math, particularly the invention of calculus, and was the basis for a lot of the math that we use today. Math at this point became as much about symbols and proofs as numbers, and they proliferation of mathematical symbols reflected this. This powered the industrial revolution and lasted right up to the computer age we’re in now.
[normal] The computer age changed a lot of long held truths about math. Now calculation is easy, so much so that it has outpaced our ability to reason about it. We still use much of the industrial revolution math systems, but it is all encoded in much looser and more scalable programming systems. Under the interface programming quietly uses binary numbers, fakes infinite values, expands out obfuscated formulas meant for ease of calculation. There is a friction in programming between our inherited system of math, and a more natural one that fits our current reality.
[Heading 3] Basic operations
[normal] Our basic math operations are addition and multiplication (and their inverses, subtraction and division). Due to mostly seeing the world as discrete objects, we don’t differentiate between repeated addition (3+3+3=9) and scaling (3*3=9). The same goes repeated multiplication (4*4*4=64) compared to repeated scaling (4³=64).
[normal] Though we have selection and repetition in some forms of math (for example the Fibonacci sequence or theTaylor series), it isn’t considered a distinct step most of the time. This is partly due to our focus on goals over processes, where the path we take is usually less consequential than where we are going. The long chain of events are often substituted by values like PI or function like sine and cosine. This is justifiable as there is no need to redo that work on every usage, but it has caused us to ignore some of the steps that can bring much clarity to the whole process.
[Heading 3] Life is anti-entropy
[normal] We know that the natural direction of the universe diffuses towards more space and less heat. With life, when something grows it accumulates more energy and organization, not less. This is so ingrained in us that we probably have many of the natural directions backwards. Higher numbers are more naturally cooler, shorter, less dense and less organized. Or perhaps it’s just that the natural direction of the number line is decreasing - more like 10, 9, 8 than 1, 2, 3. In any case, it is good to keep in mind that there are natural directions for the universe, and natural ones for life, and they tend to be opposite.
[Heading 3] Reality compression
[normal] Reality is vast, much vaster than what our brains could ever take in all at once.  This means we need to use filters and compression. The optic nerve bandwidth is around one megabyte per second, which in computer terms is like a 8mb/s internet connection. A lot of what we see is imagined by extrapolating data that seems relevant, and ignoring data that doesn’t.
[normal] The second physical issue we have with seeing, is that interpreting visual information can take up to 200 ms. That may sound fast, but it means by the time we see a fastball leave a pitcher’s hand it is halfway to home plate. The way our brain gets around this lag, is it makes predictions for everything we see, and shows us that instead. Then it will course-correct if wrong, and then through stories or edits, it will convince us that the error never happened. Words take even longer to process (about 2-3 per second), but given they usually arrive at that speed, we don’t notice.
[normal] The third thing to note (and there are many more) is memory is limited, even short term memory. One of the ways we deal with this is we carry around a context rather than every fact in a running situation. Context is focusing on traits that are relevant, and discarding the others. A book for example has many interesting things you could know about it - who wrote it, what is it about, was it good, etc. But if it is being used to prop up a short leg on a stool, we only care about how thick it is. This exponentially reduces the information that needs to be stored in any given situation. We do this a little in math as well, discarding the setup and intermediate steps to focus on the final result. Even formulas themselves have ignored every detail that isn’t important for the result. Ohms law doesn’t talk about wire color or the time of day. Math is possible because, like physics, the results are the same no matter where you do it. This is also what makes context possible.
[normal] This isn’t to say that what we see doesn’t reflect reality. It’s a very good and efficient interpretation of the world, even if it can sometimes be wrong, or even deliberately tricked. It is good to remember though, that our minds can’t be perfectly reliable. In fact nothing can. This is why we need to attack problems from multiple creative angles, with honesty, diligence and humility. It is very hard for our minds to see beyond its expectations, even on the rare occasions when we tell it to.
[Heading 3] Understanding through metaphor
[normal] Almost all our understanding is done through metaphors, built on a small number of primitives - often 2D spatial primitives. There are hints in language, in phrases like ‘in the mood’, ‘under a spell’, ‘across time’ and ‘between jobs’. Interestingly the types of spatial models used are somewhat culturally dependent.
[normal] We seem to mentally visualize math in the same way, certainly the mental number line is very familiar to most. Parts of math are also very close to the 2D spatial primitives we use to generate metaphors. When we visualize things like shapes, graphs, electric fields, or laws of motion, we may actually use shapes that are fairly close to our primitive mental building blocks. The same may be true of other artifacts we create, like written glyphs, ornamentation patterns, or simple cartoons and animation.
[normal] Importantly, we also build our mathematical systems through metaphors, where we apply patterns from one area to another, and build complex concepts from simple primitives. Group theory explores the pure patterns of relations, removed even from math itself - like the mechanics of metaphors stripped of the concepts.
[Heading 3] We magnify differences
[normal] Our brain is constantly predicting into the future, momentary, short term and longer term. It also is continually evaluating predictions and updating not only the estimates, but also the model that does the estimating - in other words ‘learning’. This is similar to predicting and testing properties of things that are beyond our ability to see directly. We do this so naturally we hardly notice it. It is more obvious when we look for electrons or exoplanets, but we are also constantly evaluating plans for a snack and what others are thinking.
[normal] This makes it very sensitive to change, so we should understand the minimum mechanics to detect change. It must start with an evaluation of the current situation, and focus on element states that are relevant. This is somehow saved, then the model moves to a later state, real or imagined, who’s relevant element states are also recorded. Lastly the two states are compared, looking for differences, and these differences are evaluated.
[normal] These differences usually evolve over a longer time. It is more like evaluating an animation than comparing two still photos. In order to view these situation all at once, we will often condense a long series of changes into some form of static 2D representation. Imagine planning to sweeping all the floors in your house. You would need to mentally model all the rooms, how they connect, where the broom is etc. There are many ways to imagine this, but what you don’t do is imagine sweeping each area at high speed, and then imagine a second path and compare them. That would be too much information to do a reasonable comparison.
[normal] We create 2D representations in order to inspect continuous differences all at once. We see these everywhere in the artifacts of our culture - graphs, maps, photos, blueprints, these are all complex fluid situations reduced to an single 2D object that can easily be evaluated and updated for different predicted paths. We certainly do this in math as well, it could even be argued that math is just a formal numeric encoding of these kinds of reductions.
[normal] Differences are often very subtle. Our minds will magnify and even misrepresent differences in order to see changes more clearly. This is generally a good strategy, as it gives us much better perception without the need for more accurate senses. We can see this in early stages of vision, where edges and luminosity change are prioritized, where flat even areas are nearly discarded. This can sometimes amplify error of course, making us overconfident in results that may not even be there. Generally though, zooming in on differences is a great way to increase resolution and filter noise, as long as we are aware of the caveats.
[normal] Math is all about predicting change. We would do well to really understand the mechanics of the ‘inspect, select, predict, simulate and evaluate’ loop.
[Heading 3] We magnify similarities
[normal] While we are very attuned to subtle differences, overall we expect similar things to be similar. This is a good bet. Our ability to categorize things depends on many traits remaining similar across instances. Because these traits are all evaluated on ranges, it allows us to stretch a few traits as long as others hold. For example we know apples are red, but also can be green or yellow, as long as they still have a lot of other apple characteristics. A blue apple though may be too big a stretch of too fundamental a property. At this point we’d wonder at least if it was a painted apple, or a toy apple.
[normal] In the common case, we only need a few measured traits to make a guess – as long as these traits were fundamental to the object definition, the object was common, and the values were expected. Every time we see a new object, we categorize it. This not only reinforces the category, but it also can move the potential ranges of some attributes if they were unusual. Over time the default ‘center’ of that category would also change. A dog, a small dog, and a big dog are estimates that are influenced by the interactions we have with dogs over the years. Everyone’s estimate would be broadly similar, but people who have tiny dogs as pets would have a different ‘default dog size’ than someone raising sled dogs.
[normal] All of these trait ranges that form a category allow us to not only categorize new objects, but they allow us to make reasonable guesses about their traits we haven’t verified. Of course we are sometimes wrong about these guesses, but that type of error helps us update the categories ranges and expectations, or even start new categories.
[normal] We expect similar things to be similar in math as well. Math is roughly organized into categories, and these categories tend to investigate a common area. Sometimes math is duplicated in different categories with slightly different syntax and calculations, such as the various ways matrices are described across domains. More fundamentally, we expect the same results when expressing the same equation in different ways, and we are very aware when changes matter (3/2 vs 2/3) and when they don't (2+3 vs 3+2). Our intuition tells us when new situations feel like math we’ve used before, and often guides us into finding the right solution to novel problems. This is largely left out of formal math, but the field would benefit greatly from a better understanding and harnessing this type of predictive reasoning.
[Heading 3] We are made of desire
[normal] While we aren’t that great at computationally simple problems like addition and multiplication, our minds are very well adapted to much more complex ‘organic’ things like language and planning. Perhaps the most difficult of all is our ability to navigate human social complexity. There is even some thinking that our brains evolved to be large due to the outsized rewards of winning the social game. It seems simple to us, but if you try to account for all the mechanics involved it is a monumental ability. We know where information comes from, how reliable it is, who knows about it, and who knows who knows, and how to try hide it. We know who wants what and how badly, the history of micro-pacts and payments over years, the changing of moods, and all the mind games that try to influence reality and perceptions in the pursuit of advantage. It makes 3D chess look like tic-tac-toe.
[normal] The underpinning of all social relations comes down to breeding and resources. This isn’t just competition for these, although it is obviously a large part of it. We have also evolved to be very weak alone, and almost unstoppable together. At a certain level we all understand the social group is the machine, and we are the parts. Every part looks to its own interest to maximize its potential, but clearly the fate of an average individual is more tied to the group than their ranking within it. And without a group, the individual’s fate is nearly certain.
[normal] There is a lot of uncertainty in human behavior. Some due to randomness, some due to an unpredictable environment, and a lot due to the advantages that come with secretly being a few steps ahead. Knowing what people actually desire would be extremely helpful to predicting behavior. Sometimes we wear that on our sleeves for all to see, sometimes we hide and misdirect, but often we even fool ourselves. There is no better way to keep a desire secret than to not know you want it.
[normal] While math itself is not set up for this type of calculation, there are many fields that are. Economics, psychology, game theory, and political studies to name a few. They have had pretty dismal track records so far, mostly because these are fields that are actually orders of magnitudes more complex than they seem to us. But also because our math is historically based on precision and perfect information, and things like probability, causation and interpretation are kind of bolted on the side. As we get closer to understanding ourselves, we will be better served by a system of calculation that better reflects our mental models and the organic world they interpret.
[Heading 3] We see objects as primitives, not traits
[normal] We identify everything using concepts, and concepts are easiest to understand when presented as discrete things. Common categories, things like oranges, chairs or horses, are so normal to use that we see them as universal objects that are building blocks of reality. When looking closer we can see that they are categorized using their traits. Tangerines, sofas and mules feel nearby, or perhaps special cases. The reality is that they fit common patterns of traits that we use to describe a useful concept area, not a universal truth.
[normal] When combined with our feeling that the truth is infinitely precise, we get a feeling that these objects are the starting point for describing the world, and that everything should fit precisely into some divine taxonomy. This tends to work fairly well as early guideposts for default concepts, but usually unravels with deeper understanding. When faced with evidence that not every object category has exact bounds, some even retreat to the idea that all categories are illusionary, that reality only exists in the mind, or some such thing. Clearly at a basic level reality maps pretty well to our mental perceptions of it, given we can’t walk through walls. But the main confusion is that we imagine the world as exact discrete concepts, rather than common patterns found in multiple traits and their ranges of values. A chair with a leg missing is still a chair, but a chair cut in half is half a chair. The second has too many traits that violate their ranges to fit into our definition of a whole chair.
[normal] In math, counting 1,2,3 might seem like the basis for all that comes after, and things like ratios are built from them. When flipping this and looking at traits as primitives, things are suddenly more natural. Traits can be imagined as lines, and their values measured places along them. We can easily compare two lengths or two temperatures without resorting to numbers. In fact we can derive numbers from these comparisons, where one length being twice as long as another would define the number two.
[normal] Ironically the earliest math system of the Babylonians was based quite strongly in ratios, and by Greek times non-numeric geometry was still foundational. The simplicity of calculating with discrete values, and the efficiency of symbolic calculation moved us further towards numbers, until geometry and ratios themselves were numeric, and the number line itself was imbued with the infinite. Again, this made perfect sense for the needs and capabilities of the time. But times have changed, and it may be time to once again rethink this orientation.
[Heading 1] What has changed?
[Heading 3] Changes in math
[normal] Computation is no longer the bottleneck. This is of course mostly due to computers and improvements in the algorithms that run them. This is also a form of computation that incorporates decision making and interactivity, with the ability to hide complexity with visual interfaces.
[normal] The ability to scale without leading to chaos is drastically better than ever before. This is as true in economics and resources as it is in engineering and software. And scale begets scale, so this is an ever increasing area. Math historically was limited in scale and complexity, so it is designed to explore and understand small areas. There are good reasons we don’t use mathematical syntax for programming languages.
[normal] Simulation is now possible, with ever increasing levels of accuracy. While a model will always be limited, they are also much easier to work and experiment with. In many fields they are essential, such as modeling airframes or engineering stresses. Great scientists and mathematicians of the past could simulate ideas in their minds, and often this would lead to great insight. We are now at a point where we can go much further, to dynamically test whole ranges of ideas, and in many cases even generate solutions.
[normal] The latest directions in math are heavily relying on machine ‘intelligence’ in some form. It is early days, but certainly computation is being pushed into areas that were not historically thought of as mathematical. This is broadening our concept of ‘numerical’, into something much more organic and informative.
[Heading 3] Changes in engineering
[normal] Computation is no longer the bottleneck. This is repeating the opening for the ‘changes in math’ section — not an error. Changes in math have always been in lockstep with changes in engineering, as well as changes in society. It is hard to tease cause from effect in these things, but certainly this time the changes in our ability to calculate things has changed everything.
[normal] There has been an explosion in sub fields in math and its related fields. Specialization is near universal, to the point there isn’t really a good overall system for understanding where all the parts fit in. As esoteric as some fields are, they are investigating relations of magnitudes and the concepts (real or imagined) they define. If math were code, it would be thousands of functions, with a minimum of structure or convention. Knowing what we know about scaling complex systems, it seems this could be improved.
[normal] Our levels of precision are many orders of magnitude better than even 100 years ago. With this precision comes a much better understanding of how things function, and a much better ability to reproduce results. When interacting with the real world, our precision is now often the bottleneck. This makes old ideas like significant figures very relevant, unfortunately our non-engineering compute process tends to be ‘add more precision than you need’ and call it good enough. This is the luxury of excess compute power, but it does obfuscate what is really going on. The edges of precision are where discovery happens, we would do well to treat that area more formally.
[normal] Math has been well encoded in computer languages and libraries. It has become normal for people to use high level math without a deep understanding of it. One can understand the utility of sines and arctangents without a deep understanding of the Taylor series. This has allowed many more people to leverage math as a tool, and is certainly overall a good thing. It has also made math quite a bit more abstract, where for many people it is more about Mathematica than even math101.
[Heading 3] Changes in society
[normal] There are way way way more literate and numerate people in the world today than anytime in the past. This has been true for hundreds of years. Much of the rapid progress we have made is simply due to more people building on the work of more people. People are by far the most important ingredient in any progress we make.
[normal] One of the biggest changes in human history was the invention of writing. We could always communicate, but it was very hard to preserve information long term. Something like 10,000 years ago, there was a profound shift in our ability to thrive in this world, and it was because we could preserve information with writing.
[normal] We now are in a new phase of history, where we can easily communicate information, as well as retrieve it, test it, discuss it, document it, and collectively advance it. We are still adapting to this profound change, but it does significantly increase our potential to make progress on all fronts. We normally attach ‘trust metadata’ to information — who sourced it, who else knows it, and who gains from it. This has always been as important as the information itself. In this new information avalanche, we unfortunately haven’t had the equivalent avalanche of metadata. Reputations of institutions and individuals disseminating information have proven a poor substitute for trust. We would do well to develop a rigorous and honest metadata system for information, ideally based on a chain of receipts rather than ad-hoc groups of ‘fact guardians’.
[normal] Overall, we not only have more powerful tools, and a more connected society, but we have a better understanding of our minds, and a better understanding of how we interact. This will drive much of our future progress. Like all technology, this will be both a gift in the hands of many, and a weapon in the hands of few. If I can offer advice, tread cautiously, and err on the side of the many.
[Heading 1] Deriving the Math
[normal] With a list of universal things, we can now attempt to derive a universal math from it. It is important to account for every step required when making a calculation. The idea of a calculation should be broadly interpreted, and exhaustively examined. We should end up with a very generic template that can be used to structure calculation, and if it is truly universal, it should be applicable beyond traditional math.
[Heading 3] Assess and select
[normal] The very first step in making an assessment of any sort, is to decide what to assess. This may seem obvious, but there is a lot to unpack when trying to examine this completely.
[normal] Starting with a common, if not simple idea, imagine selecting apples from a pile in a grocery store. Unpausing this, we must first decide we want to buy apples, and decide collecting them should be our next task. We then assess the pile, and then select and retrieve them one by one until we have enough to complete the task.
[normal] We could have decided to collect something else, recheck our shopping list, or imagine what we want for supper. These all require focus. Because we have approximately a single focus, we are most comfortable with single selections, and tend to group multiple tasks into a single task (filling a bag vs selecting an apple six times). This is true for mental tasks as well, we generally can only think of one thing at a time, so we imagine a single broad category rather than the many concepts it involves.
[normal] Single selection works fine for our minds, but of course in the real world, more than one thing can happen at the same time. Somewhere else in the store someone is running the checkout, perhaps a drop of rain just hit the roof, and somewhere in the galaxy some grain of sand just blew against a rock. When looking at parallel events like this, selection is too narrow a word - perhaps it is more just ‘existing’.
[normal] Traditionally math has been about the things we inspect (mentally or physically), but with the advent of powerful computation, we can now simulate as well as calculate. This makes the selection step more of a ‘select all’, where we just run things for a number of steps and inspect the results. Simulation lies somewhere between theory and experiment, but we still select what we wish to simulate. In the case of the universe itself, it is always selecting all, and assessing all as it goes.
[normal] Our concept of selection needs to accommodate single and multiple selections, that might be assessed one time or repeatedly. These choices can be guided by minds or algorithms, or like most things, a result of natural forces. Most fundamentally, an assess and select step is required before any calculations are possible.
[normal] To demonstrate this is math, we can look at something as simple as 1+1=2. The ones here represent the selection. The utility is more obvious when looking at sequences, as in the Fibonnaci sequence: 1,1,2,3,5,8,13,21... Here the next total is created by selecting the previous two totals and adding them. There are many such solutions in math that rely on algorithmic or dynamic selections. Even in simple cases, focusing on the initial selection can clarify a process.
[normal] Selection is the initial step in any mathematical process. It sometimes comes through human assessment, and sometimes it is already selected by being part of a larger system.
[Heading 3] Select is unselect
[normal] As the first law of thermodynamics tells us, energy can not be created or destroyed. This requires the things we select to already exist, so we are actually just mentally transferring them from the set of all things to the set we have selected. The total does not change.
[normal] Even when we imagine things, there is a physical process that conserves energy as it invokes mental images from memories. It seems natural to us that objects can be created out of nothing because this process is totally hidden from us. But they can’t be. All operations must balance once everything is accounted for.
[normal] By being aware of what we don’t select, it is easy to see that the total group we choose from can be a selection itself. When we pick apples at the grocery store pile, we are ‘not selecting’ the other apples in the pile, not all apples in the world. This ‘total possible’ is often ignored, but is essential information for calculating things like potentials and probabilities.
[normal] This means selecting is also unselecting, leaving a net zero. Of course we can ignore the unselected part, and we usually do, but at the core this isn’t how things work. Note that net zero does not imply that selections are reversible, it just means there was a transformation rather than creation or destruction.
[normal] A selection ‘equation’ would be something like: total becomes selected plus not selected — where we understand the total itself is going to be a selection. What prevents ‘total categories’ from spiraling up forever is that possible selections are bounded by what is ‘nearby’ in a physical or mental context. We can build a chain of contexts to anywhere we care to imagine, but we don’t need to invoke the Milky Way galaxy every time we focus on an apple pile. Even for inanimate interactions, distance and time serve to keep selections immediate and calculations local.
[normal] It isn’t just with selecting either - add has subtract, multiplication has reciprocals, rotate has unrotate, and on and on. We see this most clearly when we manipulate an equation around the equal sign, but it is everywhere. At higher levels of abstraction this pattern is sometimes called ‘duality’, where for example a cube is the dual of an octahedron. Geometric algebra leverages this type of duality to reveal quite amazing concepts hidden in everyday geometry.
[normal] Every operation, including selection, is a rearrangement of what exists. To fully account for an operation, the books must balance.
[Heading 3] Everything measurable is a trait
[normal] A trait is any kind of property, sometimes belonging to an object, sometimes not. It is the rough equivalent of what an adjective describes in language (we say adjectives describe nouns, but in reality they quantify properties of nouns). When we say a dog is warm, small, furry and brown, we are quantifying the traits of temperature, size, texture/hair type, and color.
[normal] We can only add trait values if they are the same trait. If a tree grows one foot the first year, and two feet the second year, we know this tree is then three feet tall. However if it grew one foot the first year, and grew two branches the second year, we do not add these numbers.
[normal] In algebra, traits are the things normally represented by letters as in 3a+2b. This isn’t always true, as algebra is based on unwritten context that is filled in per use. For example the length of hair and the length of a bridge may well be two separate letters in a formula, where as they are the same trait. In math, single letters can represent constants such as e, or formulas such as Σ, vectors such as V and many other things. Traits are just properties, and these properties can be common across objects in unrelated contexts.
[normal] Traits are single things that can be measured.
[Heading 4] Multiple traits
[normal] Related traits can sometimes be combined into a new trait by a specific form of multiplying (more on multiplying later). For example width and height traits can be joined, giving an area trait. Unrelated traits can not be combined into new traits. Width and temperature can not form a new trait unless they were in a system that somehow related them. Color and temperature can be combined when referring to heating metals or the warm feeling of red and cool feeling of blue, but they can not be combined into a new trait when talking about the color and temperature of apples as that will always be two unrelated measures. As we’ll see, when unrelated traits are combined (with ranges), the result is category definitions, not new traits.
[normal] The fact that unrelated traits do not combine into new traits, and that they don’t usually decompose into multiple traits, make them the ‘primitives’ of any system involving magnitudes. They are the primitives of this math system as well.
[Heading 4] Traits in the real world
[normal] There is no list of all traits, as that would be unimaginably long. Fortunately we only care about a tiny subset of all possible traits, and nature itself cares about even fewer. The precise mass of an object is something that is often relevant to us, whereas the precise qualification of textures or smells is not — to the point that we don’t even have words for most of them.
[normal] When thinking of the physics of the unfolding universe, we might imagine it is accounting for all these obscure traits. In reality it is just reacting to local conditions and has no information on why these conditions are the way they are. If photons needed to care about a star’s corona, or even its mass, that information and special calculations would have to be stored and run on every photon in the universe. There are traits that affect physics at a high level, but as you climb to that scale, these things become more about our understanding than physics itself.
[normal] As for the traits we care about, there are many, but not unimaginably many - after all, we can imagine them all. Many of these come from our evolutionary inputs and needs, such as sensory input, motion, nutrition, safety, reproduction, knowledge, and social chess. Others are more abstract, but tend to be built on these primitive traits through metaphor. There is no specific number, but one hundred traits would cover a lot of ground, and a thousand would probably be adequate for most situations.
[Heading 4] Trait math
[normal] In math, traits are the thing a value is talking about, and all mathematical transformations are composed of trait changes. Even when we abstract away the traits, with 1+2=3, we have assumed these are talking about the same trait - perhaps distances on a number line or some such thing. There is always a trait backing a value. It can be very advantageous to abstract traits away, but they are what give these manipulations consistency. Fully quantifying these traits is what allows science to emerge from measurements.
[normal] As a mental model, we can imagine traits as a line. We know from the second law of thermodynamics that things can have a direction and gradient, so this line goes from low to high in at least some abstract way. This is not an infinite line, it will eventually have two ends, and as we’ll see later, those ends will be characterized. For now though, each trait is a line that represents all possible values, ordered, for that trait as you move along it.
[normal] The universe can be described in terms of its traits, and we can gain a high degree of comprehension with a limited number of them.
[Heading 3] Focals: every value is a segment on a trait
[normal] A trait represents all possible values of a property, and a value is a segment on it. We’ll call these values ‘focals’, as existing words like point, value or segment already have meanings. Focal suggests the part that is focused on, whether a point or segment. It also suggests that the values aren’t necessarily exact, which is correct.
[normal] The endpoints of focals can never be described with infinite precision or infinite certainly. The simple reason for this is that nothing can be measured or even described to an infinite precision. This is true in all math, though not always admitted. The reason we get away with this is that we can usually measure things with much more precision than we need.
[normal] If it is impossible to measure an endpoint with infinite precision, then it stands to reason that a single point will also have limited precision. That doesn’t make it a segment, it is more a qualified blur. But along a line, a blur has length, or at least length potential. We’ll call these focus points when referring to them specifically, but in reality they are just very short focals. Two pieces of information are considered equal when we can’t distinguish them from each other, so when a focal becomes so short that the endpoints can’t be separated, it also becomes indistinguishable from a focus point.
[Heading 3] Trait and focal endpoints must be characterized
[normal] If everything is a segment, and both scale and precision have limits, then what happens at the endpoints? They can’t be infinitely precise points, so they need to be characterized. We need to define why they end, and how they end. Traits are not a purely abstract concept, they are actual properties of things we can inspect or imagine. So the how and why of endpoints will vary, and our goal is to qualify that variation.
[normal] So how do real properties behave at their limits? It would be very useful to quantify these behaviors, as they contain meta-information that can be incorporated into calculations. This would be difficult to incorporate into terse mathematical syntax, and calculation would be difficult. However, it is straightforward to incorporate into code for a math library, where use and calculation become mostly automatic.
[normal] It should be possible to create an exhaustive list of the ways measurable things behave at their limits. Here is a first attempt at such a list.
[Heading 4] Tolerance
[normal] Very often our precision in measuring something is limited by not needing more precision. Whenever we round numbers, like a three hour drive or even a hot day, we could have been more precise but didn’t need to be. More precision implies the extra information is important, so unnecessarily adding it leads to misunderstanding. Driving 3 hours, 7 minutes and 21 seconds puts the time in focus rather than the trip.
[normal] There is often more precision available, but the context calls for a certain number of significant figures. A person’s height is usually measured to the nearest inch. People are about an inch taller when they wake up, so extra precision here would at least need an asterisk. Weight fluctuates even more, as we go through around 12 pounds (6 kg) of food and water per day. Again, 12 pounds is not exactly 6kg, but they are both very approximate numbers.
[normal] It would be nice to be able to mark numbers by the precision of their estimates. People are usually careful to use significant figures correctly in science, but it is a pretty adhoc system based mostly on trust.
[Heading 4] Limits of precision
[normal] As one moves to the extreme ends of traits and precision, things get harder to measure. There are two reasons for this, first it is physically hard to measure things that are at such different scales, and second, it’s hard to tell if you are right once you’re done. We can date rocks that are over 3 billion years old, measure distances to far away galaxies, and measure distances down to picometers. With all these extreme measurements, error bars increase until they overwhelm the measurement itself, so precision is more of a probability cutoff than any exactness. It’s also normal for these estimates to be adjusted as we find new techniques to measure things.
[normal] Limits happen at both the small and large scale. At one point numbers just become too large, distances too great, or time too distant. At the small scale, well things just become too small. There can still be information here, for example often a value will approach a value without ever reaching it. This is commonplace in calculus, but also with temperature approaching absolute zero. Numbers themselves exhibit this trait, as they approach some ideal value as you add precision, but you never reach that infinite precision.
[normal] The limits of our precision have been improving rapidly for the last few hundred years. These abilities are one of the key drivers of progress. We should be aware when a value represents ‘the best we can currently do’, as the quality of its information will likely increase over time. It also may indicate a bottleneck that needs to be overcome before more progress can be made.
[Heading 4] Transformation
[normal] Objects are defined by trait values, and these values normally remain in the ranges appropriate for the object. What happens when moving outside these ranges depends on both the trait and object, but it is common that the object just becomes something else. For example larger and larger grains of sand will eventually become a stone, then a boulder, and at the extremes a planet, a star, and a black hole. This is all just conceptually increasing the mass of an object. Increasing the temperature of ice will eventually make it steam, increasing differences in speaking go from accents to dialects and languages. If we keep dividing the amount of water in a cup, we eventually get to a single molecule of water, and after that we have hydrogen and oxygen.
[normal] Transformation at limits can either be some form of phase transition, or it can just be the limit of our definition. Often it is a mix of both, and often there are overlapping gray areas. A one year old is very different than a 40 year old. One is a child, one an adult. There is an ‘definition transition’ on someone’s 18th birthday, but people near that age could be considered either, depending on context. The trait of age doesn’t pause as the trait of childhood transitions to the trait of adulthood.
[normal] It can be important to know what values outside focal ranges mean. Sometimes this indicates an error, and sometimes it is just a change in category.
[Heading 4] Limits of computation
[normal] There are things that start easy, and get progressively harder until they become impossible at the limit. Factoring large numbers is a good mathematical example of this concept. Factoring numbers under one hundred is a grade school problem, yet factoring very large numbers is so hard that it’s the basis of modern cryptography.
[normal] When thinking of precision, the value of PI is a better example. It doesn’t have a natural limit, and people have calculated it to trillions of digits. But there is a limit, because as numbers get that precise, inconsequential things come to dominate. Even storing a number that large is a huge undertaking, and the time and cost of computation becomes a limiting factor. Even encoding a number with a predictable pattern, like 1.66666… will eventually exhaust all resources. Patterns with even a tiny amount of computation per step, like the Fibonacci Sequence, become uncomputable at scale. Exponentials or a complex series can grow beyond limits quite quickly. And long before resource limits, the numbers become uninterpretable anyway.
[normal] Some things are known to not terminate naturally, but they will still overwhelm any system at scale. This can happen with complexity, predictability, interpretability, computability or just plain size. It is useful to know when measures are limited by resources, because it usually means they are unlimited in most practical senses. We can fix a practical limit and just label it beyond our resolution. A million to the power of a million a million times is indistinguishable from 1/0. And 1 divided by this result is indistinguishable from 0, at our resolution.
[Heading 4] Error and uncertainty
[normal] Measurement error will often result in a cluster of samples around the measurement point, with positions closer to the truth being more likely. These points will almost always follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution. Understanding this probability distribution allows multiple measurements to give higher accuracy, with higher confidence than a single one.
[normal] It is important to remember that every sampled value on a segment will have the same measurement error, not just the endpoints. The difference is samples near the endpoints are less likely to lie within the segment. So when asking if a sample is within a focal range on a trait, we get a ‘true or false’ answer with high confidence everywhere except near (and especially just beyond) the endpoints. Like the best approximation with a tape measure, we can be certain our 5.19 lies between 1 and 10, but less certain it lies between 1 and 5.2.
[normal] Another common source of error comes from noise. Random noise interference in a signal will result in a normally distributed error. There are also many non random sources of interference. Overlapping signals create noise for each other in a data line, much like multiple people talking at the same time.
[normal] There are many other types of error. Breaks in a signal, signal offsets, and of course palin old mistakes in transmission. As error increases or compounds, it can swamp the signal making further measurement meaningless. Characterizing measurement error is very important when working at the limits of our precision. Even when working within tolerances, we must be careful error is uniform and doesn’t compound.
[normal] Error should be estimated and tracked directly in the mathematical system we use to calculate, rather than with an adhoc secondary step.
[normal] Within tolerance stop
[normal] Limit of precision / forever approaching
[normal] Hard stop - definition/transformation
[normal] Computation stop
[normal] Error
[Heading 3] Every comparison requires a unit
[normal] A single measurement alone contains no information. Imagine a photo that contains a single line. Without context there would be no way of knowing if it is one micron or one light year in length. When starting from nothing, all we can do is compare measured values and say something about the comparison.
[normal] Moving from one thing to two comparable things is an extremely significant step, as we now have a category. With two lines, even though we still don’t know anything about the scale, we can compare them. For example one line might be about twice as long as the other, making the other about half as long as the first. We made one line the ‘unit’, then used that unit to estimate the relative length of the other line. Switching the unit to be the second line gives the reciprocal ratio. Just as there is no universal length, there is no universal unit, so the unit selection is arbitrary.
[normal] This isn’t just for measuring the length lines of course. Two temperatures, two colors, or even two tastes can be compared. Any two focal segments on the same trait can be compared. However, two segments on different traits, or the two separate traits themselves can not be compared unless they form a single combined trait (two lengths form an area). We can’t compare 3 inches to 40 degrees.
[normal] We choose standard units for common measures because there is no easy way to communicate a unit without an already existing unit. These standards are arbitrary, but tend to be in common sizes that keep the values in practical ranges for everyday use. We usually have multiple ways of measuring the same trait based on context, and they are usually convertible to each other if need be. Lengths have inches and centimeters and kilometers. These are different systems at different scales, but with known conversions they are all compatible focal segments on the distance trait.
[Heading 3] Numbers come from ratios and definitions
[normal] Before introducing numbers, we should note how much we can do without them. For most of human evolution we didn’t have a very advanced numbering system, if any at all. We of course could tell many from few, but that doesn’t mean we had even the numbers from 1 to 10. Euclidean geometry was about constructing and comparing points, lines and circles, and was built without any numeric coordinates (which would have to wait until Descartes invented Cartesian coordinates in the 1600’s).
[normal] There are two options for generating numbers with the simple line system we’ve discussed so far.
[normal] First, we can use the ratios of two lines, making one of them the unit. If we can stretch these lines, then we stretch the non unit line to be twice as long, three times as long, four times as long etc. If we physically would do this, we can imagine the precision would be limited by our ability to measure. This gives us a continuous number system (we can create 2.5), within the precision of our abilities.
[normal] A second system could be created by just creating more lines and counting them. This will give us exactly one line, exactly two lines etc, and we don’t need a unit. The precision is limited here by the fact that these lines do not need to be the same length. This is also why this system will always be discrete - you can’t make half a line because it will still be a line. More subtly, the precision of a discrete system is always limited by the definition of the unit element in the system. In this case it is a line, but we might not count a line so short that it seems to be a dot, or a line drawn over another line. Even a Y shaped line could be 1, 2, or 3 lines depending on our element definition.
[normal] These two systems are very fundamental to how we see the world. Our number line is based on continuous stretching, and our counting is based on definitions of a discrete unit element. They do interleave though. As discrete elements move below the tolerances we care about we start considering them discrete. We don’t say ‘a sand’ or ‘a grain’, but we say ‘a pebble’ or ‘a rock’. We also build up definitions of discrete elements with multiple traits, using probable ranges of values for each. As these definitions get more specific, we can often start dividing discrete objects, like ‘half an apple’, but not ‘half a stick’. You can also use both systems together, for example by combine discrete ‘lines’ by their length rather than their existence.
[normal] It is very important to know if you are dealing with discrete or continuous measures, as the possible operations on each are very different. Combining discrete elements is fundamentally addition and subtraction, and stretching continuous segments is fundamentally multiplication and division. But more on this later.
[Heading 3] Everything that can be done with a segment on a line
[normal] Traits are properties that have magnitudes ordered from lowest to highest in a linear gradient. They can be thought of as an uncalibrated line that could be extended to the lowest and highest possible values for that trait. A focal segment is a segment of any length along this line. So we have a line and segments on it. This defines one dimension.
[normal] With such a fundamental object, we should try to exhaustively enumerate all the unique operations that can be done with it.
[Heading 4] Select
[normal] This can be done choosing an existing selection, or creating a new one. Creating a new selection can be done manually or algorithmically.
[Heading 4] Direction
[normal] Every trait has a gradient of magnitudes, and every segment has a start point and end point. This means the segments have information about which direction they are pointing - low to high, high to low, or can’t tell. Note this has nothing to do with how the trait line is drawn, rotation has no meaning here. It is better to imagine the line going from red to blue, and the segment’s end point getting redder or getting bluer.
[Heading 4] Unit
[normal] Once a segment is selected, it can be labeled the unit. Numerically this will mean the start point is zero, and the end point is one. These are the only perfect numbers in this system, because they are defined to be zero and one, not measured. The zero point is defined by the unit, not the lowest possible trait value - otherwise negative numbers would be impossible. We’ll assume the unit is pointing in the positive direction, but think about what it would mean to have a negative unit.
[Heading 4] Repeat
[normal] Whatever we do, we can do again. This implies steps done in order. Technically this brings in the new dimension of time, at least abstractly. But because everything is always moving, all things naturally exist in the time dimension. So we made a selection, now we can select a second segment. And a third. Repetition is the second fundamental action in math, after selection. In normal math repetition is, in a very limited way, expressed by exponents.
[normal] We can also select a second unit, but only one unit at a time can be used to define zero and measure. This means a second unit selection more or less deselects the first one, at least for its tasks.
[Heading 4] Count
[normal] With more than one segment, we can now count - upwards at least. Segments do not have to be the same length to count them, and we can not have half a segment, so this only counts whole numbers.
[Heading 4] Addition
[normal] With repeated selections and counting what is selected, we can now count using whole numbers. There is still no set order to what we count. Perhaps all segments are counted left to right, or top to bottom, or largest to smallest. Or for low numbers all items could be counted at once. This would be a user defined system, as there are many ways to order random segments. Initially all addition has to be by ones (1+1+1=3), though the ability to count and add bootstraps selecting more than one element. With that we can say 2+1=3.
[normal] Sometimes when we add to an ordered set, we care more about the resulting set than the total. For example adding C,E to A,B,D we might expect A,B,C,D,E rather than ((C,E),(A,B,D)). When combining two groups into one, we gain clarification by filtering information that isn’t relevant to our task. This is a choice, and what is useful is context sensitive. As always, there are insights to be had whenever we notice we are making a choice, so it is important to keep a broad view of what something as fundamental as addition actually represents.
[normal] Note that with all this information so far, we still can’t count backwards or subtract.
[Heading 4] Subtraction
[normal] At its most basic, subtraction is removing from a selection. If it is an ordered selection we are removing from, we traditionally remove from the ‘end’, or remove randomly and reinterpret the results. If we add 4 oranges to a bag (1,2,3,4), and then remove one, the remaining oranges could be (1,3,4). We usually consider oranges in a bag to be unordered, so we would either reinterpret the removed orange to be the fourth one resulting in (1,2,3), or reinterpret the oranges (1,3,4) to be (1,2,3). We would call this a bag of three oranges when focused on the unordered total, but if asked to count them we would have no trouble pointing to a first, second and third, in some order.
[normal] This may seem like hair splitting, but there are certainly cases where sets of things are ordered, and we want to delete a certain member. In these situations (1,3,4) is not the same as (1,2,3). It is important to keep a broad view of what subtraction actually is, or it will be hard to understand it in less intuitive situations.
[normal] With ordered counts (like discrete numbers), it is tempting to define subtraction as just counting backwards, but that wouldn’t cover cases where you subtract one group’s count from another’s. Counting backwards with a one to one correspondence is closer, but we still need to define what ‘backwards’ means here. If we used a heuristic for ordered counting (like say smallest to largest) then we can reverse it (largest to smallest). This makes A-B a multi step process. First make a counted ordered set (B) using addition, and place it at the endpoint of A. Reverse the order of B (mirror it over the endpoint of A) so it overlays A’s last elements. Then delete the corresponding elements from A.
[normal] Note ‘corresponding elements’ can always have multiple interpretations here as there are multiple ways of defining how things should correspond. Traditionally this is just one to one for each element in its given order. But as with addition, there are many branches of mathematics where the identity of each element in a calculation matters more than its result.
[Heading 4] Negatives
[normal] We can add and subtract, and this means the values can end up at zero or lower, leading us to values that don’t have corresponding selections. There are two ways to think about these ‘negative’ numbers. The first is they are selections that have been made but not filled (negative selections), and the second is they are still positive selections, but of an opposite type of thing. For example a person could have ‘negative ten dollars’ or just have ‘(positive) ten dollars of debt’. These are not two ways of saying the same thing, even though they seem similar. When thinking about the operation, the negative number version mirrors a value at zero, so 5 dollars becomes -5 dollars, but adding a 1 will still make you richer. This is what negative means. Moving the count from asset to debt mirrors the whole perspective of that +1 means without changing any values. The value is still 5, but it is of debt instead of credit, and now adding a dollar (of debt) makes you poorer. So negation mirrors values on a number line around zero, where the second option mirrors the number line itself. More on this crucial point later.
[Heading 4] Compare
[normal] With more than one selection, and a unit selected, we can now compare segments. This allows us to express continuous numbers, as one segment can be 2.5 times longer than another.
