===== Numbers.odt =====
Everything we understand in the universe is derived from understanding quantities. Not just by way of math and numbers either, our thoughts, our perceptions and all meaning comes from comparing and manipulating things we quantify.
Surprisingly we don’t spend much time trying to understand how exactly this all works at a
fundamental level. As in the ‘pre-elementary school’ level of understanding, “how can things be measured?”, “what is a number?”, “what is addition?”, “how can you compare things?”. This level of questions are answered with tradition, not inquiry. With the advent of AI, we face machines that have no tradition other than what we give them. It is becoming necessary to revisit our traditions, clarify them, and come up with a more complete framework for understanding quantities. This new framework quantifies concepts using webs of related perspectives, each with an inherent micro-intelligence. In this way, intelligence is distributed throughout the network in spaces of varying complexity.
All quantities derive from a measure of change. This may not seem intuitive because it is hard to isolate a single measure from its context. It’s like a deep sea fish has no idea of air, and therefore has no idea of water. Imagine living in a void - it isn’t black, it is the absence of the concept of light. You can’t be ‘here’ because there is no concept of ‘there’. There can’t be quantity, because there is no change.
It's only once there is a second thing to compare to — something different from the first — that the concept of quantity begins to emerge. It was cold, now it's hot. This is bigger, that is smaller. Two samples may not be able to fully calibrate and manipulate quantities, but it is a giant phase change in perception. The change allows us to notice a difference, and therefore notice the concept at all. This change can be over perceptible things like time, place, or scale, but it can also be fully abstract or imagined things. The most abstract ideas in math may never touch the real world, but they are only able to exist as ideas by exploring unequal things.
If existence is the transition from 0 to 1, comprehension begins at 2.
While quantities can be extended to represent anything knowable, real or imagined, this doesn’t imply that they are free of worldly rules. In fact the reason the world is interpretable at all is that these rules are very strict, and apply universally and consistently. Values can be ordered by some rule, and the interpretation of that ordering is unambiguous. Smallest to largest does not permit 4,5,7,6 as a possible order. Operations have their own logic, and it is consistent wherever applied. 2+2=4 in arithmetic, in temperature, or in imaginary unicorns. Math can be pure or applied, but the rules are indifferent to the environment that spawns them. The commutativity of addition will hold whether you're adding temperatures or debts or rotations. This is fundamental.
Rules of a space are substrate-independent, and not optional.
All this to say, the rules are paramount. They need to be extremely well defined and their implications fully explored. The mechanics of simple things like addition or multiplication should hold just as cleanly for areas, population growth, oscillations, and plain old numbers.
Unknown vs. Infinity
When thinking of number limits, you could say either:
It is unknown when or even if they end
This may seem pedantic, but the implications split into very different systems. The first gives you infinite-precision real numbers. The second gives you bounded math with uncertainty as a first-class element. Both are mathematically valid, both are useful, but only B reflects how quantities actually behave outside the abstraction. Not defining and exploring this is at least an oversight. Real numbers are a simplification of quantities, a useful subset, but they hide deeper truths needed to fully encode concepts with numeric tools. The limits of many important things large and small are in fact unknown, and this matters. We will be emphasizing the latter definition in this framework, treating real numbers as a valid subset.
The first implication of this choice is the concept of an unknown value. This can be because something is unknowable, unexamined, not yet understood, or simply random. It can also be outside a known range, like something too heavy for your scale. We tend to focus on the knowable in cognition and math, but in reality most things are partly known and partly unknown. Unknown is a first-class element when dealing with quantities (and reality!), not an edge case.
Bounds and Resolution
The second implication of unknown limits is that all measures need some ‘known’ bounds and a resolution. Infinity allows us to ignore the ranges we are operating in. Without it, we need to specify what limits exist on numbers we are using, at both the large and small ends. Everything beyond these limits can’t be expressed without changing the resolution.
We can express resolution using fractions with a slight twist. We can say 1/2 is lower resolution than 2/4, which is lower resolution than 1000/2000. The denominator matters here, as it signifies resolution. A button hole that needs to be 7/16 of an inch should be measured more carefully than a recipe that needs 1/2 a cup of flour. The value 1001/2000 would still round to 1/2 at low resolution, but they are different values in reality. The extra information is lost to the 'unknown' part of a measure at lower precision. Operations are affected by this too, for example a definition of addition needs to include rules for how 1/2 + 2/4 is handled.
Resolution matters at the high end in the same way. When you choose a precision cutoff, you implicitly choose a maximum and minimum bounds as well. If you choose not to define these, they become unspecified, which is very different than unbounded. A dog can be many weights, but outside certain ranges it is no longer a dog. Five hundred tons is not a dog. The exact boundary is unspecified, but the fact that there is an approximate boundary is part of what the word 'dog' means.
We use precision and bounds constantly in practice, whenever we estimate, whenever we choose a time step, whenever we chunk a task. But we treat these things as metadata, something written in the margins or assumed rules of thumb. This framework proposes precision and bounds are treated as first class elements of measures.
Together these two implications mean that every measure exists inside some framework that has resolution rules and information limits. There is a real separation between what is measured and what complexity space it is measured from. The space holds to rules, and the rules calibrate the measures.
Every value has a context that calibrates it. The number seven means ‘seven ones’. Seven miles is calibrated with one mile. Simple versions of these spaces appear everywhere. Perhaps most obviously in geometry - points, lines, areas, volumes, but the ideas extend much further: color, sound, social interactions or biological niches are all calibrated within some kind of framing space. Everything measurable is measured against some complexity space. Everything transformed is transformed within the rules of one. Mathematically they are akin to vector spaces, but with a wider net cast.
A complexity space is defined by the number of types it contains and how the elements created within them interact. A single space is by definition limited in scope — it cannot fully describe things more complex than itself. In practice we operate with many spaces simultaneously, each containing a mix of elements from the thing we are examining. A geometric example may help clarify this, though keep in mind that geometry is a narrow, restricted subset of this larger system.
Think of the degrees of freedom a point has within the complexity space of each: a point, a line, an area, a volume. That’s 0 degrees of freedom for a point (fully bounded), 1 for a line, 2 for an area, and 3 in a volume.
Now consider a line in each of these spaces. A line in a point: 0. In a line: 2. In an area: 4. In a volume: 6. A line in a point can’t move either end, so still 0. A line in a line allows each of its endpoints to slide, so 2 degrees of freedom there. In an area, a line can move each point vertically and horizontally, so 4. And 6 degrees of freedom in a volume. The space constrains what is possible before any other rules apply.
Now add explicit constraints. A line on a line has two degrees of freedom, both endpoints can move changing the location and size. Lock the length though, and there is only one degree of freedom. No matter which point you adjust, the effect is the same: the whole line moves in unison, like a point. It is one degree of freedom living inside a two-degree space. The math for this constrained line is the same as the math for a point. Not because lines and points are secretly the same thing, but because we have imposed the same constraints on both. The math follows from the degrees of freedom and rules of the space, not from anything inherent in a line or point.
This dimension reduction works the same way if you lock a pivot point and allow only the length to change, only the far endpoint moves. Add a unit length anchored at the pivot point, and this works exactly our standard numbering system. For these zero-anchored lengths, we know how to add, multiply, and raise to powers, and we know how transforms behave: commutative laws, distributive laws, closure. None of that is some kind of ‘law of lengths’. It is how any system behaves under these particular constraints, which is why it holds equally for areas in 2D, volumes in 3D, and any other similarity-constrained system of zero-anchored magnitudes.
What happens if you don’t constrain the start point and keep the unit? You end up with two unit lengths, one for the start and another for the end direction. This allows the start point to be based on an inverted unit that is positive left (i) and the end point in our normal positive right system. The math that falls out is exactly complex number math, but applied to segments instead of lengths and rotations. I’ve covered this extensively in other documents, and it is one of the most interesting things this system has revealed so far. This doesn't make complex numbers based on rotations wrong. Other than the rotation modulus (circles can return to zero degrees every rotation), this is just another way into the same complexity space. Because the defining characteristics of the space are the same, the math has to be the same. There are many ways to arrive at this space across many domains – in physics, electronics, algebra, and everywhere else you see complex numbers or free segments along a path.
The important thing is to understand that these ‘spaces’ are simply perspectives, and multiple perspectives can all coexist on the same elements at the same time.
Applying these dimensionality tests methodically can reveal errors in our assumptions. For example we often think of area as two-dimensional, but area is a single value (e.g. 6cm
²
Apples are actually very complex objects, with an overwhelming number of inter-related attributes. True as that is, when adding the weights of two apples we don't have to account for atoms or skin blemishes. We have reduced the apples to one dimension, the weight, and can now use simple addition that works just like all other addition. This doesn’t mean the aroma or color isn’t important in some other perspective - maybe the skin blemish prevents one from ending up on the scale. This matters, but it matters to a different perspective running in parallel. In the physical world these attributes are all running and interacting continuously. It is our minds that have managed to reduce this to separate computable heuristics, allowing us to hallucinate the truth. Our minds, and perhaps soon our machines.
If I was to guess the weight of your mother, sight unseen, how many ways could I be wrong? Leaving aside the question itself being a mistake, the errors fall into two categories. First is the guess itself is simply off - I guess 150 pounds and she’s a solid 300. This is ‘measurement error’. The second type of error is not using the right frame of reference to start with, category error. That could be wrong resolution (measuring in tons or picograms), or being out of frame bounds (9000 pounds, or 2 pounds). And just to be complete, guessing your mother’s weight to be reddish-blue is also a category error.
This separation is category vs measurement, the frame vs the contents. This is what is meant by the complexity space, and the measures calibrated within it. When we think about error, we almost always focus on the value and assume the frame. Even in math and science, the frame is usually taken for granted. When building a complexity space, though, we must specify not just the parameters and their transforms, but also the resolution and bounds. This
The opportunity in this is that error becomes quantifiable and correctable at every level. In current machine learning training, all the knowledge in the world is absorbed in each pass, and correction happens globally. At inference time, the model one-shots its best guess, from a top down whole world perspective. That this works at all is remarkable. That the whole endeavor requires computers the size of football stadiums, powered by nuclear reactors, grinding month after month, is equally unsurprising. Simpler intelligence distributed throughout the system has a chance to scale with much less compute with better heuristics, akin to machine calculation vs biological.
The reason we have one-shot error resolution is that our math can never be ‘wrong’. If I say pick a point on a numberline, there is no wrong answer. No segment is incorrect, no area is invalid, no volume is ever ‘not a volume’. There is only measurement error, but it is invisible in the system. If our measurement error is detectable within the system, every perspective will understand error pressure, and every complexity space can help correct it. Each space gains agency, each can negotiate its own goals, and each can contribute to outcomes it isn't even equipped to perceive directly. This is how biology works, because it is a more powerful architecture, compared to having some external intelligence correcting errors based on final outputs.
A geometric intuition helps here. Imagine a segment on a number line. Many points will fall outside it, but each one knows which direction they would need to move to end up inside it, or which direction the segment would need to move. Put segments on both an X and Y axis, and a random point is even less likely to fall inside their intersection. And if you have two areas on perpendicular planes, there is a good chance their projections will not intersect at all (more on this later). Each of these complexity spaces can negotiate with the others towards a preferred configuration, and each can do so using only local information. No perspective needs to understand any other, or even be aware of them, other than the tensions they create. The negotiation happens through shared substrate, not through explicit coordination.
Think again of the square moving around a plane. The bottom-left point knows nothing of the square, but it still can ‘want’ to move to the right. The area knows nothing about position, but it can ‘want’ to remain the same size. These pressures are local, but act on each other, causing all points on the square to move rightwards together. The communication happens because they are all perspectives in the same space.
This is the key. There is no need for explicit cross-level communication. The resolution mechanism is how the system responds to forces, which is inherent in the complexity space itself. And it doesn’t mean everything needs to be deterministic, as there are plenty of unknowns and ranges of uncertainty.
This is exactly why car suspension systems and analog electronic circuits can be modeled with the same math. Engineers have explicitly used this analogy (the force-voltage duality) to design F1 dominating cars.
A practical heuristic for problem-solving with distributed intelligence: start at the level of focus that matters, and reduce everything else to the minimum resolution needed.
If the problem is your chances against a bear, reduce the bear to a point, then add back only what seems relevant. The bear's weight can be estimated from its apparent size, which incorporates distance, rough fur density, and… oh my, saliva is flying. Nevermind, there is no need to focus on all that – at the resolution that matters, the size is very large. That is a one-dimensional, low-resolution estimate, and it converts immediately to 'much larger than you'. Do the same with speed: it is based on time and distance, which could be expressed in seconds or minutes, feet or inches, but again reduce it — very fast, especially relative to you. Now those two estimates can be multiplied in the complexity space of size and speed to give an estimated time of contact. Perhaps add in the flinging saliva, as a very low resolution “AHHH!”. The point of all this reduction is simplicity of calculation, and removal of distraction. Your legs will know they need to approximately “RUN!!” as soon as possible.
The point of perception and cognition is not precision. The point is for each element to be reduced to the right complexity level for the question at hand. And to have the math that applies at that level to be as straightforward as possible. This is the same principle for all levels of focus – dimensionality reduction isn't a loss of truth, it is a choice about which truth is load-bearing for this particular problem. The bear’s fur density still exists in its own perspective. It just isn't useful here.
This is complexity space reasoning in practice: reduce to the relevant dimensions, use the math inherent in those dimensions, and trust that important perspectives you've left out will have their say through other channels.
Every perspective into a system consists of a number of elements, and how they interact. The thesis is that by describing the interactions of the elements, you are defining a complexity space, and the math of this space is inherent in the description. Simple spaces, like ordering, are so common we don’t even notice how we apply the same math in a multitude of unrelated situations. Others, like mutual attraction based on scale seem tailored for gravitational equations, yet similar math appears in economics, acoustics and electrostatic forces. This is just a problem with our intuition - we would be shocked to see linear order not be linear, but as systems get more complex we feel the math is emanating from the system, rather than inherent in the complexity space we model it with. We are able to hold many of these different perspectives in our heads at once, and by melding them together we create cognition, memory, and prediction.
Every value has a context that calibrates it. The number seven means 'seven ones'. Seven miles is calibrated against one mile. Simple versions of these spaces appear in geometry — points, lines, areas, volumes — but the idea extends much further: color, sound, social interactions, biological niches. Everything measurable is measured against some complexity space. Everything transformed is transformed within the rules of one. Mathematically they are akin to vector spaces, but with a wider net cast.
To understand this all, we need to start with a single element, and see what operations interacting with new elements allow.
A geometric example would be points vs area. We know a rectangle of 2x3 has an area of 6, but it is less obvious that the area can be treated as the 0D primitive in a perspective. If you start from ‘area’ and exclude the lines and points that construct it, there isn’t even a size to it, it is just an area (it might even be a circle or other shape). With multiple areas you can sort them by size, say one is twice the size of another, and even multiply them. Area is a perfectly fine primitive unit, as are points, lines and volumes. If you want to include the side lengths and position of an area, you have to include the perspective of those lower dimensions. The position will have 2 dimensions at least (x,y), and the rectangle with have 4 elements (TB, LR) from 2 lines, along with merging operations. All of these can work together in the same space, or work in parallel in different spaces. But the key is that ‘area’, like anything else, can be a primitive in some chosen perspective.
Now notice how a single primitive, regardless how it exists in the greater reality, can not have any value attached to it without having something else to calibrate it. It can be ‘an area’ or ‘a point’ or ‘a color’, but without something to measure against, nothing more can be said about it. It is the working material, not information at this point. It is not null, it is valid, but it is uncharacterized. Mathematically we get null vs not null (not to dismiss this, it’s the mathematical equivalent of ‘let there be light’, just no information beyond that yet).
A second data point means there is a difference, and therefore information. With each point on its own we get the first example of counting, but no relationship between them.
If the two are merged it implies a line, or at least some path between them. It’s best to think of this as a path, with a straight line the simplest version of it. This difference over time implies change, and the difference over samples implies category range. It is two points merged into a 1D path, and gives us our first ‘complexity space’. There is a start and end, a potential navigable space between them, and potential extrapolations beyond them.
It is worth looking closer at what a complexity space gives us. Ultimately is a frame we can use to create, categorize, understand and manipulate things that fit inside the frame. For a given path, we can add points or other paths to it, and at an even more basic level, we can say if other data can exist in that frame or not (null or not null).
As a concrete example, two temperature measures of 20 and 40 can allow other ranges in them (25->30) and single points (38). There are two possible error states - the temperature falls outside the frame (like -100, or 35->55), or the new datapoint does not belong in the frame (e.g. a distance is not a temperature, so null).
Imagine the path of your drive to work. This is two datapoints interpolated (home->work) Adding a temperature datapoint to this path would not work, and would be null. A location in another city, or on another planet is also probably an error as it is so far outside the path it seems unrelated (unless you modify the ‘expected commute’ frame). Extrapolating beyond the ends of that path is also an error, but is something that has a fairly obvious fix (a pressure gradient that leads to a correct state). Someone else’s commute could be projected onto yours to compare, allowing things off the path to generate information. Even though the path is technically in 3D space, we can treat it like a line with bounds, and points further outside this range are in greater tension.
A very important point here is that the existence of error states in a complexity space is highly desirable. Where there is error/tension/surprise, there is a potential to learn. Our goal is to create a system where every perspective has intelligence, and the agency to express it. Agency is impossible with no information (I’m imagining a length, what is the length?), as well as with certainty (I’m imagining a length of 10 feet, what is the length?). With a bounded frame, we can apply ‘reasoning’ in reference to the frame. If someone says, ‘it’s hot today’ and it’s -5, you can adjust the frame (maybe yesterday was -20), or adjust the claim (that’s not hot!). It doesn’t mean the whole truth comes from this single frame of reference and data point, only that is allowed a say. The full context may be planning a picnic or snowboard trip, that is invisible to this perspective, but that doesn’t mean this perspective’s intelligence and agency isn’t an important part of a solution. We choose multiple perspectives that will help navigate a problem space in simple tractable ways. We don’t rate them by their size or complexity, but rather their utility.
The simplest complexity spaces have the fewest degrees of freedom. A segment of two fixed points can create a path, but it has no information as there is nothing to compare it to. The points are fixed, so we can’t generate a comparison of change over time either. If you properly isolate it, it isn’t even a segment, ‘like other segments’ because there are no other segments. It is just something that exists vs not exists. However! If we add a variable point to this segment, we enter perhaps the simplest complexity space there is, proportions. The point could be 30% along the path, or two segments could be created (0->point and 0->end) and the first would be 30% the length of the second. Other math is possible here, like comparing the first to second part (3/7), or starting from the end (70% from end). Any math you can think of with this information is valid in this complexity space.
Integers, Rationals and Real numbers all have one degree of freedom, but their complexity spaces are subtly different.
Integers are the simplest, where you have one fixed segment, the unit, and one variable segment that can only move at the resolution of the unit. The unit is by definition 0->1, and the numerator is 0->n, so one degree of freedom. More subtly there is a third segment, the numberline itself, which goes from 0->unknown for positive numbers, and -unknown->+unknown for all integers. The resolution trick to avoid decimals may seem like hand waving, but remember nothing in reality is infinite (if we choose to model reality), so the simplest system must also define resolution even if it is unknown. We define the maximum of the numberline as unknown (or as large as possible, or fixed to some value, or infinite), and the minimum resolution as the unit. We do define these lengths, and they are an important part of any numbering system. Integers in computers wrap around to negative when they overflow. That may be different in different domains, but the size of the numberline is part of the definition of an integer, even if it is defined as unknown or infinite. So in the end, integers are made of four segments (numberline, resolution, unit and value), with one degree of freedom. Unit and resolution are the same segment in the case of integers. Note, there is a lot of math you can do with integers, and as always, all integer math is valid for anything you correctly model as integers.
Real Numbers are like integers, with the only difference being the numberline and the resolution are explicitly defined as infinite. An infinite numberline matters a lot when used in computers (requiring positive and negative infinity values when things become impossible to express), but infinite resolution is the more obvious difference. Real numbers still have a fixed unit of 0->1, but now the value can use proportions to create decimals. Note that there is always a little lie happening, because technically if there is infinite resolution you can never fully express anything - you will be too busy with infinite sequences. So the reality of real number resolution is that it is variably rounded based on context, not infinite. The context is not explicit in the numbering system, so we usually default to ‘more bits that we need’. In the same way, the infinite numberline is usually just ‘bigger than we need’. This gives a unique flavor of math, the big gain is we get decimals. And again, all math valid here if valid for anything that enters this space.
Rational numbers (fractions) start with the same system as integers where the resolution is the unit, and they add a new degree of freedom with a denominator. This allows everything to work without arbitrary rounding, and it is still able to express any number real numbers can express. In theory real numbers have more precision, but in reality the numerator and denominator can both have as many digits as you want. The philosophy of the systems is quite different though, so this does lead to real differences. While rationals get around the arbitrary rounding issue of reals, they are also designed to be used by people (as they were the dominant numbering system for most of history). This explains the ‘rule’ where reduced fractions are considered to be the same number as unreduced, and the feeling is you should usually express fractions in their reduced form. You can see the issue when looking at imperial measurement wrenches. You get sequences like 3/8ths, 7/16th, and 1/2. The impulse is to have everything in 16ths, so 6/16th, 7/16th, 8/16th, however that would make 33/64th impossible if you ever want to increase precision. The metric (decimal) system doesn’t really fix that either, you have sizes like 8, 9, and 10, which is easy, but it makes the size 9.333 awkward if you ever need it. To summarize, rationals are made of 5 segments (numberline, unit, resolution, numerator, denominator) where the resolution is the unit, and there are two degrees of freedom, the endpoints of the numerator and the denominator.
Are there other number systems possible on paths? Yes, of course. Many we know, and many we can invent for some specific need. Integers where the numberline starts at zero and goes to
One of my preferences is a rational number system where you don’t simplify fractions, but use the denominator to express resolution. For example 200/500 is one hundred times more precise than 2/5. If you think of five star reviews, the first has 100 reviews and is probably pretty accurate, whereas the second implies only one person thinks it isn’t great (it might be new, or it might be unpopular, the person might be right or just cranky, so there is uncertainty). This is essentially just rational numbers without reducing, and where the denominator has to be chosen with intention. The unit is the resolution (a number of ticks that equal ‘one’), the value is the range (the extent of this number). This itself can be used as a parameterized complexity space that holds other values. Other values inside this space only need a single measure (e.g. 245 ticks), as they operate in the frame of the original unit and range. Of course if that space is 2D or complex, each element in the space will need a matching number of measures.
The one issue with all these number systems is they don’t allow error. Any number is considered valid, no matter how large and small, even if it can’t be fully expressed. While this seems (and is) normal in math, we always use numbers with implied and actual resolutions and bounds. If we make those implications explicit, we can mathematically detect when values are out of range or precision, and mechanically adjust things without relying on human judgement for intervention.
First, evidence that we actually do this. If we shift our definition of infinity to ‘larger than we use’ rather than infinite, we acknowledge the idea of a boundary at both large and small scales. This doesn’t lock us into anything, we can always create more capacity if we need, but it does force us to consider boundaries and their behaviors. This is how numbers in computers work, because like everything else we understand in the world, they are finite machines. We use integers, which are limited resolution, and switch to floats for decimals. We move from bits to bytes to ints to ints to ‘big numbers’ as we need more scale. There are many options, but there isn’t a universal ‘everything is true’ number, because there physically can’t be. This is just as true outside computers, albeit less obvious.
Second, evidence that we do this because it is both natural and useful. We use limits in both science and engineering, not just with significant figures, but also with units. We don’t express the distance to the sun in millimeters, nor the size of an atom in miles. There is an implied resolution to these units, and an implied scale. We express tolerance and error as ranges, and we need to make sure our units error doesn’t swamp calculations. We can’t measure a turtle’s speed over one second with a stopwatch using markers every mile). We also use ranges all the time, for example everything measured as a percent is based on a range of 0 to 100. This is the first complexity space we encountered that gave us proportions, calibrated to a round number in base 10. This doesn’t mean we must discard our regular use of numbers, you can choose the bounds to be larger than you use, and the precision 100+ decimal places if you like. It’s just that recognizing these limitations as a real thing allows us to leverage them when it is useful (which is very often once you get used to it, and all the time if you’re a machine).
Adding error to the above number systems (complexity spaces) does not require much change. Integers already have built in resolution based on the unit size, meaning decimals are not possible. To create a range, all that needs to be done is to make the upper and lower bounds explicit, like 0 to 100 (percent), or -1000 to 1000. Proportions have the opposite problem, there are two fixed points forming a path, and a variable point inside that can move however it sees fit (no specified resolution). To specify resolution, you need a ‘tick’ size segment, or divide that path into a known number of segments. With 1000 ticks, you have a resolution of 1000, so 999/1000 is as close as you can get to maximum without being maximum. Note that these two systems now look more similar, a fixed number of divisions along a fixed length path.
Real numbers can be made finite by combining both of these systems. The unit is divided into a known number of ‘ticks’, and the scale of the numberline itself is specified. Again, this is not that unusual. If you have a tape measure, you will get 10 (or 16) ticks per division, and it will have a finite length. The decimal system itself does this, where we need to pick the number of decimal places to specify precision. The main issue is that it has to be a power of 10, which is not very precise. If you are counting 5 star reviews, it makes sense to have 5 ticks per number. 100 reviews would create a range of 100 to 500 (you can’t specify 0 stars for a review). You can see the complexity space that emerges here, it has a dynamic min and max range based on the count of reviews, and each review is a fixed number of 5 ticks. The math is inherent in that space, you don’t ‘decide’ that the lowest possible score is reviewCount/5. It is part of the space, not the review system, and is easily discoverable by both people and machines.
With this error, we can not only spot problems, but we can evolve the system to improve at the level it is at. With a little intelligence involved, one can imagine the review system discovering (over time) that expected range of 100 reviews will be 100->500 rather than 0->500. It then could adjust many of its outputs to be more accurate based on this new parameterization. The five star review system itself is usually part of a larger system that accommodates cost, seasons, reviews, country, UI, returns, self interest etc. The 5 stars still get a vote here, but other algorithms put pressure on it, and it may well adjust its range and precision over time. An intelligent local algorithm may discover that 4 stars are high praise in Japan and yet lukewarm in the US. It could then automatically adjust its output over time, with this new and improved calibration. This doesn’t have to come from a star rating algorithm looking at country data, it just feels different error pressure in each locale and adjusts itself to create more accurate predictions. This localized intelligence that can push and be pulled by external tensions (without inspecting and understanding things outside its domain) is the key to distributed intelligence, and highly capable machines.
We now have a few complexity spaces that are both bounded and have a specified resolution. One aspect that we glossed over it the case where the bounds can be -1000->1000, or in the ‘100 five star ratings’ case, 100->500. This is obviously a range, which takes two numbers to encode, requiring two degrees of freedom. There are many ways to encode this, but most will lead to slightly different complexity spaces, so it does matter which you choose. Two numbers based on order works (100->500), but this does require rules to clarify ambiguity. For example, is (500->100) equivalent? Is the order min->max, or start->end? What would (500->100) imply here if order mattered? It seems to imply some kind of inversion of the numberline, and that would need to be clarified before the space could be used.
Another way to think about it is to embrace the inverting of the numberline and see what space this leads to. If a segment has a start and end, and we think of the end as ‘rightwards’ (in our positive-right system), then the start would be leftwards. What does rightwards mean? It means the unit points from zero to the right, which makes all numbers on the right of zero positive, and all on the left of zero negative. So by this logic, there would be an equivalent ‘start unit’ that points leftward (positive left), and this would encode the start point. We can call this the inverted unit (i), but it is as valid a unit as the rightward unit, it just encodes the start point, and the normal unit encodes the end point. This means that a start point at the -2 position would be encoded as ‘+2 inverted’, or 2i for short (positive is to the left for the start point). An end point of 6 would just be 6, as we normally encode numbers with this unit, as ‘positive-right’ segments from zero. We can now combine the start and end points by appending them, and we get 2i+6 to encode the segment from -2->6. Our star-rating system is -100i+500. Note that this is order invariant, 500-100i means the same thing. The start being leftward is just a choice, rotating the number line to be upside down would make the end point leftward and none of the math would change.
And speaking of the math, the math of this complexity space is pretty much the same as the math of complex numbers. Using a start point instead of a rotation means that there is a MOD option for the i variable, and of course it is parameterized differently (a numberline instead of radians). In spite of that, essentially all operations work the same even though the intuitions are very different. There are additional Boolean operations that make sense in this space, so the traditional complex number space is more a subspace of this. (I’ve written much more about this space elsewhere if you are interested).
This is not to say traditional complex numbers are wrong or misrepresented. They are a path into this type of space, one that has two degrees of freedom and two orthogonal units. Where the spaces are conceptually the same, the math is the same. There is no right and wrong here, as the truth comes from the space, not the model that brought you.
In that spirit, one can imagine the model where there is an X and Y axis and all segments start at zero being exactly the same as this segmental complex number space. And it is, as long as you choose to interpret it the same. You will discover things like positive area and negative length/area in both systems, but that isn’t too surprising when you consider 3*-2=-6 (we tend to default the area to positive, which is maybe the weird part). There are lots of things to explore in these spaces with two ‘types’ and two degrees of freedom, going forward we’ll use segments not anchored to zero as our mental model for it as this casts a pretty wide net into the space.
We’ve touched on parameterization of complexity spaces already, but we’ll make it explicit. If you have a proportion type space, it doesn’t matter how long it is or what the resolution is, it will be the same space. If you are 30% of the way between Fargo and Winnipeg, or 30% of the way through your coffee, it is the same space. It can be parameterized in metric, imperial, with large volumes or small frequencies. The space is structural, and the rules and relationships are what creates the structure.
The five-star review system has a dynamic range (1->5 vs 100->500) based on review count, and this can vary like the dynamic star count or sample count itself. This can still be considered one degree of freedom though, as the scale and resolution are either defined explicitly or calculated through rules. Only the number of stars on each review is not predictable. Expressed as an equation (which all complexity spaces can be), there is only one unknown that isn’t structural.
There are three ways to scale this system of complexity spaces discussed so far, in serial, in parallel, and increasing complexity by merging. First, flesh out more spaces by exploring things like new operations and behavior sequentially, over time. Second is to combine multiple spaces to run in parallel to give a higher conceptual understanding of what is being modeled. Third is to move to higher order spaces by adding degrees of freedom, or merging existing spaces together.
We will dive further into operations over time when discussing equations, but in short these are somewhat recursive in nature, and therefore
serial
Running spaces in parallel is the key to conceptual understanding, where we have a variety of perspectives and get a ‘gist’ of the whole. Imagine seeing something moving towards a tree. We might make a size estimate along some expected size path, cat to truck. We can estimate speed with a few samples, distance over time, and that gives us momentum using speed and size. This tells us it will probably hit the tree, given the physics. However a parallel circuit tells us it is in the bear size range, and therefore is probably alive, so it will probably adjust course. Meanwhile the tree is tree size, has a large round vertical base, and is probably not moving. All this ‘negotiates’ in our mind to expect no collision, and we can use that new information to inform our ‘danger incoming’ mode to activate and adjust accordingly. This parallel execution of small commingled intelligences is the key to fast reaction and good prediction. A large model that considered the whole world for each thought would not be effective here, regardless of how well or poorly it scored in a classification metric.
Lastly we look at merging to expand into higher complexity spaces. Note first that merging is not running two in parallel. A length and a width separately can describe 2D paths, but only when they are merged can they describe an area. And no matter how many areas you use, it is only when two are merged that you get a volume.
Spaces can be scaled by adding degrees of freedom. This can be done by just adding a variable, such as we do going from 1D lines to 2D area to 3D volumes. This is always valid, as long as it can map to your problem space. We won’t go heavily into this, just to say these are all new complexity spaces, and they have the same ‘lack of error’ feature/problem as the number systems above. They work very well for certainty, and less well for uncertainty.
Note exactly what is happening to create these ‘higher order’ spaces, the values are being merged (multiplied) together. If they remain independent, like an XYZ 3D space, you can only define points in that space. The points can be merged into paths, areas or even volumes, but that will still require merges. And crucially, if you create a volume with say an area merged along a path, that volume is now 1D (it can be described with 1 degree of freedom, e.g. 30 liters). If you want to use the volume as well as the shape, you need to also preserve the line and the area it was extruded along, and use that information in that space. This is how complexity spaces naturally interact, even when there is no uncertainty – different perspectives contain different portions of the truth which work in tandem to construct a concept.
Another way to look at expanding complexity spaces is continually squaring them. So two points make a line, two lines make an area, and two areas make a volume. We usually think of three lines making a volume rather than two areas, however this binary-like progression has some interesting differences. If you think of intersections, it is easy to see that two values along X and Y will always create a valid rectangle when merged (2X and 3Y gives a rectangle with an area of 6). This is still true with non zero segments, where the segments (-2i+4)X and (-4i+7)Y intersect to create an area of 6, offset from zero in the top right quadrant. There are also invalid areas here, where anywhere outside the intersection could be considered ‘wrong’ and correctable.
The change comes when two areas combine to create a volume rather than 3 lines (an area using 4 numbers rather than 3). In this situation, two planes connect completely orthogonally at zero, tip to tip, with one plane rotated 90 degrees (see image). Now when creating areas on each of these planes you can see that it is not always possible to get an intersection. In many situations this is desirable, as it shows that increasing the complexity narrows what is valid, or even possible. For a contrived example, imagine temperature, water, and flowrate through a pump. For temperature and water, all states are possible, just not always desirable - very hot is steam, very cold is ice, and we prefer the range of liquid. Now when adding the pump speed, things outside certain ranges are just not computable - you can send ice or steam through a water pump, so the correct answer is more like null than 0. You can move parameters around to get to a non-null state by looking at valid areas where the three intersect. With three lines, you just get three numbers with flow rate being zero, but there is no way of knowing that there is error in the mechanism - that would be a valid zero if the pump was turned off for example. As you scale up in dimensions, it is generally harder to get a conceptually meaningful intersection. Every extra parameter has a chance of being an outliner, or just being incompatible with the interpretation of the system. This also gives a natural projection into much higher dimensions, where a ‘super volume’ is just two volumes merged (and of course this isn’t just about geometry, there are plenty of systems with more than ‘three’ dimensions).
We can think of operations as synthesising new elements, or modifying existing ones. This distinction is important, but it is blurrier than it may seem, so it is worth a closer look. If you have independent horizontal and vertical lines, you can stretch or shrink either one. This is modifying existing elements, and is necessarily a sequential step, because there is a before and after. You can also group them to make an XY grid, or you can merge them to make an area. These are new elements that have been synthesized, but we must be careful with the ‘new’ word here. They are not new in the atomic variable sense, where they sever all connections with what created them.
Creating an area by merging two orthogonal lines does synthesize a new perspective, however the area we created is not independent of the original lines unless we explicitly make it so. I can measure the surface area of a balloon and then blow it up. Depending on the perspective I choose, that value will now be larger (always measure the surface area of said balloon) or stay the same (the original surface area). Either way, that value is tied to some state of the balloon, and comes from some measurements on it. We can choose to wipe all history of the measurement, and just use it as a unit of some sort, like we do with horsepower or ‘foot’, but that needs to be a choice. If my foot or horse grows, I don’t expect to change my unit, where if my balloon surface area is estimated by its diameter, I expect it to change as the diameter increases. Most ‘new’ synthesized elements retain their connection to the original source, which is why we can multiple perspectives all usefully contribute to the truth of a concept.
This goes the other way as well, modification of an existing value is also subtly a synthesis. We can take a segment of 3 units, and add 2 to make the segment 5 units. Or we can stretch it to be twice the length, to 6 units. These are both modifications of the original, but there is a merge step in there. 3+2 is 5, not two segments that add up to 5 (that would remain a grouping). Stretching a segment (multiplication) does need to specify how much it will stretch by, 2 in this case. There are many ways to mentally model this, but they all involve a second value that participates in the amount of stretching. Even along a line you have in some sense merged these two values. So while it is easy to imagine you have the same element after the operation, it is important that your process clarifies what exact modify/synthesise behaviour you are modeling. This is less important in one simple equation, but as multiple equations connect into different perspectives of the same conceptual object, these distinctions become material.
Most operations are between two elements, and there are surprisingly few of them. First, for a single element, the only operation they can do on their own is create/delete. In computers, increment and decrement are considered ‘unary’ operations for chip architecture reasons, but they require the +1 or -1 so are in fact addition. Two element operations boil down to grouping, appending, scaling, and boolean operations.
Grouping is akin to a set in its most basic form, but also includes constructing complexity spaces. For example, two lines can be grouped as a set of two, but also can be partially merged by joining the zero points and making them orthogonal. They are merged but not fully solved (fully merged would be an area), in that the original lines still exist, and they can be used to calibrate other values that exist in the new complexity space. This partial grouping is similar to the difference between solvable and partially solvable equations (3*2+1 vs A*B+C). In the latter, values can be plugged in to explore the equations, where in the former there is no such flexibility.
Appending is addition, which of course includes subtraction. This is a two step process, first grouping values, and then merging in a way that preserves all their values. Thinking geometrically we need to imagine some algorithm, like sorting tip to tail, but it is better to think of something like weight, where the positions don’t play a part. You can put apples in a bag, and from that bag you can get a 1D weight that is independent of all sorting. In fact that bag could be a blender, and the addition would still be valid for the resulting applesauce. That value becomes its own thing, and the original apple attributes are not visible from its perspective.
Scaling is multiplication, which includes division. We can think of this geometrically as stretching, which is recursive in the sense of increasing or decreasing relative to its original self. And again, it does require a second value to be involved, but more as a director than ‘contributor of stuff’. Notice that scaling can be thought of as continuous over time, where addition is a two step process of group->merge.
Boolean operations are a one step operation, and have a wider variety of outcomes that can even move into higher or lower dimensions. They are under-represented in our school curriculums, but are vital to things like logic and computation. There are commonly known operations like AND, OR, and NOT, but in fact for two elements, there are 16 possible bool operations, and all of them matter. We usually do bool operations on true/false, or bits, but the same logic applies in higher dimensions. We see higher dimensions with the union and intersection of rectangles or segments, and this is probably a more useful way to develop a good intuition here.
First thing to notice is bool operations are one-shot. You have source and target segments, one operator, and the result is instant. If two segments don’t touch, the intersection (AND) of them is null. The target segment doesn’t gradually get shorter and disappear, it is immediately gone.
Second thing to notice, we had one target segment, and now we have no result segment. That is a reduction of elements from 1 to zero. In the same way, if we union the same segments (OR) we start with one target segment and end with 2 result segments. We have increased the complexity.
The third thing to notice is in simpler complexity spaces, bool operations can mimic scaling or appending, but this doesn’t mean they are the same. My favorite example is the way explain 2*3 to a child using a grid. It creates a rectangular box in the top right quadrant with an area of 6. Yet -2*-3 is also 6, and we feel less comfortable putting the same resulting box in the same position. -2*3 is even stranger, as we have no way to display negative area. Viewing this as an ‘OR’ operation, with segment intersection makes more sense here. This is explained when we leave our anchored zero point, and let both of those segments moved freely (detached segments as complex numbers). Here the intersections are still intuitive, where to get a rectangle of area 6 sitting at any position in the grid. Multiply this gives a different answer, the same answer you get when multiplying complex numbers. And yes, this is still intuitive, and it still can describe reality. It is a much more complex perspective though, and probably isn’t suitable for explaining multiplication to children.
Here are the 16 boolean operations for reference. This may seem like too much detail, and indeed they can be categorized in simpler sets, but this is the raw form of them. They are key operational primitives for combining elements, and very much worth internalizing.
Before equations can be usefully sequential, they must be able to adjust to the previous steps output. This pressure can come from the results of running the equation. Imagine stretching something to be twice as large in slow motion, there is a ‘larger’ pressure at each moment until the equation is resolved. The ‘times two’ is slowly used up as it approaches equilibrium.
We often model decisions as choices and branching, but in a dynamic system it is often more useful to resolve over time. This allows all inputs and perspectives to ‘have a vote’, meaning potential solutions can be probed and even reversed.
Imagine the example of a dog running towards a tree. We can calculate its range of motion given its speed and weight, giving some range from the left to the right of the trunk. We can ‘NOT’ the tree part, leaving a left side or right side path. At this point we might randomly pick left or right, if/then style. However in a dynamic equation with multiple perspectives we don’t need to go that far. The ‘vote’ from this level is maybe left, maybe right. Some other perspective may know about the rabbit it’s chasing, or the stream it wants to drink from, and weigh things in that direction. The goal is to allow each perspective to contribute accurate information from its view, which means not underspecifying, but also not over-specifying.
Many common equations are actually dynamic adjustments over time. This allows the equation to examine the output and recycle that into new values. Every sequence works like this, as well as sign waves and most of calculus. Sometimes we can jump ahead with clever calculation, but we may not want to do that when we have many variables interacting. Not only does this allow a negotiated truth, but it allows us to narrow in on local truths as new information comes in. What starts looking like a line, may look more like a curve after a few more data points, and eventually resolve to assign wave.
This time difference can be backed into other simple equations such as multiplication, and even addition. This is, of course, the choice of the perspective, but the only truly one shot equations are creation, deletion, and Boolean operations. This allows complex dynamic operations to run in parallel over time, even if some are not considered continuous.
To reiterate, there is no ‘always correct’ way to set up a complexity space, it will depend on what you are modeling and how you choose to interpret it. Take two orthogonal unit lines. If you just add them together you get an L shaped path, and then merging them with multiplication gives an area. As you look at this over time, you can imagine a stair step diagonal that seems more continuous with finer resolution steps - the result looks like a diagonal line, but its length is always 2. Alternatively it could be continuous merging of the lines, and you end up with a diagonal, with the length being sqrt(2). These are all valid, and they have different implications. The important thing is these choices are first class properties of equations, and should not need to be inferred from notes in the margin. Or worse, not even noticed in their absence.
This brings us closer to the final form of complexity spaces, calibrated equations. When a full equation has no variables it is just a fact, 2*3=6. With one variable it can be solved (or not), 2*3=?, so it has use, but only in its exact context. With higher variability equations have different interpretations, which is bad for calculation, but good for exploration. Equations like 2a+2b<24 are unsolvable, but fit questions like “I have 24 inches of moulding, what sizes of picture can I frame?”. An equation like this allows you to plug in multiple values and compare them, and is more useful with other equations, like “how much space on the wall”, “what is the smallest reasonable frame”, “how are the people in the photo positioned” etc. Having resolution, ranges, and free variables allows all equations to work together to negotiate a solution through iteration. It is also true that the mathematical behavior of 2a+2b<c is not something that needs to be invented or declared, it is inherent in appending and scaling.
Choosing the correct equations to model a problem is usually the difficult part, especially for a machine. The advantage of multiple equations iterating towards a better solution is you don’t have to know the solution before starting, and the answer doesn’t need to be perfect before being useful. The machine may start modeling squares (4a<24), and while not perfect, it does give a good approximation. Later it can add an aspect ratio equation, and the two can negotiate a size. These may even merge into the single equation above over time. It also allows higher resolution adjustments, like how the inner diameter will be smaller than the outer one, how that depends on the thickness, and how a mat overlay can affect usable size. All of these are valid, but some are lower levels of detail and may only become important at later stages. Using multiple partial equations with simple math and knowable error is a much more flexible system, and is much easier for machines to learn with.

If you add two lines on the same numberline (same type) they append, but if you add orthogonal lines you get an L shape.
