===== Relational contexts.docx =====
[normal] Relational contexts
[normal] All information is the result of comparing something measurable with a ‘ground’, and this ground value is always external to the object in question.
[normal] There are no yardsticks in the universe, so by necessity our meaning comes from the potential of everything being compared to everything else. This does not mean it’s just a 24/7 free for all though. We always select a non random frame of reference to encode information. This choice is as important as the value we are interested in, but it is so taken for granted that it is often invisible to us. The height and depth of an iceberg is referencing the water level, a color is a material’s ‘reaction’ to visible light, a width is the relation of two sides to space, and a big dog is referencing normal sized dogs. There is no color material attached to a tree, and no depth property inherent to an iceberg. It feels like a dog has a size all on its own, but without comparison it is just an arbitrary volume – and what is the size of volume? Is a sphere big?
[normal] All of our concepts, primitive, compound or metaphorical, spring from the physical world, but it is important to remember that the physical world contains no information. It doesn’t compare anything to anything else - it just is. It is numerators without denominators. You could argue that two points exist and the distance between them is information, but who’s two points? Those must be selected by something else, as the two points know nothing about each other. Then they must be compared with another two points someone chooses, otherwise it is just a length, and a length isn’t long, short, or 72. It’s just a length with no information other than it’s a length.
[normal] The physical world has energy, matter, space and time. Even if conceptually combining these (space to space is distance, matter and space is density etc) there is still no information. All states and changes just ‘are’. Is speed fast? If I’m thinking of two points, the only information you have is what I’ve already told you - that I’m thinking of two points. A value between them exists, but a) that is already an implicit comparison and b) it has no meaning and no way to be expressed.
[normal] It is like a numerator without a denominator, but that implies the top and bottom are both capable of being a number. In reality (and in math) a number itself requires a denominator (7 is 7/1), without it the numerator is just a ‘floating value’. Math rightly doesn’t commit to what numbers represent, but numbers are assumed to represent something – even if that something is  just an abstract transferable unit in a numbering system. What that something actually is will be expressed in the denominator. More concretely, in LanguageMath, ‘seven dogs’ would be 7/’a-dog’. A group of seven dogs might be 1/’a-pack-of-dogs’.  The numerator alone is just a floating value, without meaning until it is grounded with a denominator. A big dog is ‘big/a-dog’. With the denominator alone you still have a dog, but the numerator alone is a floating ‘big’ that actually tells you nothing about the size (a big ant or a big planet?). We don’t have a word for this floating value really, it’s like if I say ‘this much’ but you can’t see what I’m referring to. It’s a measurable thing that exists, but without context (a denominator) it could represent literally anything and therefore means nothing. Maybe it’s just an adjective or adverb, but without connotations. The universe then isn’t full of numbers, it’s full of floating values that only become ‘language numbers’ when minds enter the scene, with their categories and expectations.
[normal] What we do then, is always always have a ground — a frame of reference of some sort, that the property in question relates to. And this ground is always extrinsic to the object itself, because it has to be in order to generate a comparison. So a property isn’t an attribute of an object, it is the way an object relates or reacts to something else. Sometimes this dependence is clear, like color being a relation to visible light, other times it is based on context, like how balanced an object is depends on a fulcrum, and ultimately a gravity field. When comparing an object to itself, it will always be identical, which only tells us ‘same things are the same things’. So an external calibration must be used. A heavy dog’s perceptual weight is based on some average dog weight, and the numeric weight is based on some agreed unit of weight like a pound or kilogram which is based on our gravity field. If you dissect a dog, you won’t find a ‘weight property’ in there. A way to think of it is the grounded property (denominator) is on ‘a dog’, while the focused value is on ‘the dog’. This isn’t the whole story though, as objects have grounding beyond their physical form - a table of data uses the grounding of a table as ‘a place to spread out objects of interest’, while ‘a table’ filters out metaphorical groundings that aren’t relevant to a physical table. The ‘table concept’ not only includes all these groundings, it is made of all these groundings and nothing else.
[normal] The more common a ‘ground’ is, the more likely it will become a category or concept in our thoughts. Pinks, browns and oranges can be thought of as types of reds, but this would leave the ‘ground red’ doing a lot of work - light red, dark red, yellowy red etc. Sub colors feel natural for red, but we don’t do the same for blues or greens. Dark blue, cyan, navy blue, and baby blue are describable, but don’t get the full orange, pink and brown color status. The color monikers make them easier to use as a ground themselves, think ‘hot pink’ vs ‘hot baby blue’. The important thing is we choose these grounds by habituation, and we do the same with non-words (like dog sizes, and the water level relating to icebergs).
[normal] There is a certain math with grounds that language uses very flexibly. We can set the ground (say the water level) and then create a positive or negative expectation (height or depth) and calibrate them (a little high, very deep). We can also negate these expectations directionally (‘he was less than helpful’) and invert them (‘very unhelpful’). We are also very good at tagging a resolution along with our grounding (‘about a day's journey’ vs ‘three and a half hours at a brisk walk’). Our minds do this all invisibly with great speed, and our numbers extend the accuracy to the extremes. Ironically numbers do not allow flipping the positive expectations (‘un-‘) or expressing the resolution, unless, shameless plug, you use the number system I’ve been working on, which does :).
[normal] So we can imagine now, instead of a concept having some giant amount of properties with expected ranges, we have concepts that just interact with things they encounter in the world. There are a lot of interactions, but we only ground the common interactions we care about. This means all things have all properties, even if they aren’t commonly associated together. All things react in some way to visible light, so they all have ‘color’. We don’t need to attach a red color to an apple, we just expect it to appear red in visible light. And seeing it in the orange light of a sunset doesn’t surprise us, as we expect things to react differently to different light values. The ‘math’ of red is not stored in an apple definition, and a blue apple is still an apple, just some extrinsic property of it has been modified. This means that we only need to understand how things interact with visible light, and everything known and unknown automatically gets a color. And we can even apply color perception to things that don’t intrinsically interact with light at all, like a blue mood or white knight.
[normal] Properties being an interaction with something external is why metaphor is so easy in language. Legs on a house seems wrong, but in a flood zone you see it a lot, they are called legs, and nobody is confused. I can even say ‘a walking house’ or ‘an angry house’ and an expected image comes to mind. A house walking upside down with the legs coming out the roof however, just seems wrong. This is because legs are a common grounding we can apply to any concept (this idea has legs!), but the grounding has them underneath.
[normal] Everything we can imagine can have legs, but unless we have a context that focuses on them they aren’t mentally present. This is true even for things defined by legs, like a table or chair. ‘He served all six tables at once’, does not invoke a mental concept of legs. A table includes concepts like four legs, a flat surface, a place to gather, an eating location, a work surface, something you sit in front of, and so on. These concepts aren’t part of the table itself though, and the only one that needs to be valid is the one that fits the active context. If you suggest we ‘go sit at the table’, and then go to the ping pong table, that would require clarification. And when you do your homework on the floor, there is no need to borrow concepts and math from the table’s ‘place to do work’ modality. ‘Place to do work’ lives independent of tables, and it can be applied to literally anything, just like every other property. Again, this is because it is how an object relates to using it as a place to do work, not that it is inherent in the objects themselves.
[normal] This also explains how for every ‘requirement’ needed to define table, I can give a table example that doesn’t have that requirement. Made of wood? Aluminum. Four legs? How about three. Flat surface? Warped table. And floors have flat surfaces, are they tables? In the end, a concept is how we use an object for grounding, not the object itself. You can table a proposal while chairing a meeting, while standing on one foot in a park. The concept of the table is in the grounding, not in the wood.
[normal] So this seems like everything affects everything, and there are a lot of things, so how can we possibly compute all this? First, we reduce things to context, which is probably not more than five or six properties at once. Second, we expect things to react in similar ways. Heating anything up will make it warmer, usually, and too much will melt or burn it, usually. This allows broad reuse of default expectations, and then learning variations as we drill down (metals behave a little differently than average, and copper a little differently than that). Third, these properties also tend to affect each other in similar ways. A larger dog tends to be heavier, and ‘larger is heavier’ is the default expectation for everything. This doesn’t mean we die of shock seeing a helium balloon, just that registers as surprise, and surprise remembered is learning. This allows us to not just tweak our balloon expectation, but creates a new size/weight algorithm that we can use to associate to other things (say clouds) and use this new concept as a ground (“your idea will go over like a lead balloon”).
[normal] The fourth ‘compression trick’ we use takes advantage of the fact that patterns in one area are often similar to patterns in another. This lets us map these patterns separately from their embodiment, and reuse them as we see fit. Heat transfers through metal like the way panic moves through a crowd like the way a fart disperses in a room. You can be between jobs, between the sheets, or between a rock and a hard place. We separate out the pattern, in what I think of as ‘super prepositions’ - words that describe a reusable pattern, including things like jagged, corner, filtered or endless. Properties are always compared to some extrinsic ground, and the expected/allowable patterns and constraints that result are also extrinsic to the comparison. This results in an extensive toolbox we can mix and match to assess familiar and novel things.
[normal] When we see a brand new object, we are pretty well equipped with default expectations. These defaults don’t just give us better than random predictions, they give us a ‘ground’ to calibrate with. “An otter is like a wet cat but more playful”. The denominator is the familiar default cat with its many known relations to the world, and numerator is how otters relate to social environments (giving context to the denominator, which is now the quiet, aloof, independent, and certainly dry cat). This tells us a great deal about the unknown otter, as we have so many cat defaults, and playfulness was chosen as a major difference (which drags with it hints of energy levels, speed, safeness, curiosity). Notice how ‘playful like a puppy’ would be less informative, because it just compares one property, rather than relate to a ‘ground’ animal with selected differences.
[normal] CAD
[normal] “Sure, maybe”, I can hear you say, “but what does this all have to do with computer aided design?”. Well that’s the thing, CAD is at the intersection of human concepts and mathematical computability. So a good CAD model needs to leverage computation in the same way we do. So not only does this apply to CAD, CAD is the best tool for discovery here.
[normal] Normally a CAD model will take a conceptual object, say a trace in a PCB, and add properties to it, say path, endpoints, width, branches, thickness etc. Then elsewhere you model the edge of a table and you add other properties, say position, strength, straightness, material, texture, joint adhesion, scale, precision etc. In reality though, all things have all properties, because the properties are not inherent to the thing, they are a relation to something external. The edge of a table has a conductivity (it has a reaction to a voltage difference) just like a copper trace. And a trace has a texture, even though we may not care about it. If you try welding on a wooden vs metal table, you will care about electrical properties of tables, and you won’t have much trouble with it because you already understand charge flow to that level. So all properties will be applicable to all things, even if you don’t always focus on them.
[normal] Second, you apply metadata like working ranges, elastic ranges, and breakdown ranges. You aren’t specifying the actual current or frequency in a trace — that will be from its environment. You are just specifying how it behaves in the normal ranges of its expected environment, and when it fails. If you attach the trace to a pin, the pin will also have these properties and expected ranges, and here we can compute predictions. Perhaps there is too much current and we need to widen the trace. Or the voltage may sag and we add a capacitor. The point is we can ALWAYS map values to properties we care about at these junctions, because all things will react to and potentially transform the environment. You can imagine AI being able to insert a capacitor when it detects voltage sag by working to keep properties in expected ranges. The way we do it now is to show it capacitors, and expect it to derive ‘why’ they are there and extrapolate this to other situations. People would also fare poorly in this situation.
[normal] CAD is normally constraint driven, you specify two lengths are equal, or an intersection is at a right angle etc. Then with all these constraints, you end up with a fully defined object. However, you always need at least one grounded element, much like in the real world. Unlike the real world, these specifications are very concrete, and operate at the same low level of abstraction. We can’t say ‘this edge is smooth’ or ‘that hole is big’. It more this distance is mm, that line is parallel.
[normal] We also can’t take information from other levels in CAD. The software may say this pin is used as a high frequency clock signal, an antenna, a led signal, or a power source. That isn’t inherent in the chip or the PCB layout, only the software has this information. Yet this is crucial information that informs trace routing decisions!  Neither the input nor the output of PCB designs encode such things. It might be in a noisy environment with lots of vibration, or it might be in space. It might be a military future project, or a cheap toy. This is all important context all the way down, and it informs everything in the CAD model. Any attempts to ‘AI generate’ circuits are doomed to fail without this context, much like humans would be.
[normal] Another missing tool in CAD is permissive constraints rather than restrictive ones. A line that is allowed to change its path or have branches is more actionable than specifying a single possible path using restrictions. These are more like observations than constraints, like one edge is sharp on a knife. You don’t specify anything concrete, like which edge, how long it is, or if it’s curved. It is a grounding element, a concept, that applies to the knife you are designing. And with that information, and the fact that it is going to be gripped, we get new design observations, like ‘make sure the grip doesn’t easily slide into the sharp edge’. The whole thing can be designed with these different levels of concepts, and then instantiated repeatedly in custom ways, akin to parameterized concepts.
[normal] Really, any time you see numbers in CAD, that is an embodiment of a concept being specified, not the concept itself. If we list affordances and constraints, at all levels, many satisfactory embodiments can be created. If we require a game controller to ‘feel comfortable in the hands’ (how it relates to hands), then a kids version would look different than an adult one. How do we encode this? Same as above. We know how things relate to other things, we know various patterns (smoothness, tactile clicks, color contrasts), and we have AI+people. We do the math, much like our language and mental models do, and we get output we can iterate on with more conceptual guide rails.
[normal] The future is coming, and it no longer wants us to work at the numeric instance level. We need to get used to expressing things conceptually with grounded concepts, much like we do with each other. You won’t program the numeric motions of a robot any more than you specify the footfall positions when giving directions to a stranger.
[normal] This is all totally doable with our current technology, we just need a fresh look at formats, at math, at concepts, and the fresh worldview that comes with all that.

===== Segments.docx =====
[normal] number is 0 based segment, we only change the endpoint
[normal] Adding is just merging two values bit by bit (+3 always adds 3)
[normal] multiply is stretching by an input ratio bit by bit (*3 adds a larger value based on original size)
[normal] segment is number with a startpoint and endpoint.
[normal] start point is an opposite number, not a subtraction (handicap/head start)
[normal] the length shows the total distance, so has a direction
[normal] both sides move in the dominant direction, i is ->| and 1 is |-> numberline is positive right ->
[normal] inverting the numberline flips those arrows, but only because it changes the dominant direction to <-
[normal] Adding is still shifting by the values
[normal] multiply is stretching by the input ratio
[normal] - total minus head start, and then proportions to account for where that force is on the line.
[normal] The start can be 'positive', where i would be -i. This is a mirror, as it heads to zero on the right. |<-
[normal] A mirror is literally a mirror, so zero can start with +i,-1 and end with +-
[normal] An equal length is not an equal number (2->5 vs 12->15) force, proportions

===== sessions\Axioms of Multi-Dimensional Structural Fusions.docx =====
[normal] Axioms of Multi-Dimensional Structural Fusions
[normal] Axiom 1: The Primitive Measure The foundational primitive is a single, isolated measure. A single measure does not possess an implicit zero; it represents a single reading that is entirely uncalibrated.
[normal] Axiom 2: The Origin Before an extent or distance can exist, a single measure must be frozen to act as a fixed origin point.
[normal] Axiom 3: The Unit Interval An interval is created by recording a second measure relative to the frozen origin. Freezing this interval establishes a unit—a portable denominator with a fixed magnitude that persists independently of changing values around it.
[normal] Axiom 4: Polarity, Perspective, and the Zero Unit Because units are derived from directed intervals from an origin, they inherently possess direction, establishing dominant and recessive perspectives (e.g., growing vs. shrinking) which are structurally inverted. However, a detected value that cannot be interpreted within these known unit directions manifests as a Zero Unit (0). The Zero Unit acts as an unknown "tension potential"—geometrically orthogonal to the established dimensions, like a value moving on a z-axis slider straight out of a 2D page. This uncalibrated energy seeks resolution by attaching to a newly defined unit that can explain it.
[normal] Axiom 5: The Four Modalities of Number Once units and intervals are established, numbers dynamically fulfill four observer-dependent intentions:
[normal] Claiming (stating a structural fact, e.g., "There is a segment").
[normal] Measuring (recording a new fact against a unit).
[normal] Inspecting (interpolating within a structure, e.g., finding a midpoint).
[normal] Generating (acting upon another segment to scale or translate it).
[normal] While driven by observer intention, these modalities inherently self-adjust when balancing structural tensions within the system. The system can observe itself, and use all these modalities with local structure, data and tension.
[normal] Axiom 6: Data vs. Fused Structure Recording multiple values against a single, shared unit produces uncalibrated data (sequential arrays), which are fragile and require external rules to interpret. Combining multiple values with differing or opposing units internalizes these rules into a physical, self-describing fused structure.
[normal] Axiom 7: The Directed Segment (1D Dual-Unit) Fusing two opposing units—one recessive and one dominant—creates a stable dual-unit. This structure inherently represents a bounded range or directed segment, allowing calculations like total length to fall out naturally via addition.
[normal] Axiom 8: Orthogonality and Area (2D Dual-Units) Fusing two independent, orthogonal units defines higher-grade 2D structures. Fusing aligned orthogonal units generates bounded positive or negative area, while fusing opposed orthogonal units causes the axes to act against each other, generating complex rays that define a length and angle.
[normal] Axiom 9: Unit Self-Fusion and Non-Linearity When a unit pairs and fuses with itself, rather than an orthogonal unit, it becomes self-interacting. This internal repetition alters the calibration of the unit so that intervals are no longer linearly spaced. This yields power progressions (squared, cubed) that model dynamically changing attributes such as acceleration, volatility, or changing intensity.
[normal] Axiom 10: Multi-Dimensional Change and Subunit Scaling To fully describe structural change across two dimensions, a system generally requires four values forming two directed segments (one structural dual-unit per orthogonal axis) to capture both the start and end states of the dimensional plane. However, this subunit fusion is dynamically scalable: expressing change requires fewer subunits if a dimension remains constant, but can scale to involve more than four final elements when self-interacting potentials (powers) multiply the relationships.

===== sessions\sessions.docx =====
[normal] I have been running on the assumption that an extent exists and that is the basis of growth in this numbering system. However in reality an extent is already something that has 2 ends, so it can't really be primitive. We think of it as primitive because we're used to measuring from zero for example the height of something, the time of a 100 meter dash, the weight of a bag of apples. This works because we have a convenient zero point that makes sense, but we cannot rely on this in the real world. A light sensor measuring a light level may never experience total darkness. A thermometer measuring temperature will never experience absolute 0. so the correct way to start this is with measures, and the simplest a system of a single measure will have a default 0. We can bootstrap from this.
 when we measure many people in a race, they can run one after another or all at the same time. We're starting from zero, and none of them run backwards, because there are no negative values. There are no negative values because we have an implicit 0, temperatures don't go below absolute 0, and absolute darkness does not get darker. So this single digit measure is by default a positive number and negative numbers do not exist. We still cannot create a unit from a single measure or even many measures. For this we need to pick some arbitrary position along this line and  store it for reuse. This can be one meter, or one second, or one abc.  we now have an interval, because we started at zero and went to ABC,  and we can use this interval to compare with all other measures for the same property. we did not create a  numerator/denominator relation, we simply took a value and froze it, declaring it a denominator.  this unit is not attached to any value at this point, and if you would inspect it you would find it to be just a regular measure like the others, other than it doesn't change value, and it persists. You can use this to measure any runners time, but you cannot use it to measure a runner that is going in the opposite direction. That's like asking how long will it take me to  get to the finish line if I run in the opposite direction. This would just be error and tension, even though I am still  running and being timed.
 that example sounds a little nonsensical, because it is a unit that has a pinned 0 and no negative values. However for something like temperature it is a lot more obviously useful.  if you have a temperature sensor it will give you some reading throughout the day, and that reading will be higher when it's hotter lower when it's colder. But it may be just a voltage, so you really don't know how to describe it. To do this correctly you need to take at least 2 readings, set the first one to origin and then remember the difference to the second one. this is an interval, and you can use it to measure both positive and negative values that you encounter based on their distance from zero, and in how many times larger or smaller than the unit they are. Notice that both of these situations require an interval with two numbers, it's just in the first that number is always 0 so we don't record it. There has been one assumption here though and that's that the second number will be larger than the first number. It is very possible somebody else calibrates this in the evening, and the second number is smaller than the first number. This works for calibration just as well, however bigger numbers will be colder now not hotter. even if you align the calibration in these two systems to be the same size and have the same zero point, they will not be compatible because the units point in opposite directions. That does not mean they are not both measuring temperature correctly, it just means there's two perspectives at play. With some formula you could convert these because they're the same underlying physical thing being measured, but that does not happen automatically.
 so now you have two  perspectives to measure temperature, and both work fine in their own way.  you can put it in any situation and you will get a single value of temperature that is accurate based on the calibrated unit. You can store many of these values and get a history that can be meaningfully compared.  the unit here is portable, and all temperature values can attach to it for calibration.
[normal] Now let's say you want to measure an interval, or the high and low of each day. both scales are able to do this,  you check the temperature, wait a little bit, and check the temperature again. Or you continuously check the temperature and record in two columns the lowest it gets, and the highest it gets. the default way to do this is 1 unit and two values, but there is a second way.
 If you combine the  cold unit with the hot unit to create a new dual-unit, you can also use this to measure temperature ranges. You could record the first reading in cold partial units (recessive) and the second reading in hot partial units (dominant), to get a single two value number with a dual unit. So a temperature range of-2°C to plus 5°C would look like 2r+5d. this may seem strange at first, it's like measuring the height of an iceberg by saying 20 deep and six high. But it is not too different than measuring a rectangle by saying 2x5 inches = 10 square inches.
 both systems work, multiple values with the same unit leads to data that is UN calibrated, as in you need to impose the spacing and meaning on raw values. For example you don't know that they are pairs instead of triplets, and if you ever miss a single recording, they will all be opposite after that time. If you use a dual unit with two values as a number, it is less fragile 2 missing data, you don't need to delineate values into pairs, and therefore you don't need to impose rules making it  a more physical representation of the underlying data. Other interesting things is 2r+5d gives you the range (total length) by running the addition, where -2d+5d doesn’t.  you could record the total length separately, but 7 degrees is extra data, and it doesn't include the zero point, so you don't know no the overall temperature, just the range. you need either extra data or an extra rule to get the range  if you use the same unit for two values.
[normal] now let's do the grade increase 2 area. Let's go with the iceberg, where we're measuring the width and the height.  if we go with both of those we can measure the two sizes and *roughly* estimate how much ice there is with some formula. What we can't do is measure change in either of those components without either going to data, or a dual unit. I think the data version is fairly straightforward, we just make recordings, create rules, pair things up and calculate. But a more physical version of this would be to create a dual unit that allows intervals.
[normal] vertically, this could be a growing or shrinking unit, and horizontally this could be a widening or narrowing unit. remember if we record using 2 growing units (or any same units), we just get datas that is a shared unit. if we pick two opposite units like growing and shrinking, we get horizontal or vertical intervals. The new thing is we can pick one of each, and create a fused unit. If we fuse the growing and widening units, larger numbers will mean more ice and smaller numbers will be less ice. If we fuse the shrinking and narrowing units, larger numbers will mean less ice and smaller numbers will mean more ice. This is positive area and negative area. Then if we go diagonally and pick growing and narrowing units, or shrinking and widening units, then larger or smaller numbers do not necessarily tell you about the amount of ice.  This is why they act like rays rather than areas. And This is why complex numbers are shaped like this, and can be described as a length and an angle, rather than an area. They can tell you volume only by a complex number formula that accounts for all 4 possible quadrants, because they act against each other. remember, regardless of the units you choose, the values attached to them can be either positive or negative. So if you've chosen growing lightening units, and your values are positive and negative, you are in the same situation where you cannot be certain about creating area, and you have to subtract 1 from the other.
 I think this might be a better explanation of growing an increasing the grade compared to what we have now, especially at the low level, could you integrate this into the axioms, or maybe better take the axioms into account but rewrite them with this taking precedence. Like you would freeze in area before you could measure larger and smaller areas etc. I don't think it makes a difference to the logic of it, just to cleaner re application of the rule.

===== Symmetrical Numbers Explained.docx =====
[Heading 1] Numbers from first principles
[normal] To construct numbers from first principles, you must first imagine a world without numbers, without values, and without references. This is hard, so it’s good to have a few models to work from, models that get you from nothing to something. One option is to imagine a universe with nothing in it at all, totally empty with no previous knowledge. No size, no color, no time, no naked ladies. Start from literally nothing.
[normal] Another option is you can model limited information, perhaps a sensor that you haven’t yet read, a bacteria without perception, or some imagined thing I haven’t told you about. However you model it, the model is unable to make assumptions beyond the information it has –  it exists isolated from the rest of the world, so comparisons to known references aren’t possible.
[normal] As more information comes in, it gives our model new ways to describe, define and manipulate what it already knows. Each new observation, no matter how seemingly trivial, is a tool that can be used for math. And as I hope to convince you, while we need at least four pieces of information to create numbers, there is a lot of math before and after that point we are ignoring.
[Heading 2] Zero to One
[normal] So we have empty space, an unread sensor, or someone’s secret. We have no information. Note that this isn’t ‘zero’, it’s the absence of information. It is null rather than zero. Now if we imagine the same system with one piece of information, what can we say about it? We of course can’t give it a size, a length or a color, as there is only one value and we don’t know anything about it without bringing in more information. You don’t even know what property is being described, never mind what object it belongs too. It could be a grain of sand or it could be a planet, and it could describe the size or prescience of kryptonite. We can’t even really call it zero, as that implies the potential to scale, or be compared to another value that isn’t zero. We CAN say there is something rather than nothing, and not much else – though to be fair that is a pretty big step.
[Heading 2] One to Two
[normal] Now imagine two pieces of information. Note this is not a new piece of information appearing, as that would imply ordering, which implies change over time, and we haven’t derived either of those concepts yet. It's just two pieces of information.
[normal] Let's dig into the implications of this. If I hand you a paper with dots, each dot is a piece of information. The number of dots I made and the amount of information on the page are not necessarily the same though. I may have put 100 dots in the same spot and you'll see one, or I may have made them all line up and you'll only see a line. If you stand further away you may see less dots than if you're close. THIS ISN'T TRIVIA. The system is the system you perceive or imagine. The freedom is you can imagine things however you like, not that you can misinterpret what you imagine.
[Heading 3] Resolution
[normal] A piece of information (a value of some property) depends on separating it from other values. If you glance at a thermometer for 5 seconds, you will get one, or hundreds, or millions of readings, depending where you draw the line between your axons and your brain, and how you define ‘a reading’. This means the resolution of the system matters when encoding values, real or imagined. It doesn't mean you can't have two identical numbers, just that they need to be separated somehow. Two values can be separated by time, in a table, or I can take your word for it that one dot is actually two. But in a system where there are only two pieces of information, you need to be able to separate them somehow so they are ‘not equal’, otherwise you only have one piece of information. Going backwards now, we can say a single piece of information has a difference of zero, because we don't actually know if it’s a single value, or many identical values that are ‘equal’. It is a ‘distance’ of zero, at the resolution we know it by. Separate things are not equal, but they may appear equal at a different resolution. Every value in the history of the universe comes with a resolution, observed or not, ignored or otherwise.
[Heading 3] Direction
[normal] While we don’t know the order of the samples we have, we do know for sure there is a separation between them. This means they have two possible orderings, A to B, and B to A. This is NOT a positive and negative direction, it is a length of ‘n’ from A to B, and the exact same length of ‘n’ from B to A. This is akin to the Y axis point up and the Y axis pointing down. Either one of these orientations can have negative changes (when values move in the opposite direction of the orientation), but there are two orientations, not one. This is a crucial point to internalize, not because it is complicated, but because our math doesn’t use it and it’s important. Essentially here we are choosing a direction for greater, and the opposite direction is less, which only requires two points.
[Heading 3] Length?
[normal] You would think that with two samples we would have a length, but we don’t. In the empty space model, we can have two positions and still have no idea how far apart they are. They might be the distance between two fingers, or the distance between two stars, and without fingers or stars there is no way of telling. If you imagine a line, I have no idea how long it is without more information, even though I know it has two endpoints. In fact all measures, real or imagined, are relative to other measures – the universe doesn’t come with a universal yardstick.
[normal] While we certainly can’t quantify the distance between our two samples, we do know it has a length, and we therefore can attempt to extrapolate and subdivide it. We can take two readings from a sensor, and imagine this growing and growing until it is as large as we care to imagine, or subdividing it into smaller and smaller pieces until it is way smaller than we can possibly work with. We also can imagine positions twice as long or half as long. A few caveats though. Just because we can imagine it doesn’t at all mean it represents real information. Math operations are a bit like predictions based on starting values, which might be useful. These predictions also do NOT imply things can be infinitely large or small. In fact you can’t actually imagine infinity even though the ‘not stopping’ algorithm is trivial. However, you can imagine that you can imagine infinity, and you can still ‘do math’ on abstract concepts like this. Lastly, can’t imagine an extrapolated position somewhere along A and B without coming into possession of a third value, so let’s segway to…
[Heading 2] Three Pieces of Information
[normal] Three values allows operations like greater than, less than and in between. We can use two values to define an orientation, and then decide where the third point lies in regard to this segment. We could already measure ‘equal’ with a single piece of information as we can’t separate any further values that may or may not be there. With two values we understand ‘not equal’, because a second distinguishable value is by definition not equal. In quantifiable systems where all measures have to be relative to something else, comparisons are the cornerstone — and three values give us our first glimpse of this.
[normal] Let’s enumerate everything we can say with three values (not three numbers to be clear, think three levels of light). We take any two points and extrapolate them. Then the third point lies somewhere along this extrapolation. Again, this may not actually be ‘true’, I can extrapolate my age to 500, but that doesn’t mean I’ll live to 500. The units also may not match, our values might be temperature, distance and time. But our information is more like ‘this much’, ‘that much’, and ‘that other much’, no units in sight, and this is all we need to do math with.
[normal] Now in orientation A to B, C can be less than A, less than B, greater than A or greater than B. And then these values reverse in orientation B to A, and change again with A to C, C to B etc. This gives us 6 orientations, and the third value has two comparisons available. In English, this is simplified with prepositions like before/during/after, or behind/between/ahead. Language will often assume an orientation (higher is larger) but can usually flip it with context (deeper is larger). Math assumes a context and encodes it in the culture, leading to many arguments about things like the correct positive direction of the Y axis, and yet surprisingly little thinking about it.
[normal] We can also, sort of, create a number with three values. We can say A to C is three times longer than A to B, and that can represent the number 3. The problem is we can’t do that without using A to B as well as A to C, which is using the A value twice. This is like saying there are two A values and they are equal. So really that’s four values, not three. Oh, Mr. Segway man…
[Heading 2] Four Values – and Numbers
[normal] Every number is made up of (at least) four values. If you see two sticks on the ground, you can say one is about three times as long as the other. This is the number 3, but notice how it is made up of four values - the start and end of one stick, and the start and end of the other. We are comparing lengths, so we don’t care about orientation here, but certainly there is a way of thinking about two sticks where one is -3 times longer than the other. We would have to move them into a line (mentally or physically) and call the place where the ends met the start point. As they now point in opposite directions, one is -3 time longer than the other. Even when doing a normal comparison, we are lining them up somehow, as it is complex to include the ‘here to stick’ part in your calculations.
[normal] Note that when we line up two sticks, we end up with two values in the same place. This doesn’t mean we can’t distinguish them like back in the one peice of information case. In that case we had one piece of information, in this case we have two. If I make ten dots on a paper, all one on top of the other, it can be either one dot or ten dots to you, depending on what you know. We do math on information, not on physical reality.
[normal] So numbers. What we are really doing when creating a number is taking a reference ‘unit’ (a distance, a duration, a standard, or some other knowable interval of some precision) and using it to estimate how a second known range differs from it. Five inches, 40 degrees, twice the returns, half as good, partly true, lost it all – these all imply ‘numbers’, because they have a unit made of two values, and an implied two value range being compared. Notice how ‘more than a mile’, ‘a color range’ and ‘same as it ever was’ only require 3, 2 and 1 values, conceptually. Things can be measured without numbers, but the operations are more limited.
[normal] So really really, we are saying that all numbers have a numerator (the thing your number represents) and a denominator (the unit). In our numbers, both the numerator and denominator are represented by single numbers, but that is only because they both start at zero, and they both assume ‘positive right’. And even though we treat a segment from 0 to 3 the same as a point at 3, these are very different things, obviously. A point at 3 is really a value that starts at 3 and ends at 3, somewhat similar to zero, which starts at zero and ends at zero. It can’t actually have zero length, but it has a length smaller than we can use, or smaller than we care to use, just like zero. Remember back at the start, with empty space vs a thing we know nothing about. The point at 3 exists, and is very different than nothing at all. The point at 3 is also different than the point at 2 or the point at 0, showing there is something to it rather than nothing to it.
[Heading 2] Our Numbers
[normal] We now have all the primitives to define exactly what our numbers are made of, and what constraints they work under. This may seem trivial, but with an accurate model we will be able to understand the mechanics of the operations we do on them. With this we will find some separate operations are considered the same, and some very basic operations are missing. We will also be able to relax and expand these constraints to create new number systems, so familiar, and some fairly alien, but all useful.
[normal] Our numbers are created with two segments, a unit, and a value that is some scaled version of that unit. Each segment starts at zero, and the unit segment always ends at one (it defines 1). The positive direction is always considered to be rightwards in a numberline sense, but regardless of visualization, there is only one positive direction. Our numbers move towards the negative in the opposite direction of this. Any value segment that isn’t a whole multiple of the unit is some form of a partial number, fraction or decimal.
[normal] While these do require four separate values, the unit segments zero and one are definitional, the zero on the value segment is required, leaving only the end point of the value segment dynamic. This makes it very useful, as one free parameter is far easier to reason about than four. Note that this comes at a price — values we use in our math will often need to be adjusted to fit this system. If we find two sticks in the forest, it’s unlikely that they both share a common zero point and share a direction like this. Generally though, it is worth paying this price, and we will always prefer one free parameter when possible, even with multiple units (3 meters per second vs 6 meters per 2 seconds).
[normal] Note that this doesn’t consider the base of the number yet, or deal with rational vs real numbers, as these are all subcategories of these basic rules. A base 10 decimal or a base 12 fraction both have a unit and a value made of segments that are anchored at zero, and all operations on them are mechanically the same.
[normal] Also this does not cover the point at 8 vs a segment from 0->8, in spite of these being a very intuitive version of numbers to us. These actually require 8 values, and relaxing some of these constraints (essentially similar to what we know as complex numbers, which we will get to).
[Heading 3] Operations on Numbers
[normal] Values only become information when they relate to other values in non-random ways. This makes predictable operations the backbone of information. Addition and multiplication are some of the most basic arithmetic operations, and we need to elevate other things like ‘group those values’, ‘reference a calculation’ or ‘make a copy’ to operation status, rather than assume we have these abilities and everyone will understand what we mean.
[normal] However one chooses to define the mechanics of these, they really need to be explicitly defined with no assumptions, as the model we choose will inform how things behave as we scale and transform these values into more advanced numerical concepts. It is kind of surprising this isn’t done in math already regarding these basic concepts, but here we are.
[normal] Addition is grouping. Here is a question: with 2+3=5, are the 2 and 3 values ‘destroyed’ and you create a new ‘5’ value, or are they preserved and we now treat them together? In terms of apples, it seems the summed apples remain intact. In terms of segments, our intuition might be that we join the two value segments tip to tail into a new segment that stretches from 0->5. In terms of weight, we are just placing values together on a scale. All of these are fine — they encode different operations but have some fundamental similarities. For apples, to start with we need a definition of an apple, and some kind of container, mental or physical. For lengths, think of the rules you need for ‘tip to tail’, and the merging step. Is 2 merging with 3 or vice versa? For weights, we need the idea that all the values are considered together as one value.
[normal] The simplest version is we are now considering multiple values together, and nothing changed other than that. No need for moving things, sorting them, merging them etc. We are really just changing our categorization, not modifying the objects we are categorizing. Just five apples in one bag instead of two, same apples. Addition is grouping of values, the total is just a computable side effect of that. If we want to move forward with the number 5 we can just make a copy or reference of this calculation, but we haven’t altered or destroyed the 2 and 3.
[normal] Multiplication is scaling. 2x3=6 takes some initial value and expands it by a certain amount. It is the 2 getting scaled here, as in, if the 2 is red and the 3 is blue, the resulting 6 will still be red. The x3 is just ‘instruction’, the 2 is what is transforming. Note that while we are ‘scaling’ the 2, it doesn’t need to be a transform, we could just be moving closer or changing our measuring unit. This ratio scaling is in fact very related to how numbers themselves work, the unit segment is compared with the value segment creating a number. Notice how these operations can be a fact (A is 3x bigger than B), a question (how much bigger is B than A), an action (make A 3x larger), or an ‘action question’ (how do I make it 3x larger?). These four interpretations also hold true for addition, and in fact for all operations (and in fact for all information!). Are there other basic ways of using information?
[normal] So we can select and reference values, measure them, group them, and compare amounts and ratios. We can choose our frame (what change is considered ‘bigger’, what is our unit, at what resolution, what is our start point), and what operations we want to do. This gets us numbers and basic arithmetic.
[normal] All this may seem obvious or too trivial to be meaningful, but it does have some serious implications right off the bat. For one, the answer to 2+3 is really just 2 and 3 as a set, the ‘weighing’ them is just an observation. 2+3 is not the same as 1+4 unless you erase information which would require some erase operation. The Fibonacci sequence relies on not erasing this source information for example. But more fundamentally, 2+2+2 is a very different operation and result than 2x3 - one is a bag of 6 apples, the other is a big apple becoming much bigger or closer. We are rightly obsessed with totals because a single dynamic value is easier to interpret than many dynamic values. But as we relax various constraints and new math emerges, the differences between these ‘operational equalities’ will start to matter.
[Heading 3] Decimals and Fractions
[normal] The way we encode numbers is a big deal to us, but it actually has very little effect on the mechanics of mathematics. Whether ticks, decimals, fractions, hexadecimal, Roman numerals, or the Babylonian sexagesimal system, at their heart they work the same. Scaling is still scaling, grouping is still grouping, and the numbers that emerge come from comparing a unit to a value. The reason we have number systems at all is they help us with both standardization and variable resolution. This helps keep numbers interpretable as we communicate them more broadly, and helps us resume complex value groups into categories, as we do with object definitions.
[normal] To this point we are creating a number using the ratio of a value segment to a unit segment. This unit segment is arbitrary, it might be the length of a stick, the smallest size we can measure, or a perfect  value we imagine. I could measure my yard using 50 steps, and it would be good enough. If you want more precision, you change units, using feet or mm. The problem comes later when you want to change precision using the same unit. If you get a more accurate version of a step, you need a new unit for it - you can’t say 50 ½ steps, it needs to be 101 ‘something elses’. A system that allows partial values allows you to change the accuracy of a unit without making all your other measures invalid. A fraction system doesn’t obviate the need for multiple units to describe things of different scales (this also helps our intuition), but it does give the units we use a lot more latitude.
[normal] The way all numbering systems do this is by dividing the unit into parts (ticks if you will), and then appending this to the unit measure for more precision. A good way to understand the utility and limits of this is to look at five star reviews online. One review is divided into 5 possible ticks, 2 reviews have 10 possible ticks. If you get one 5 star review and one 3 star review, you have 8 ticks out of 10, so a 0.8 review score. Now if we switch to 10 stars per review, a higher resolution, nothing really changes. One review (the unit) is still one review, and a 0.8 review score is still a 0.8 review score. If we treated a star as the unit, then some perfect reviews are worth 10 stars and others only worth 5. The fractional part protects us from changing resolution, but note that the price of this convenience is that we are subtly throwing away information.
[Heading 3] Precision
[normal] In decimal we will convert 12 stars out of 15 to 0.8, or 80% perhaps. In fractions we will reduce 12/15 to ⅘. In both cases we’ve converted 3 reviews to an infinitely precise 1 review equivalent, but the ‘true’ answer is the unreduced (and unwieldy) 12/15. As you know, a 5 star review with one rating is very different from a 4.9 star review with thousands of ratings.This is numeric information we had, but our number system consolidated it into something easier to understand by removing information. The same goes as we scale up, 100 miles away probably doesn’t mean you counted every mile – it is acceptable if it is actually 97 miles. We consolidate the resolution to something useful by removing distracting information. Our modern numbers are infinite precision, and we organically add back resolution with context and gut feelings.
[normal] This is great for people, but a real problem when trying to teach computers about the world. Resolution is important in our world and in our language, and our numbering system erases it automatically. Math with resolution requires new encodings and rules, but is the major unlock to getting computers to think more organically.
[Heading 1] Relaxing and Adding Constraints
[normal] And this opens up a whole wonderful rats nest of mathematics that is new. The point at 3 starts and ends at 3, so what about a number that starts at 3 and ends at 4? And what if our unit points in the opposite direction or isn’t anchored at zero and one? How would we add this to another number made of four unaligned values? What about multiplying these kinds of numbers, how would you multiply two offset segments on a numberline? What does it mean to have a unit that is positive like 2/7 vs a negative unit like 2/-7? And if I can divide a stick into 10 parts and pick a midpoint (5/10) isn’t that more accurate (higher resolution, more information) than if I can only divide it into two (1/2)?
[normal] By answering these questions to your satisfaction, you will not only have a novel way of looking at mathematics, but your mathematics will be in a position to describe and understand the conceptual world we so deftly navigate. And back down to earth, this may sound very abstract, but remember that it's our math that has abstracted reality, these values are the norm in both the real world and our pure imaginations.
[normal] If an amoeba has two light sensors that change as it moves, there is no zero point, no universal calibration, and yet it is able to do enough math on these two signals to usefully navigate its world.
[normal] If you take two sticks in a forest, call yourself a zero point (a fifth point ‘observer’ position if you will), you now have two things you can measure to some approximate resolution, where neither one is a zero based length. One can be the unit, the other the value, and two other sticks could for a similar number. If non zero measures like this are impossible to add or multiply in a useful and systematic way, it isn’t me coming up with some wild esoteric example – it's a failure of our mathematics to quantify and manipulate a very large portion of reality.
[normal] Organic two values: stim response, twice as hot (no unit)
[normal] three values: prev average, dynamic zero, change over time
[normal] Dynamic direction: steering
[normal] simultaneous direction: complex numbers
[normal] dynamic unit: hue/lightness
[normal] Multi dim: multiplied symmetric numbers
[normal] dynamic unit multi dim: paths through color

===== The Core4 Bootstrap_ Ordered Relation and Structural Integration Rules.docx =====
[Heading 3] Core4 Experimental Bootstrap Note (Revised)
[normal] This note captures a newer bootstrap picture for the experimental relation model 1. It is intentionally separate from earlier notes to sharpen meanings aggressively, specifically focusing on the physical constraint that fully partitioned structures cannot legally add together through structural merging 1, 2. The goal is to state the smallest physical picture capable of generating basis, value, operation, fold, power, and orientation from one shared ordered integration substrate 1, 3.
[Heading 4] 1. Bootstrap Stance
[normal] Before anything is related or committed, a carrier presents a field of long-valued potentials 3. Nothing deeper than ordered potential is assumed yet 3. The first primitive act is to choose one potential as A, choose another as B, and relate A -> B in that order 3. This ordered relation is the bootstrap act 3.
[Heading 4] 2. Ordered Extent And Tick Matter
[normal] Relating A -> B creates a directed extent 3. This does not require pinning either endpoint to a globally fixed substrate location; the relation may slide on the substrate while remaining perfectly lawful internally 4. This means later structures can be stable internally while moving relative to the wider substrate 5.
[normal] At bootstrap grade, the distance between raw values determines the structural partition count 5. If A != B, interior tick matter exists; if A < B, it is dominant/expansive; if A > B, it is recessive/inverted; if A = B, no interior tick matter is created 5. This means extent and raw partition count coincide physically at this earliest grade 6.
[Heading 4] 3. Open Site, Point Claim, And Calibrated Basis
[normal] The cleanest current bootstrap ladder uses three importantly different cases 6:
[normal] 0/0: Open site or unresolved coincidence 6, 7. It does not claim a usable magnitude 7.
[normal] m/0: Point claim 6. It has a committed magnitude present, but its interior tick matter, flow orientation, or support structure is not yet disclosed 7. It is present in magnitude without disclosed interior partitions 7.
[normal] m/u: Resolved value through a known basis 6, 8. The magnitude is present, the basis is present, and the value can be read through the basis partitions and orientation 8.
[Heading 4] 4. Grade 0 And Grade 1
[normal] Ordered raw relation gives the seed basis 8. For example, 4/0 is a point claim of magnitude 4, while 4/4 is a unit in the dominant orientation with four structural partitions 8. These project to values (e.g., 8/4 projects to value 2), but projected values are not the structure itself 9. The structure 8/4 is an extent 8 resolved through partition basis 4, and this distinction matters because structural partition count must remain available for later fusion 9.
[Heading 4] 5. Orientation
[normal] An inverted basis is the same basis with an inverted orientation, not a separate species 9. A dominant basis traverses expansively, while a recessive basis traverses in the inverted direction 10.
[normal] An i-oriented basis should be read as operating through inverted orientation, inverting the current resolved structure as it is taken up 10, 11. In repeated fold (like 2i * 3i), each new inverted participation acts on the whole currently resolved host, flipping both placement and denominator perspective in sequence 11, 12.
[Heading 4] 6. Higher Grade Partitioning
[normal] Partitions scale upward into higher grades 2, 12. If one resolved structure is fused with another, the higher-grade structure inherits the partition availability of its ingredients 12. Fusing an 8/4 vertical structure with an 8/4 horizontal structure results in a squared unit carrying the product of those partition opportunities 2.
[Heading 4] 7. Operations Are Relations Read As Integration
[normal] There is no separate primitive for "operation" 2. Operations (addition, multiplication, fusion) are different uses of the same ordered relation substrate, read as integration rules 2, 13. An operation dictates how to integrate operands using a specific number of partitions, repeated a specific number of times 13.
[Heading 4] 8. Operation Core: Partitions And Repeats
[normal] The operation core consists of partitions and repeats 13.
[normal] Repeats specify how many times the integration acts (1 = one pass, >1 = power-like, fractional = root-like) 14.
[normal] Partitions specify how the integration is exposed 15. The system uses a precedence rule to determine partitions: explicit operation partitions, then reused basis partitions, then raw tick fallback 16.
[Heading 4] 9. The Merging Constraint: Addition vs. Multiplication
[normal] Because fusing resolved structures forces their partitions to merge and scale (multiplying the partition opportunities), two fully partitioned structures cannot physically merge without the operation becoming a multiplication 2, 12. If internal units are allowed to merge to normalize total ticks, a scaling occurs 2.
[normal] Therefore, true addition requires that we only add the numerators (magnitudes) while strictly preventing the structural denominators from interacting.
[Heading 4] 10. Addition As Zero-Mixing Integration (The Override)
[normal] To accomplish addition without illegal structural merging, the system applies a denominator of 0 directly to the operation 15. This acts as an explicit override 16.
[normal] An operation with zero partitions means: append whole resolved values, but do not mix interiors during the operation itself 15, 17.
[normal] It functions as a structural safeguard that tells the system to accumulate the claims (the raw ticks or numerators) while preserving their lack of fused interior 17.
[normal] It relates separate members into one collection-like result without fusing them into one continuous extent 17, 18.
[normal] By keeping the 0 on the operation rather than stripping the operands down to m/0 point claims, the operands get to keep their structural identities (m/u) intact, safely appending their magnitudes without cross-multiplying their bases 15-17.
[Heading 4] 11. Multiplication As Basis Substitution
[normal] When interior mixing is legally allowed, the operation acts as multiplication 18. Multiplication-like behavior is defined as basis substitution: taking every unit proportion of the first operand and replacing or filling it with the whole of the second operand 18.
[normal] The first operand provides the host basis 18.
[normal] The second operand provides the inserted structure 18.
[normal] This fusion is done at the tick level, resulting in the shared interior and scaled partition availability expected when structures genuinely merge 2, 12, 18, 19.
[Heading 4] 12. Linked Fold Versus Snapshot Fold
[normal] Fold always produces a new output stage, which can be a one-shot snapshot or a linked result 19, 20. In a link calculation, the fold relation is preserved, and later changes to reused input can retune the output 20.
[Heading 4] 13. Structural Equality Versus Projected Equality
[normal] Two constructions may project to the same visible value while remaining different structures 20. For example, 6 * 2 and 2 * 6 project to the same scalar but differ structurally in host basis, inserted structure, and aspect 21. Projection equality must not erase construction lineage 21.
[Heading 4] 14. What Still Feels Open
[normal] Repeat Semantics: The exact meaning of rational repeats, compression optimizations, and root alignments need tightening 21.
[normal] Point, Carrier, And Flow: Does an m/0 point commit to a carrier family while withholding orientation, or is it looser? 22.
[normal] Selection and Reuse Windows: Mechanisms for sliding windows, recurrence, and trolley movement across preserved structures likely require one more layer above this bootstrap encoding 22, 23.
[Heading 4] 15. Current Working Summary
[normal] Carriers present ordered potentials; relation A -> B creates extent 23.
[normal] m/0 is present magnitude with unresolved interior flow; m/u is resolved magnitude through a known basis 23.
[normal] Fully partitioned structures cannot legally add by merging, as merging scales partitions (multiplication) 2, 12.
[normal] Addition (0-partition operation) safely appends magnitudes while actively blocking interior mixing 15, 17, 23.
[normal] Multiplication is basis substitution or filled host integration 23.
[normal] Fold always produces new output, but reuse can keep it linked 23.

===== twitter\Property keys.docx =====
[normal] In this first set of experiments from a few years ago, I wanted *everything* to be values on gradients that could combine, link and interpolate with each other. We did this a little at Pixate, this was the ‘all in’ version.
[normal] Samplers
[normal] All properties can be based on gradients (ranges) with samplers. In this example, all the properties for the middle elements are calculated rather than stored - only the end points have actual values. Eg. Shapes have [3,12] points.
[normal] These ranges are sampled over t, and t itself is sampled from a range. The number of sides is discrete samples from 3 to 12. These will never ‘fail’ though - if the range of sides is 3 to 6 it will just adjust based on a rounding rule.
[normal] This is more like GPU/shader programming than CPU, but it works well on both. The properties that can be set are based on universal enums. Upcoming iterations use “typed numbers”.
[normal] Slider Input
[normal] Here hue and saturation are based on the x,y ranges of the mouse. The scale and pointiness are set by sliders, and number of points on the ‘clicked range’. All properties of all things can be defined on these types of ‘trait gradients’, but first there needs to be a way of combining for new traits.
[normal] The shapes, color and location - all calculated here. The property ranges cross the entire sequence of 56 elements even though it is arranged into a 8x7 grid. This uses a grid sampler, where horizontal overflow increments the vertical. The shape pointiness is an additive combo of two ranges.
[normal] The location is set by layout samplers (rings, grids, random). These animations are all just a single blend from 0 to 150 (as in, a segment defined with 0, and 150). They are sampled differently over time. Because all values work with each other on gradients, all properties can be interpolated or linked with each other.
[normal] Disjointed layouts with exceptions
[normal] The layout can also nest, here the range is a ring layout to nested flower layouts with the same elements. Also the properties can be completely calculated (layout) or have stored values per instance (the colors of the flower patterns are stored). Stored patterns allow simple overrides (thus the red pentagon)
[normal] Spherical effects with mouse input
[normal] These gradient numbers can also be applied to input. Here the x and y inputs of the mouse are converted to gradients, and the gradients are combined in a circular sampler. This is applied to the rotation, size and location of stars in the grid. This combining of values is key to creating higher order traits.
[normal] Gravity simulation to layout and back:
[normal] A purely calculated layout can also be instanced into other layout engines - at the extreme a 2D physics engine interpolates with grid layouts. This allows interesting transitions from one UI to another, regardless of the underlying engine.
[normal] Bezier - The layout samplers aren’t limited to simple shapes, they can be any ‘equation’. Here the placement is based on a Bézier curve sampler.
[normal] The most basic information required for a magnitude are its value, its max/min range, its resolution, and its repetition properties. Later we’ll add direction.
[normal] The maximum and minimum ranges of a value can be expressed as the endpoints of a gradient. There are many ways to compare two ranges, boolean overlap tests being the simplest. The bezier above bounces off the limits of its ranges.
[normal] Repetition is usually handled by calculating repeatedly along a gradient until some condition is met - a test condition. Each step can apply some equation that modifies a result, but test conditions can adjust the equation itself as it steps. The simplest action is a halt condition, where the cycle ends.
[normal] Level of detail hex compression
[normal] Resolution is set here by looking for certain conditions (looking at the amount of change and centeredness in the image iirc?). The resolution of a number (LoD) always matters, this is ‘significant figures’ in science. Unfortunately ‘real numbers’ throw this information under a bus.
[normal] Hex automata with evolving conditions
[normal] There are a lot of experiments with test conditions. This is hexagonal automata, where conditions that change equations are triggered by changes in the local environment. I have wasted a lot of time with these, and it has been fun.
[normal] Hex automata
[normal] A similar type of automata, but this time preloaded with images. The changes in the images are based on the local information of the picture – hue, saturation, lightness, location, sample distance etc. Many interesting things happen with these, and they are easy to explore as any properties can be linked to any other properties. For example the size of the color hexagon here is related to color/size information nearby.
[normal] Histogram sort
[normal] Here images are sorted in a histogram by color, and then recreated. When transitioning from one image to another, the pixels migrate based on their histogram sorting. A pixel in image A will migrate to its nearest pixel in mage B, while interpolating the minor color shift required.
[normal] Ultimately the problem with this approach was it didn’t have a good understanding of discrete vs continuous, making it changing between them somewhat forced.  It stored values as real numbers, and then sampled integers, floats, while clamping ranges and calculating step sizes. The right way to look at this is to have the number itself hold these properties, and more.

===== twitter\Tweet threads.docx =====
[normal] Tweet threads
[normal] The motivation: What the heck are the thoughts in our head made of? Are they in a coherent structure that is walled off from us? Is this structure just too basic to notice, like the smell of air? Are they made of language, or is language made of them?
[normal] The goal: Understanding our own thought mechanics so we can better emulate it, and ultimately interact with AI at a conceptual level. I think this is a computationally simpler problem than deep learning, and AI will be a combination of both eventually.
[normal] Maybe that seems hand-wavy. When we hear 'car' and get that concept, what is the concept made of? Is a car a whole bunch of mini-ideas, or a single one? Is it just a picture? How much overlap is there with 'truck', or is that totally different?
[normal] We can *quickly* tell the difference between "feeling the blues" and "feeling the oranges". What are those things made of that they can jump around so easily? If they're made of mini-concepts, what are the lowest level 'primitive' concepts there?
[normal] Even in single words, we can see many things going on. A concept like 'move' is very generic and simple. We append other concepts to it as it gets more specific: give, toss, send, deliver, distribute.
[normal] 'Distribute' has multiple copies of something going to multiple locations, what is our mental model of that, just words? A 2D image with moving shapes? Some specific thing actually getting distributed? How can we figure out what we're hallucinating to give us these ideas?
[normal] Can we reverse engineer our 'output' to figure out what is going on inside? Look at the simplest things like gestures, ornamentation, cartoons, sounds, glyphs, physics sense, or memes. Are these minimal concepts reduced to minimal representations?
[normal] In computer languages, there are things called terminals (primitives) in the grammar. These are things that can't be further reduced. Are all concepts made of primitives? Would our primitives be things like food, friend, danger? Maybe motion, energy, quantity, size? Emotions?
[normal] Are there a fixed number of these primitives that all thoughts are constructed out of? Are they constant? Inate? Universal? How many would there be -- 10s, 100s, 1000s, millions? Is there overlap? Does 'struck by a hand' and 'struck by an idea' reuse anything?
[normal] How to figure out these 'primitives'? What are the simplest gestures that convey big and small? The fewest lines that make happy and sad? The minimum sound to convey disappointment? The fewest strokes to capture a pattern?
[normal] At a higher level: words, sentences, stories, music, sports, numbers, logic, emotions, processes, organizations... These are complex, but there is something similar with a story arc, a gestural arc, a ball's arc, and the arc of a process. A goal, shit happens, a result, repeat.
[normal] Lastly, as we figure these things out, how do we encode it? An encoding exists that is low bandwidth enough for us to all sync on, because we do. Is this more dependent on how our brains are wired, or on the limitations of what the world can be?
[normal] I'm trying to pull together these threads. Lots of prototypes, some wins, lots of fails... But I strongly feel all of these things boil down to something similar at their essence, because that essence is mostly limited by what is possible. Will post more on each over the weeks.
[normal] Change is the basis for all perception and understanding, because without it we have nothing to compare.
[normal] When you dig right to the bottom, the thing that we lock onto for all perception is change. We track it at all scales relevant to us, and we are very attuned to the characteristics and patterns of changes. We easily transfer these patterns across domains.
[normal] At the lowest level there are sensory changes, changes over time (motion and scaling), and changes of focus. We are sensitive to slight changes in light, sound, texture or motion. We understand static photos through changes in light.
[normal] It is worth looking really really close at what change is then, as it is the basis for everything. When looking at these kinds of ‘mind primitives’, it is important to look with first principles. Our intuitions are mostly correct, but are far too embedded to be easily understood.
[normal] Most simply, change has a start, a duration, and an end. The start and end is chosen by the observer, as everything is always changing. The duration isn't just over time. For example, the change from a city to country happens over a distance.
[normal] This describes change in properties that can be measured. Things that can be counted (objects) are made of collections of these property ranges and their relations (definitions). More on those later.
[normal] The start and end points of a change are chosen, so they map to some definition of the chooser. Duration is the measure between them. The one rule of the duration of change is it can't be zero length.
[normal] This feels right and wrong to our intuition - something is moving or not moving, no in betweens. Yet if there is zero distance between those states, how can there be change? The confusion comes from how easily we can scale and ignore precision, our superpower.
[normal] So start, motion, end. There are two more obvious elements to add here. First, there must be potential for change at the start point, otherwise there would be no change. It follows that by the end, that potential has been reduced by the amount of change that happened.
[normal] Second, the potential for change doesn’t mean it’s certain - all transforms require work, and other things can affect that. A rock may never roll down a hill, or it may get pushed. It may hit a wall half way down, or might miss it. Interactions that assist or impede transformations are always part of our change calculus.
[normal] So select something with potential, define a start condition, duration with obstacles until some defined end condition. These are the primitives of how we perceive change. Is this because of how our brain works, or how change works?
[normal] We use 'change' as the encoding for everything. Not just motion or senses, but stories, music, sentences, equations, paths, emotions, plans. At all scales, and over moments or eons. Mini-stories are the predigested change-patterns running our conscious minds.
[normal] I’ll die on that hill. Maybe alone :).
[normal] Not only do our thoughts run on these change sequences, but reuse the change patterns themselves as the basis for all metaphor. You can drop a ball, then you can drop a call, a boyfriend, or just drop by. Something is held, then let go, ending on the ground.
[normal] The last part of change we care about, and the most important to us, is the predictability. We broadly divide predictability of change into animate and inanimate, because animate things are much harder to predict (and tend to be tasty and hungry).
[normal] To predict inanimate things, like the motion of a falling tree or a setting sun, we can extrapolate using previous experience and physics. We aren’t perfect at this, but we aren’t usually too surprised. When inanimate change becomes too surprising we assign animate forces to it.
[normal] Change with living things, like watching a bug or passing a car, requires us to get ‘in the other mind' to make predictions. A lot of what we care about is animate, so many of our change models are based on the forces acting on other animate things.
[normal] Our minds are constantly predicting the future (everything we see is a prediction of up to half a second into the future!). We are keyed to notice differences with expectation and reality (surprise), as that is where we adapt and learn.
[normal] The primitive for encoding thought in this system, the ‘number’ if you will, is directed segment. A start, a transition, and an end. It can get more detailed with start and end conditions, different resolutions and limits, relations and equations.
[normal] I think this pattern should be the basis for encoding concepts in AI, and is what I’m using. This has led to many experiments with animation, patterns, design, machine teaching, and…
[normal] …ultimately a fairly different, more organic math system for encoding it. More on this next.

===== Universal Math - 5.docx =====
[normal] Everything that can be done with a segment on a line
